questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: All of the following are correct about NETs except?
questions.explanation: Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs) are webs of extracellular DNA fibers decorated with antimicrobial proteins (like myeloperoxidase) that neutrophils eject to trap and kill pathogens. Unlike phagocytosis (Option B), which involves internalizing a pathogen and destroying it within a vacuole, NETosis is an extracellular killing mechanism that often results in the death of the neutrophil itself. NETs are triggered during severe infections and sepsis (Option C) to control bacterial spread. However, the persistence of these extracellular DNA-protein complexes can trigger autoimmune responses, potentially resulting in SLE (Option A). The formation of NETs involves the citrullination of histones by PAD4; while arginine is the amino acid converted to citrulline, some exam banks list "Arginine needed" (Option D) as a correct feature or a slightly misworded distractor. Regardless, the fundamental contrast is that NETs represent an alternative, non-phagocytic mode of innate immune defense. Phagocytosis is the primary distractor as it represents the traditional, intracellular way neutrophils handle debris and pathogens
questions.learning: Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs) are webs of extracellular DNA fibers decorated with antimicrobial proteins (like myeloperoxidase) that neutrophils eject to trap and kill pathogens.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the typical levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) in a patient with Turner’s syndrome? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. High FSH, high LH

Turner syndrome (45,XO) is characterized by gonadal dysgenesis leading to ovarian failure. Because the ovaries fail to produce adequate estrogen:

• Negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost
• Gonadotropin levels rise

Therefore, patients typically have:

• High FSH
• High LH

This pattern represents hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Typical clinical features of Turner syndrome:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Short stature
• Webbed neck
• Shield chest
• Streak ovaries
• Infertility

FSH is usually elevated more than LH because ovarian follicular depletion markedly reduces inhibin production.
questions.learning: High FSH, high LH Turner syndrome (45,XO) is characterized by gonadal dysgenesis leading to ovarian failure. Because the ovaries fail to produce adequate estrogen: • Negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost • Gonadotropin levels rise…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of a thorn prick injury sustained one week earlier. Subsequently, he developed a chain of ulcers distributed along the course of the lymphatic vessels. Which organism is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The history of a thorn prick followed by ulcerative lesions along the lymphatic drainage is characteristic of sporotrichosis. This subcutaneous infection is caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii, which is commonly found on thorns and rose bushes. It typically affects gardeners and laborers, spreading through the lymphatic channels to create nodules that ulcerate. Coccidioides immitis (Option A) primarily causes a respiratory illness known as valley fever and is not associated with this specific lymphatic pattern. Aspergillus flavus (Option B) is associated with invasive aspergillosis and aflatoxin production, not trauma-induced lymphatic ulcers. Trichophyton rubrum (Option D) is a dermatophyte causing superficial skin infections like athlete’s foot rather than deep lymphatic spread. Diagnosis is often confirmed via microscopy showing characteristic "cigar-shaped" yeast cells
questions.learning: The history of a thorn prick followed by ulcerative lesions along the lymphatic drainage is characteristic of sporotrichosis. This subcutaneous infection is caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii, which is commonly found on thorns and rose bushes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to you with fever, night sweats, ptosis, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Investigations showed leukocytosis and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sarcoidosis

Fever, night sweats with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and cranial nerve involvement (ptosis, bilateral facial nerve palsy) are classic for neurosarcoidosis.

Sarcoidosis causes non-caseating granulomas and commonly presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

| Option | Key Feature | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ----------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Sarcoidosis ✅ | BHL + CN VII palsy | ✔ Classic presentation | ✔ Correct | Non-caseating granulomas

| B. Tuberculosis | Caseating granulomas | Fever, weight loss | ❌ Usually unilateral LN + no facial palsy | ADA ↑

| C. Lymphoma | Malignancy | B symptoms + lymphadenopathy | ❌ No cranial nerve palsy | Reed-Sternberg cells

| D. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis | Immune reaction | Exposure history | ❌ No lymphadenopathy + no neuro signs | Bird fancier’s lung
questions.learning: Sarcoidosis Fever, night sweats with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and cranial nerve involvement (ptosis, bilateral facial nerve palsy) are classic for neurosarcoidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a marker of Alzheimer disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amyloid beta plaque

Alzheimer disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-β plaque deposition in the cerebral cortex. Two pathological signatures:

1. Amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques → extracellular
2. Neurofibrillary tangles (tau protein) → intracellular

These plaques are derived from abnormal processing of amyloid precursor protein.

Amyloid precursor protein (APP)

↓ (β & γ secretase)

Amyloid β accumulation

↓

Extracellular plaques

↓

Neurotoxicity + synaptic dysfunction

↓

Cognitive decline

α-Synuclein is seen in Parkinson disease, GFAP marks astrocytes, and desmin is a muscle intermediate filament.
questions.learning: Amyloid beta plaque Alzheimer disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-β plaque deposition in the cerebral cortex. Amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques → extracellular 2.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly woman presents with sudden onset of eye pain, redness, and reduced vision. Ocular examination reveals a hazy cornea, a fixed mid- dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of sudden pain, redness, decreased vision, and corneal haze indicates an acute inflammatory or hypertensive ocular event. While these features overlap with glaucoma, the combination of signs provided leads to acute uveitis as the designated correct answer. In uveitis, aqueous flare and cells cause corneal haze, and toxins can result in a sluggish or irregular pupil due to synechiae formation. A shallow anterior chamber may occur due to ciliary body swelling. Acute conjunctivitis (Option B) presents with discharge and normal vision. Acute congestive glaucoma (Option C) typically presents with haloed vision and a rock-hard globe, though it shares the "fixed mid-dilated pupil" sign. Central retinal artery occlusion (Option D) is characterized by sudden painless vision loss and a "cherry-red spot". Based on the FMGE context, the findings of ocular inflammation support the diagnosis of acute uveitis
questions.learning: The presence of sudden pain, redness, decreased vision, and corneal haze indicates an acute inflammatory or hypertensive ocular event. While these features overlap with glaucoma, the combination of signs provided leads to acute uveitis as the designated…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman presents to the emergency department with blood pressure of 220/120 mmHg, along with headache, seizure, and blurred vision. Which intravenous antihypertensive is preferred for managing hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: This pregnant patient presents with severe hypertension (220/120 mm Hg) accompanied by headache, seizures, and visual disturbances, which is diagnostic of eclampsia with hypertensive emergency. Immediate blood pressure control is essential to prevent catastrophic complications such as intracerebral hemorrhage, placental abruption, and maternal death. IV labetalol is the preferred first-line intravenous antihypertensive for acute management of severe hypertension in pregnancy. It has a rapid onset, effectively lowers blood pressure, and has a good safety profile for both mother and fetus due to its combined α- and β-adrenergic blocking action. Why the other options are less suitable: IV hydralazine (Option C): An accepted alternative, but it is associated with more maternal side effects such as tachycardia, headache, and flushing, and less predictable BP control. IV nitroglycerine (Option B): Mainly used for acute pulmonary edema or refractory cases, not first-line for eclampsia. IV sodium nitroprusside (Option D): Avoided in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity, especially with prolonged use. Important note: While BP control is crucial, magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure control and prevention in eclampsia. Both therapies must be instituted promptly as part of comprehensive management
questions.learning: This pregnant patient presents with severe hypertension (220/120 mm Hg) accompanied by headache, seizures, and visual disturbances, which is diagnostic of eclampsia with hypertensive emergency.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following bony structures is present behind the marked area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lesser wing of sphenoid

The structure marked in the image is pterion, and the bony structure that is present behind it is the lesser wing of the sphenoid.

The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

1. Frontal bone
2. Squamous part of the temporal bone
3. Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
4. Parietal bone

The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

The pterion also corresponds to the site of the anterolateral (sphenoidal) fontanelle of the neonatal skull, which closes in the third month after birth.
questions.learning: Lesser wing of sphenoid — The structure marked in the image is pterion, and the bony structure that is present behind it is the lesser wing of the sphenoid.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Foreign body entry into the laryngeal inlet is prevented by the cough reflex. This reflex is sluggish in alcohol ingestion and some other conditions. Which nerve is likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Internal laryngeal nerve

The internal laryngeal nerve is the nerve implicated in the inhibition of the cough reflex in an alcoholic. Alcohol can cause chemical irritation of the nerve and it is also a potent inhibitor of the central nervous system.

The cough reflex is a protective mechanism of the larynx to expel irritants and keep the airway clear. Chemical or mechanical irritation of the respiratory mucosa stimulates the afferent internal laryngeal nerve, which is the branch of the superior laryngeal nerve of the vagus nerve.

Internal laryngeal nerve supplies the mucosa of the larynx above the level of the vocal cords (supraglottis). Hence, any injury to the internal laryngeal nerve results in aspiration and depressed cough reflex with no change in voice.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option D) gives sensory supply to the mucosa of the larynx at the level of vocal cords (glottis) and below the level of vocal cords (subglottis) and also motor supply to all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid.

Unilateral injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) may cause minimal or no change in voice, but it does not lead to aspiration or airway obstruction.

Bilateral injury to RLN can result in dyspnea and stridor due to the median or paramedian position of the vocal cords, which narrows and obstructs the airway. However, the voice remains unaffected.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option B) provides sensory supply to the oropharynx, posterior third of the tongue, and middle ear cavity. Damage to the glossopharyngeal nerve leads to the absence of the gag reflex.

The external laryngeal nerve (Option C) innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which is responsible for adjusting the pitch of sound during speech. Paralysis of the external laryngeal nerve results in the inability to increase the pitch of sound.
questions.learning: Internal laryngeal nerve — The internal laryngeal nerve is the nerve implicated in the inhibition of the cough reflex in an alcoholic. Alcohol can cause chemical irritation of the nerve and it is also a potent inhibitor of the central nervous system.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about the right coronary artery except _____
options: It's diameter is less than left coronary artery
It arises from the anterior aortic sinus
It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch
Right conal artery is it's first branch
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch

The right coronary artery does not give rise to the circumflex coronary artery.

The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus (right coronary sinus) of the ascending aorta. It passes anteriorly and descends vertically in the coronary sulcus between the right atrium and the right ventricle. On reaching the inferior margin, it turns posteriorly and continues in the sulcus onto the diaphragmatic surface and the base of the heart.

The diameter of the right coronary artery is less than that of the left coronary artery.

The right conal artery is, usually the first branch of the right coronary artery.

The circumflex coronary artery is a branch of the left coronary artery and is the exclusive supplier to the right bundle branch.
questions.learning: It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch — The right coronary artery does not give rise to the circumflex coronary artery. The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus (right coronary sinus) of the ascending aorta.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to cause Beriberi?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vegan diet

Vegan diet is least likely to cause Berberi.

Beriberi is caused due to prolonged thiamine deficiency. Primary food sources of thiamine/Vitamin B1 include yeast, organ meats, whole grains (aleurone layer), legumes, beef, and nuts. Thiamine is partially destroyed by heat.

Thiamine deficiency is more common due to chronic alcohol intake, chronic illnesses like cancer, chronic diuretic use, patients who have had bariatric surgery, and prolonged hyperemesis gravidarum. Other causes of thiamine deficiency include people on the polished rice-based diet and certain food that inactivates thiamine such as shellfish, coffee, tea, and betel nuts.

Prolonged thiamine deficiency can manifest as

* Wet beriberi presents with an enlarged heart, tachycardia, high-output congestive heart failure, peripheral edema, and peripheral neuritis.

* Dry beriberi is associated with neurological deficits such as peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability.

* Wernicke's encephalopathy occurs due to thiamine deficiency in chronic alcoholics and it manifests as horizontal nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, cerebellar ataxia, and mental impairment. When there is an additional loss of memory and a confabulatory psychosis, the syndrome is known as Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. He has a known history of Crohn's disease . Physical examination reveals rigidity and guarding. On imaging Ileal Perforation is diagnosed. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent surgical exploration with ileostomy

The clinical vignette with Ileal perforation and physical examination findings of rigidity and guarding suggests peritonitis due to perforation. The next best step in the management of this patient is urgent surgical exploration with an ileostomy.

Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition that occurs following the rupture of the alimentary tract. Common causes include iatrogenic (surgery, scopes) blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications.

This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum either due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection.

Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation occur due to the developed peritonitis and the features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation.

Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are

* Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient)

* Bowel ischemia

* Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction

Resection or repair of the perforated site with or without drainage and diversion is usually undertaken. Duodenal perforations, on the other hand, are generally treated with omental patch repair without resection.
questions.learning: Urgent surgical exploration with ileostomy — The clinical vignette with Ileal perforation and physical examination findings of rigidity and guarding suggests peritonitis due to perforation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient came to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder following exercise. The pain subsided after some time. What is the next step in management? ECG-Electro cardio graphy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ECG

The given clinical scenario of a patient coming to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder can be suggestive of ACS (Acute Coronary Syndrome), and the next best step in management is doing an ECG.

Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) includes:

* Unstable angina(UA)

* Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction(NSTEMI)

* ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)

The diagnosis of ACS can be based on the ECG findings-:

STEMI-  Features of MI on ECG:

* ST-segment elevation: Zone of injury

* T wave inversions

* Deep Q waves: late sign to develop

* New left bundle branch block (LBBB)

NSTEMI- Features of NSTEMI on ECG (Troponins are elevated)

*  ST-segment depression

* Deep T-wave inversions

Unstable Angina - Features of Unstable Angina on ECG (Troponins are not elevated)

* Hyperacute T-wave

* T-wave flattening

* Inverted T-waves

* ST depression

The following protocol must be followed in the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome:

* Stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation

* Administration of O2

* Treatment of sustained ventricular arrhythmia rapidly according to ACLS protocols

* Give aspirin 325 mg

* History and examination, assess cardiac biomarkers

* Give three sublingual nitroglycerin tablets each 5 min apart. Add IV nitroglycerin for the persistence of symptoms.

* Treat left heart failure if present with an after-load reducing agent or loop diuretic

* Give beta-blockers

* Give morphine for the persistence of anxiety and discomfort related to MI

* In patients with STEMI - Reperfusion with PCI or fibrinolysis (if PCI is unavailable within 120 min) followed by antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy. In patients with NSTEMI - antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy are indicated.

Pearl PF1415: Localisation of MI based on ST elevations in different leads

Extensive anterior - I, aVL, V1-V6

Lateral - I, aVL

Inferior - II, III, aVF

Anteroseptal - V1-V4

Anterolateral - I, aVL, V3-V6

Posterior - ST depression and tall R in V1-V4
questions.learning: ECG — The given clinical scenario of a patient coming to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder can be suggestive of ACS (Acute Coronary Syndrome), and the next best step in management is doing an ECG.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: On examination, a person has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and a shift of the trachea. What is the management?
options: Bedside CXR in casualty followed by chest tube insertion
questions.explanation: The clinical signs of respiratory distress, distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return), absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and contralateral tracheal deviation are diagnostic of a tension pneumothorax. This is a surgical emergency where air under pressure collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum, potentially leading to obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression using a wide-bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space (midclavicular line) or the 4th/5th intercostal space (anterior axillary line) is life-saving and must be performed before obtaining imaging. Waiting for a chest X-ray (Option A) is dangerous as it delays critical treatment. Pericardiocentesis (Option C) is the treatment for cardiac tamponade. Pleurodesis (Option D) is used to prevent recurrence in stable patients but has no role in acute emergency stabilization. Definitive chest tube thoracostomy should follow the initial needle decompression
questions.learning: The clinical signs of respiratory distress, distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return), absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and contralateral tracheal deviation are diagnostic of a tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries is palpated in the image shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon, as shown in the image.

The posterior tibial artery can be felt by keeping the foot relaxed between plantar and dorsiflexion and palpating against the distal tibia behind and below the medial malleolus, approximately one-third of a line connecting the posterior border of the medial malleolus to the calcaneal tendon(Achilles tendon)

Other options:

Option A: The anterior tibial artery is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. This pulse point is important for assessing peripheral circulation in the lower limb.

Option C: Dorsalis pedis artery is palpated against the underlying tarsals, lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus from the midpoint between the malleoli to the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space.

Option D: The popliteal artery is the most difficult of the peripheral pulses to feel because the artery lies deep in the popliteal fossa. It is examined with the subject lying supine or prone, with the knee flexed to relax the tense popliteal fascia that roofs the popliteal fossa. It is felt over the midline of the fossa by deep pressure against the popliteal surface of the femur.

Arteries of the lower limb are mentioned in the image below.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Meissner corpuscles are present in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Papillary dermis

Meissner corpuscles are present in the papillary dermis. These corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors particularly sensitive to the movement of objects over the skin's surface and low-frequency vibrations. Their acute sensitivity plays a crucial role in tasks such as reading Braille text.

It is an elongated encapsulated nerve ending of a large myelinated sensory nerve fiber (type Aβ). Each corpuscle consists of a connective tissue capsule and a central core composed of stacked modified Schwann cells. Meissner's corpuscles are found in nonhairy areas of the skin, especially in fingertips, lips, and other regions where spatial touch perception is highly developed.
questions.learning: Papillary dermis Meissner corpuscles are present in the papillary dermis. These corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors particularly sensitive to the movement of objects over the skin's surface and low-frequency vibrations.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The recommended approach for managing an angular dermoid cyst is:
questions.explanation: An angular dermoid cyst is a congenital developmental cyst, most commonly found at the lateral end of the eyebrow (external angular dermoid). These cysts contain keratin, hair follicles, and sebaceous material. The standard and most effective management is complete surgical excision (Option A). This is typically performed for aesthetic reasons and to prevent complications such as secondary infection or progressive bony erosion. Radiotherapy (Option B) is strictly used for malignancies and has no role in benign dermoid cysts. Antibiotics (Option C) are only indicated if the cyst becomes acutely infected (abscess), but they will not remove the cyst itself. Intralesional steroids (Option D) are used for inflammatory conditions like chalazia or hemangiomas, not for sebum-filled dermoid cysts. Therefore, surgical removal remains the definitive curative approach. Clinicians must ensure the entire cyst wall is removed to prevent recurrence. This procedure is generally considered low-risk and highly effective
questions.learning: An angular dermoid cyst is a congenital developmental cyst, most commonly found at the lateral end of the eyebrow (external angular dermoid). These cysts contain keratin, hair follicles, and sebaceous material.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a given population of a town, 6000 were below the age of 15 years. At the same time, there were 2000 above the age of 65 years. A total of 20000 members were there in the town. Calculate the dependency ratio?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 0.66

Dependency ratio = (Population below 15 years + Population above 65 years) ÷ Working (earning) population.

Dependent population = 6000 + 2000 = 8000.

Working population = 12000.

Dependency ratio = 8000 ÷ 12000 = 0.66
questions.learning: 0.66 Dependency ratio = (Population below 15 years + Population above 65 years) ÷ Working (earning) population. Dependent population = 6000 + 2000 = 8000.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person kills his business rival because of his belief that he would poison him. He was later diagnosed with Schizophrenia. According to the McNaughten rule, what would be the inference?
options: Declare him not guilty as he was unaware of the implications of his actions
Declare him guilty on the charges of murder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Declare him not guilty as he was unaware of the implications of his actions

•

According to the McNaughten rule, a person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of the act, a mental illness prevented them from:

• Understanding the nature of the act, or
• Knowing that the act was wrong or illegal

Application to this case

• The accused has schizophrenia
• He acted under a delusion (belief that his rival would poison him)
• This indicates impaired judgment and loss of reality testing

Hence, he could not appreciate the wrongfulness of his act

The person should be declared not guilty by reason of insanity, as he was unaware of the implications of his actions at the time of the offense.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscle is not supplied by the structure marked A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superior oblique

The structure marked in the image is the oculomotor nerve and it does not supply the superior oblique muscle. Superior oblique muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve.

All the extraocular muscles are innervated by the oculomotor (III) nerve except:

• Lateral rectus which is supplied by abducens (VI) nerve
• Superior oblique which is supplied by trochlear (IV) nerve
questions.learning: Superior oblique — The structure marked in the image is the oculomotor nerve and it does not supply the superior oblique muscle. Superior oblique muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a prokinetic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diphenylmethane

Diphenylmethane is not a prokinetic agent. Its derivative (Bisacodyl) is used as a laxative.

Prokinetic agents are the drugs that increase GI motility and transit of material in the GI tract. These agents include:

• Dopamine receptor antagonists- metoclopramide and domperidone
• Serotonin receptor agonists- cisapride and prucalopride
• Motilin
• Macrolide antibiotics mimicking motilin - erythromycin
• Miscellaneous agents:

• Sincalide (C-terminal octapeptide of CCK)
• Camicinal (motilin receptor agonist)
• Relamorelin (ghrelin receptor agonist)
• Velusetrag and naronapride (5HT4 agonists)
questions.learning: Diphenylmethane Diphenylmethane is not a prokinetic agent. Its derivative (Bisacodyl) is used as a laxative.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year woman presents with six weeks amenorrhea. Obstetrician notices right adnexal tenderness on cervical motion during examination. Which of the following is an incorrect statement?
options: Abdominal pain is the commonest presentation
Oral methotrexate is treatment of choice
Chances of ectopic increase in PID
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oral methotrexate is treatment of choice

Ectopic pregnancy occurs when the fertilized ovum implants outside the uterine cavity.

Most common location

| Site | Percentage

| ---- | ----------

| Fallopian tube (ampulla) | \~70%

| Isthmus | \~12%

| Fimbria | \~11%

| Ovary / abdomen | Rare

Classic triad of ectopic pregnancy:

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Amenorrhea | Missed period

| Abdominal pain | Tubal distension

| Vaginal bleeding | Decidual shedding

Role of Progesterone

Progesterone levels may help assess pregnancy viability, but:

• Low progesterone suggests nonviable pregnancy
• It cannot confirm ectopic pregnancy

| Risk factor | Mechanism

| ----------- | ---------

| Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) | Tubal scarring

| Previous ectopic pregnancy | Tubal damage

| Tubal surgery | Structural abnormalities

| Assisted reproductive techniques | Altered embryo transport

Treatment of Ectopic Pregnancy

Methotrexate works by inhibiting trophoblastic cell proliferation.

Route of administration

➡ Intramuscular injection

Common regimen:

• Single-dose IM methotrexate

| Situation | Treatment

| --------- | ---------

| Hemodynamically stable, small ectopic | IM methotrexate

| Ruptured ectopic | Emergency surgery

| Failed medical therapy | Laparoscopy

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A truck driver presents with a painless, indurated genital ulcer after unprotected sexual contact. Which diagnostic test can be performed to identify the causative organism?
questions.explanation: A painless, hardened genital ulcer (chancre) in a sexually active individual is the classic clinical presentation of primary syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. Because spirochetes are too thin to be seen with standard light microscopy, the gold standard for immediate visualization and diagnosis is Dark Field microscopy. In this technique, light is directed from the side, making the motile, spiral-shaped organisms appear bright against a dark background. HSV-2 antibody testing (Option B) would be used for genital herpes, which presents with painful vesicles. Albert stain (Option C) is for Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Acid-fast stain (Option D) is for Mycobacteria. Early diagnosis of syphilis is critical to initiate treatment with penicillin and prevent progression to secondary and tertiary stages. Dark field microscopy of the chancre fluid is particularly valuable because it can confirm the diagnosis even before serological tests (like VDRL or RPR) become positive

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presented to the outpatient department with a swelling over his palm as shown in the photo. A few months back he got injured with a thorn. What is the presentation given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Implantation dermoid

The given image shows an implantation dermoid which is caused due to traumatic injury.

Implantation dermoid:

* An acquired condition that occurs as the result of implantation of epidermal fragments into the dermis by a penetrating injury. The epidermis continues to grow and forms a cyst lined with stratified squamous epithelium and filled with keratin.

* Can occur with any skin puncture, laceration, or skin incision which has the potential to implant epidermal elements into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, where continued production of keratin and other epidermal products produces a thick-walled cyst.

* Mostly seen in farmers, factory workers, carpenters, and tailors who are subject to repeated minor traumas to the hand.

* Risk factors of palmoplantar epidermoid cysts-HPV infection, ultraviolet exposure, and eccrine duct obstruction.

* Presents as asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, painless, superficial localized swellings over the volar aspect of the hand, especially the distal portion of the digits.

* Investigations-X-rays, Ultrasonography, FNAC(CT and MRI may be helpful in delineating the anatomy of the soft tissue tumors, although unnecessary to guide the treatment).

* Histologically, the inclusion epidermoid cysts are lined with stratified squamous epithelium with granular cell layer and are filled with eosinophilic lamellated keratinous material.

* Most of the hand dermoid cysts are benign and asymptomatic, and hence surgical intervention is not needed.

* The surgical treatment is needed for symptomatic cysts causing interference with hand function in which complete excision is done with regional anesthesia under a pneumatic tourniquet.

Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types:

* Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development

* Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube/duct

* Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma

* Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto, meso, and endoderm)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 63-year-old woman is diagnosed with differentiated thyroid carcinoma after undergoing partial thyroidectomy. Which radioactive iodine isotope is routinely used to ablate the remaining thyroid tissue in such patients?
questions.explanation: In the management of differentiated thyroid cancers (papillary or follicular), radioactive iodine ablation is used to destroy residual microscopic thyroid tissue or metastatic disease following surgery. Iodine-131 (¹³¹I) is the isotope of choice because it emits gamma rays (useful for imaging) and beta particles, which produce a localized cytotoxic effect with a tissue penetration of about 1–2 mm, making it effective for therapeutic ablation. Iodine-125 (Option A) has a very long half-life and is mainly used in brachytherapy, not thyroid ablation. Iodine-127 (Option C) is a stable, non-radioactive isotope present in dietary salt. Iodine-123 (Option D) is a pure gamma emitter with a short half-life, ideal for diagnostic scans but ineffective for treatment. Before ¹³¹I therapy, patients must have elevated TSH levels, achieved by thyroid hormone withdrawal or recombinant TSH, to maximize radioactive iodine uptake by remaining thyroid cells

questions.text: An elderly male patient comes with foul-smelling breath and dysphagia. A barium swallow X-ray is attached. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zenker's diverticulum

The given clinical scenario of foul-smelling breath and dysphagia, and the given barium swallow X-ray showing the collection of contrast in a posterior pharyngeal pouch-like structure, are suggestive of Zenker's diverticulum.

It often presents with the following:

• Dysphagia
• Regurgitation
• Halitosis
• Gurgling sound on swallowing
• Aspiration

A barium swallow study may show a diverticulum arising from the midline of the posterior wall of the distal pharynx near the pharyngoesophageal junction. The diverticulum is typically noted at the C5-6 level. The outpouching may be transient, sometimes referred to as a pharyngeal pouch. The pouch is best identified during swallowing and is best visualized on the lateral view.

questions.text: Which one of the following drugs is not a secondary cause of weight gain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroxine

• A. Sulphonylureas: Can cause weight gain by increasing insulin secretion.
• B. Glucocorticoids: Cause weight gain through increased appetite, insulin resistance, and fat redistribution.
• C. Thyroxine: Correct. Thyroxine is generally associated with weight loss, not weight gain, when given appropriately. Excess thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic rate.
• D. β-blockers: Can cause modest weight gain, partly by reducing energy expenditure and physical activity tolerance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the case of a 7-year-old school-going child, which would be the most appropriate indicator to measure the current nutritional status?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Weight for height

In school-aged children (5–19 years), weight-for-height is the most appropriate indicator for assessing current nutritional status, as it reflects acute malnutrition (wasting) and is independent of age. Indicators such as birth weight, head circumference, and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) have limited utility in a 7-year-old child.

High-Yield Pearls

• Weight-for-height: Best indicator of current nutritional status (wasting/acute malnutrition).
• Height-for-age: Indicates chronic malnutrition (stunting).
• Weight-for-age: Reflects underweight but cannot differentiate between acute and chronic malnutrition.
• Birth weight: Assesses intrauterine growth, not current nutritional status.
• Head circumference: Useful only up to 2 years of age for monitoring brain growth.
• MUAC: Primarily used to screen acute malnutrition in children 6–59 months, not school-aged children.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of Ethosuximide?
options: Inhibits calcium channels in thalamic neurons
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide is the first-line and highly specific treatment for Absence seizures (petit mal). Its primary mechanism is the inhibition of T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons. These channels are responsible for the rhythmic, oscillatory activity in the thalamocortical pathway that drives the characteristic "3-Hz spike-and-wave" discharges seen on the EEG during an absence seizure. Enhancing GABAergic inhibition (Option A) is the mechanism for benzodiazepines and barbiturates. Blocking sodium channels (Option C) is how medications like phenytoin or carbamazepine work; these are effective for focal and tonic-clonic seizures but can actually worsen absence seizures. Increasing serotonin (Option D) is the mechanism for antidepressants. Absence seizures typically occur in children and are characterized by brief "staring spells" with immediate recovery. Ethosuximide's ability to selectively target the thalamic T-type channels makes it uniquely effective for this specific epilepsy type while causing minimal side effects
questions.learning: Ethosuximide is the first-line and highly specific treatment for Absence seizures (petit mal). Its primary mechanism is the inhibition of T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to cause mucormycosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Broad spectrum antibiotics

Among the given options, the condition least likely to cause mucormycosis is the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised patients. Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use.

Risk factors for the infection include the following:

* Uncontrolled diabetes

* Acidosis (especially diabetic ketoacidosis)

* Steroid treatment

* Lymphomas and leukemias

* Immunodeficiencies

* Severe burns

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Patients can have local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resembling the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis.

Treatment includes intravenous administration of amphotericin B and wide excision of necrotic tissues. Along with the reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.

•

Sudden stimulation or dysfunction of the otolithic organs (utricle/saccule) due to endolymphatic hydrops → abrupt loss of postural control → patient suddenly collapses.

Differentiation:

• Tulio phenomenon → vertigo induced by loud sound
• Lermoyez syndrome → hearing improves after vertigo

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with itchy, flat- topped, polygonal, violaceous papules on the inner wrists and flexor surfaces of the forearms. The lesions have a shiny surface and appear in a linear arrangement. There is no history of recent medication use. What is the appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of itchy, flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules on the flexor surfaces of the wrists is pathognomonic for Lichen Planus. These lesions often display a characteristic shiny surface known as Wickham striae and can demonstrate the Koebner phenomenon, where lesions appear in a linear pattern along sites of trauma. The first-line treatment for localized Lichen Planus is topical steroids, which work by reducing the T-cell mediated inflammatory response at the dermo-epidermal junction. Antibiotics (Option B), immunosuppressants (Option C), and anti-fungals (Option D) are not the primary treatments for this autoimmune condition. While systemic steroids or other immunosuppressants may be used for widespread or recalcitrant disease, topical therapy remains the standard of care for initial management. Clinicians should also screen these patients for Hepatitis C infection, which has a documented association with Lichen Planus

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following demographic indicators is used to compare the life expectancy of two different countries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HDI

The demographic indicator used to compare the life expectancy of two different countries is Human Development Index(HDI).

Human Development Index (HDI) is a measure of a country's average achievements in three dimensions of human development. The components include:

* A long and healthy life, as measured by life expectancy at birth

* Knowledge (literacy), as measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling, and

* A decent standard of living, as measured by GNI (gross national income) per capita.

HDI values range from 0 to 1, with 1 as the maximum value.

Life expectancy at 1 year, literacy and infant mortality rate are components of the Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 37-year-old woman presents with headaches for 6 months. She has been taking analgesics regularly. The headache recently increased in severity for 3 days but was reduced on stopping the analgesic. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medication overuse headache

The clinical features are suggestive of medication overuse headache.

Medication overuse headache:

It is also known as analgesic rebound headache, drug-induced headache, or medication-misuse headache. In this condition medications that are used for the treatment of headaches become the cause for headaches. It usually resolves when the overuse is stopped.

Diagnostic criteria: According to ICHD-3 (International Classification of Headache Disorders-3)

• Headache occurring on ≥15 days/month in a patient with a pre-existing headache disorder
• Regular overuse for >3 months of one or more drugs that can be taken for acute and/or symptomatic treatment of headache.
• Not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis.

Management: It includes the following steps:

• Withdrawal of the overused medication
• Rescue therapy or the treatment of withdrawal symptoms
• Initiation of preventative therapy if required
• Alternative symptomatic medication for future headaches

Other options:

Option B: Tension headache is a chronic headache syndrome characterized by bilateral, tight band-like discomfort. It can be episodic or chronic in nature. It is usually not associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, photophobia, etc.

Option C: Chronic migraine - Diagnostic criteria for migraine headache is as follows: Repeated attacks of headache lasting 4-72 hours in patients with normal physical examination, no other reasonable cause for headache, and

At least 2 of the following features
Plus at least 1 of the following features

Unilateral pain
Nausea or vomiting

Throbbing pain
Photophobia and phonophobia

Aggravation by movement

Moderate or severe intensity

Option D: Cluster headache is characterized by deep, excruciating, nonfluctuating pain which is usually retroorbital. The classical feature of this condition is its periodicity.  At least one of the daily attacks of pain recurs at almost the same hour every day.
Typically the patient has daily bouts of one or two attacks of relatively short-duration unilateral pain for 8–10 weeks a year. In between the clusters, there is a pain-free interval.
questions.learning: Medication overuse headache — The clinical features are suggestive of medication overuse headache. Medication overuse headache: It is also known as analgesic rebound headache, drug-induced headache, or medication-misuse headache.

Richardson and Koeppe are direct gonioscopes.

A gonioscope is used for the measurement of the angle of the anterior chamber. The types of gonioscopes include:

• Indirect gonioprism: Provides a mirror image of the opposite angle. Indirect goniolenses include Goldmann, Zeiss, and Posner.
• Direct gonioprism: Provides a direct view of the angle. Direct goniolenses include the Koeppe, Richardson, Medical Workshop, Barkan, and Swan–Jacob.

Applications:

• To view the angle of the anterior chamber. The structures visualized in order from front to back are:

• Schwalbe’s line
• Trabecular meshwork
• Scleral spur
• Ciliary body band
• Root of iris

• The localization of foreign bodies, abnormal blood vessels or tumors in the angle.
• Demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae.
• During goniotomy, a surgical procedure for the treatment of congenital glaucoma.

The below instrument is an indirect gonioscope of four-mirror type, which is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber.
questions.learning: 2, 4 Richardson and Koeppe are direct gonioscopes. A gonioscope is used for the measurement of the angle of the anterior chamber.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
An elderly patient on a vegetarian diet presenting with easy fatigability and pallor was investigated. Peripheral smear showed findings of macrocytic anemia. What is the probable cause of anemia in this patient? Other lab findings are as follows:

Hemoglobin - 9 g/dL

Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) - 112 fL

Serum homocysteine - Elevated

Serum methylmalonic acid - Normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Folate deficiency

The probable cause of anemia in this patient of folate deficiency.

The given clinical scenario of macrocytic anemia in a vegetarian with elevated homocysteine levels is due to megaloblastic anemia, which can be caused by the deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid. Vitamin B12 deficiency is associated with raised serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) levels, which are normal in this patient; hence, folic acid deficiency is the cause of megaloblastic anemia in this patient.

Folic acid deficiency is associated with the following clinical and laboratory findings:

• Raised MCV (normal range: 80–100 fL) - macrocytosis
• Normal MCHC (normal range: 33–36 g/dL)
• Increased MCH
• Elevated RDW
• Decreased reticulocyte count - due to destruction of abnormal erythroid precursors
• Elevated homocysteine level
• Normal MMA level

where MCV, mean corpuscular volume; MCHC, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration; mean corpuscular hemoglobin, MCH; RDW, red cell distribution width

In vitamin B12 deficiency, neurological abnormalities, elevated homocysteine, and elevated MMA levels are seen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following hormone–receptor interactions acts via the IP₃–DAG second messenger system?
options: Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle and vasopressin acting via V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle and vasopressin acting via V2 receptors on epithelial cells
Angiotensin II acting on epithelial cells and vasopressin acting via V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
Angiotensin II acting on epithelial cells and vasopressin acting via V2 receptors on epithelial cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle and vasopressin acting via V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle

Hormones that act through Gq protein–coupled receptors activate phospholipase C (PLC), which generates the second messengers IP₃ (inositol triphosphate) and DAG (diacylglycerol).

• IP₃ → releases Ca²⁺ from the endoplasmic reticulum
• DAG → activates protein kinase C

Key hormones using the IP₃–DAG pathway:

• Angiotensin II (AT₁ receptors) on vascular smooth muscle → vasoconstriction
• Vasopressin (ADH) acting on V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle → vasoconstriction

Important contrast:

• V2 receptors of vasopressin act via Gs → cAMP, causing water reabsorption in renal collecting ducts.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child underwent adenoidectomy for adenoid hypertrophy. Postoperatively, the child develops a hypernasal voice and occasional regurgitation of fluids through the nose. What is the most likely cause?
options: Submucous cleft palate unmasked after surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Submucous cleft palate unmasked after surgery

Persistent hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation following adenoidectomy suggest velopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI). The most common cause is an occult (submucous) cleft palate that was previously compensated for by enlarged adenoids. Removal of the adenoid pad unmasks the inability of the soft palate to achieve complete velopharyngeal closure during speech and swallowing.

Why not the other options?

• B. Choanal atresia unmasked after surgery: Causes nasal obstruction, not hypernasality or nasal regurgitation.
• C. Adhesions in the nasopharynx: May cause nasal blockage but do not typically produce velopharyngeal insufficiency.
• D. Uvular injury post surgery: Minor uvular trauma may cause sore throat or edema but is not a common cause of persistent hypernasal speech.
questions.learning: Submucous cleft palate unmasked after surgery Persistent hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation following adenoidectomy suggest velopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with fever, weight loss, and a persistent cough for the past 2 weeks. A lung biopsy is performed, which reveals small yeast forms measuring 2–4 μm in diameter, showing narrow-based budding and predominantly located within macrophages. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histoplasma capsulatum

Identify Histoplasma capsulatum by its characteristic histopathological appearance: small (2–4 μm), oval, narrow-based budding yeast located within macrophages. Histoplasmosis commonly presents with fever, weight loss, cough, and pulmonary infiltrates, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or those exposed to bird or bat droppings. Demonstration of intracellular yeast forms in tissue is highly suggestive of the diagnosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cryptosporidium parvum: An intestinal protozoan causing profuse watery diarrhea, not pulmonary disease or intracellular yeast in macrophages.
• B. Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Produces caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli, not budding yeast forms.
• D. Blastomyces dermatitidis: Appears as large (8–15 μm), broad-based budding yeast, usually extracellular, unlike the small intracellular narrow-based budding yeast of Histoplasma.

High-yield Pearl

| Fungus | Characteristic Histology

| ------ | ------------------------

| Histoplasma capsulatum | 2–4 μm, narrow-based budding yeast within macrophages

| Blastomyces dermatitidis | Broad-based budding yeast (8–15 μm)

| Cryptococcus neoformans | Encapsulated narrow-based budding yeast (India ink positive)

| Coccidioides immitis | Large spherules containing endospores

Exam Tip:

• Histoplasma = “Hides in Histiocytes (macrophages).”
• Bird/bat droppings + Intracellular 2–4 μm narrow-based budding yeast = Histoplasma capsulatum.
questions.learning: Histoplasma capsulatum Identify Histoplasma capsulatum by its characteristic histopathological appearance: small (2–4 μm), oval, narrow-based budding yeast located within macrophages.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following statements about Psoas abscess are true?

1. Fluctuant swelling in the hip
2. Cold abscess can develop from Pott's abscess
3. Pain on passive extension of hip joint is seen
4. It develops more commonly through hematogenous route in immunocompromised patients and elderly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3, and 4

The correct statements regarding psoas abscess are 1, 2, 3, and 4.

Psoas abscess occurs due to a collection of pus due to an infection in the iliopsoas compartment. The compartment is retroperitoneal and hence, the abscess is also called a retroperitoneal abscess. The compartment contains iliacus and iliopsoas muscles.

Psoas abscess is either primary or secondary.

• Tuberculosis of the spine leading to pott's abscess was the leading cause of psoas abscess (statement 2).
• Recently, hematogenous spread of infection from an occult primary site (gastrointestinal or urinary tract) has become common, especially in immunocompromised patients and the elderly (statement 4).
• Due to contiguous extension of infection from neighbouring structures.

Features include

• Back pain and fever.
• Soft, fluctuant swelling pointing towards the groin (hip) (statement 1).
• Pain on passive hip extension or active flexion of the psoas (statement 3).

CT scanning is useful in diagnosis. Percutaneous CT-guided drainage and antibiotic therapy are useful in the treatment of the condition.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following muscle filaments has a fixed length and does not change during contraction or relaxation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

According to the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction, the length of individual filaments remains constant during contraction and relaxation; instead, the degree of overlap between filaments changes.

Filaments with fixed length:

● Actin (thin filament): slides over myosin but its length remains unchanged.

●  Myosin (thick filament): also maintains a constant length.

●  Titin: an elastic structural protein that stabilizes the sarcomere and connects myosin to the Z-disc; its structure does not shorten during contraction.

During contraction:

●        Sarcomere length decreases

●        Z-lines move closer

●        I-band and H-zone decrease

●        A-band remains constant
questions.learning: All of the above According to the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction, the length of individual filaments remains constant during contraction and relaxation; instead, the degree of overlap between filaments changes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 32-year-old female presents with fatigue, paleness, and dizziness. Laboratory tests reveal low serum iron levels. Given these findings and her negative iron balance, what changes in iron metabolism would be expected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)

The given clinical scenario of a 32-year-old female presenting with fatigue, paleness, and dizziness and the laboratory tests showing low serum iron levels is suggestive of iron deficiency anaemia which is associated with increased TIBC.

Iron deficiency anaemia is a common type of anaemia that occurs when the body lacks sufficient iron to produce adequate levels of haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying component of red blood cells. This condition can result from various factors, including insufficient dietary iron intake, chronic blood loss (such as from gastrointestinal bleeding or heavy menstrual periods), or malabsorption disorders like celiac disease. Symptoms typically include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, and dizziness. In severe cases, patients may experience brittle nails, hair loss, or pica.

The diagnosis of iron deficiency anaemia is based on laboratory tests that often reveal low serum iron levels, reduced ferritin (Option A), a marker of iron stores, increased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), decreased transferrin saturation(Option B), decreased hematocrit (Option D), and a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV), indicating microcytic anaemia. Treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause and replenishing iron stores, often through oral iron supplements or dietary adjustments. In more severe cases, intravenous iron or blood transfusions may be necessary. Early detection and management are essential to prevent complications and restore normal red blood cell production.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient presents with a history of loss of interest in day to day activities, weight loss, insomnia, and sadness for six months. She also recalls hearing a voice once that ordered her to kill herself. What is the DSM-V diagnosis?
options: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

Since the patient fulfills the DSM-V criteria for major depressive disorder and has had an episode of auditory hallucination, a diagnosis of major depressive disorder with psychotic features is made.

Diagnostic criteria for depression:

1. Depressed mood most of the day
2. Anhedonia- diminished interest in day to day activities
3. Significant weight loss or weight gain. Change in appetite.
4. Insomnia or hypersomnia
5. Psychomotor agitation or retardation
6. Fatigue or loss of energy
7. Feelings of worthlessness or excessive, inappropriate guilt
8. Diminished ability to think or concentrate, indecisiveness
9. Recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation

At least five out of nine symptoms must be present over a two week period and one symptom must be depressed mood or anhedonia.

In major depressive disorder with psychotic features, delusions and/or hallucinations are present along with the depression symptoms.
questions.learning: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features Since the patient fulfills the DSM-V criteria for major depressive disorder and has had an episode of auditory hallucination, a diagnosis of major depressive disorder with psychotic features is made.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman is in labour, and during delivery, the baby's head is delivered, but the shoulders get stuck. The baby's head is at the introitus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Shoulder dystocia

This clinical vignette of a 28-year-old woman in labour with the baby's head at the introitus and the shoulders being stuck is suggestive of shoulder dystocia.

Shoulder dystocia, defined as a head-to-body delivery time >60 seconds, occurs when either the anterior or the posterior (rare) fetal shoulder impacts on the maternal symphysis or the sacral promontory respectively.  A positive turtle sign may be seen which refers to a definite recoil of the head back against the perineum.

Risk factors for the development of shoulder dystocia include maternal diabetes mellitus, obesity, post-dated pregnancy, excessive weight gain during pregnancy, etc.  Wood's corkscrew maneuver is used to deliver the impacted shoulder in this condition.

Woods corkscrew maneuver: Progressive rotation of the posterior shoulder 180 degrees in a corkscrew fashion releases the impacted anterior shoulder.

Other options:

Option A: Face Presentation - In a face presentation, the baby presents with the face as the presenting part instead of the vertex. The baby’s head is typically fully extended, leading to complications during delivery. However, once the head is delivered, the body usually follows without significant issues. The scenario described involves difficulty after the head is delivered, specifically with the shoulders, which is not characteristic of face presentation.

Option B: Occipito-sacral arrest- This refers to the baby being in a persistent occiput posterior position (with the baby facing up towards the mother’s abdomen rather than down). Labor may progress more slowly or stop when the baby’s head fails to rotate and descend properly. However, like with CPD, occipito-sacral arrest typically results in difficulty before the head is delivered, not after. If the head has been delivered but the shoulders are stuck, it indicates a different issue.

Option C: Cephalopelvic disproportion(CPD) - CPD occurs when the baby's head or body is too large to fit through the mother's pelvis. This can lead to labor not progressing or being arrested before the baby’s head is fully delivered. In CPD, labor arrest or failure to descend is seen, and the baby’s head may not pass through the pelvis at all. Since in the scenario described above, the head is already delivered and the shoulders are the issue, CPD is less likely to be the cause.
questions.learning: Shoulder dystocia — This clinical vignette of a 28-year-old woman in labour with the baby's head at the introitus and the shoulders being stuck is suggestive of shoulder dystocia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with spinal cord injury shows loss of recurrent inhibition of alpha motor neurons, leading to increased muscle tone. Dysfunction of which of the following interneurons is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renshaw cell

Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord that provide recurrent inhibition to α-motor neurons.

• An α-motor neuron activates a muscle fiber and simultaneously sends a collateral branch to Renshaw cells.
• Renshaw cells release inhibitory neurotransmitters (mainly glycine).
• This inhibits the same α-motor neuron and neighboring motor neurons, preventing excessive muscle contraction.

Clinical significance:

• Loss of Renshaw cell inhibition → increased α-motor neuron activity → muscle hypertonia/spasticity.
• Tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release from Renshaw cells, leading to muscle rigidity and spasms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 37-year-old male who is a chronic alcoholic abstained from alcohol. 3 days later, he was brought to the emergency with complaints of disorientation, tremors, hallucinations, and hypertension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Delirium tremens

The clinical features are suggestive of delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens occurs after 2-4 days of abstinence in a heavy or chronic drinker. It usually resolves spontaneously in 7 days but may cause the death of the patient due to cardiovascular collapse or infections or self-injury.

The characteristic clinical features include:

* Clouding of consciousness with disorientation in time and place.

* Distractibility and lack of attention.

* Visual, auditory, and/or tactile hallucinations.

* Autonomic disturbance with tachycardia, fever, hypertension, sweating and pupillary dilatation.

* Psychomotor agitation and ataxia

* Insomnia

* Dehydration with electrolyte imbalance.

Delirium tremens is treated using benzodiazepines starting with a higher dosage which is gradually tapered as withdrawal symptoms disappear. In cases of chronic alcohol use, vitamin deficiency (especially thiamine) may be co-existing and hence bolus doses of thiamine are given to prevent/treat Wernicke encephalopathy.

Other options:

* Alcoholic hallucinosis is characterised by the presence of hallucinations (usually auditory) during partial or complete abstinence. However, the other symptoms given in the question are not seen, and the patient present with clear consciousness.

* Korsakoff ’s psychosis: It is seen n patients with chronic alcohol use usually followed by Wernicke’s encephalopathy, together referred to as Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Patients with korsakoff's psychosis present with memory disturbances, which is not seen in the given case.

* Marchiafava-Bignami disease is a rare disorder seen in chronic alcoholics, associated with epilepsy, ataxia, dysarthria, hallucinations, spastic limb paralysis, and deterioration of personality and intellectual functioning.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with increased urinary frequency, hesitancy, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He has no history of urinary tract infection or kidney disease, and evaluation suggests benign prostatic hyperplasia. What is the most appropriate initial management for his urinary symptoms?
questions.explanation: For a patient presenting with bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) due to BPH without secondary complications, the initial management is usually medical. Tamsulosin, an alpha-1 blocker, is the most appropriate first-line choice because it rapidly relaxes the smooth muscle of the bladder neck and prostate, providing quick symptomatic relief (often within days). Finasteride (Option C), a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, is also used but typically takes 6–12 months to significantly shrink the prostate and is best suited for larger gland volumes. TURP (Option A) is the gold standard "surgical" treatment but is generally reserved for patients who fail medical therapy or develop complications like refractory urinary retention, bladder stones, or recurrent hematuria. Observation (Option D) is only suitable for patients with very mild, non-bothersome symptoms. Since this patient reports progressive symptoms, initiating tamsulosin is the most effective and commonly prescribed initial intervention to improve his quality of life
questions.learning: For a patient presenting with bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) due to BPH without secondary complications, the initial management is usually medical.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: How is this contraceptive inserted?
questions.explanation: The device shown is an intratubal contraceptive micro-insert (classically known by the brand name Essure). It is a non-incisional form of permanent sterilization. The coils are inserted hysteroscopically (Option A) through the vagina and cervix into the fallopian tubes. Once in place, they induce a localized inflammatory response that leads to the formation of scar tissue (fibrosis), which permanently blocks the tubes. Abdominal (Option B) and Laparoscopic (Option C) methods are used for traditional tubal ligation (e.g., Pomeroy’s technique or applying Falope rings), which involve incisions and general anesthesia. Oral (Option D) refers to birth control pills. The primary advantage of the hysteroscopic coil method is that it can be performed in an office setting without incisions. However, users must use backup contraception for three months until a follow-up test confirms the tubes are completely occluded. Therefore, the visual of the micro-coil coil uniquely identifies the hysteroscopic delivery route
questions.learning: The device shown is an intratubal contraceptive micro-insert (classically known by the brand name Essure). It is a non-incisional form of permanent sterilization.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the condition based on the non-contrast CT scan of a patient given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hydatid cyst

The given CT image shows a cyst in the liver with the serpent sign and areas of calcification, which are suggestive of hydatid disease.

Hydatid disease or echinococcosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the Echinococcus species of flatworms. Its life cycle consists of dogs as definitive hosts and humans as accidental intermediate hosts.

Primary hydatid cysts most commonly occur in the liver. Most patients are asymptomatic but when symptomatic, the patient presents with hepatomegaly, pain, and obstructive jaundice.

The first/initial imaging test is USG, and CT scan can be used to diagnose the condition. CT scan shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline and septa. CT scan has an accuracy of 98% in the detection of hydatid cysts and high sensitivity to the detection of daughter cysts and extra-hepatic cysts.

On CT imaging, serpent sign is seen as wavy membranes within the cyst:

The USG of an active hydatid cyst shows multiple septations and a rosette or honeycomb appearance:

The ball of wool sign is seen on USG when the contents settle in the dependent portion of the cyst, as seen below:

On USG, the water-lily sign is seen in hydatid infections when there is detachment of the endocyst membrane, which results in floating membranes within the pericyst that mimic the appearance of a water lily.

The image below shows the structures present within a cyst.

Other options:

Option A: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is diagnosed with contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) or MRI. On a non-contrast CT, it appears as a low-attenuated lesion with occasional calcification. On CECT, HCC lesions show enhancement in the arterial phase and washout in the portal phase.

The following image shows the triphasic CECT of HCC:

Option B: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign solid lesion in the liver. Histologically, it is composed of normal liver elements, but the biliary elements are not connected to the normal biliary tree. On CECT, they exhibit homogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase of IV contrast.

The image below shows late arterial and portal venous phase CECT of focal nodular hyperplasia:

Option C: Liver abscess may be caused by various infections. It begins as a local inflammatory reaction and later develops liquefactive necrosis in the center, with an inflammatory margin.

On a non-contrast CT, it appears as an ill-defined lesion with low attenuation, as seen in the image below:

The given image shows a liver abscess with rim enhancement on CECT.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The sulcus located deep to the marked structure is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stem of the lateral sulcus

The area marked by an arrow in the given image is pterion and the stem of the lateral sulcus lies under it.

The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

• Frontal bone
• Squamous part of the temporal bone
• Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
• Parietal bone.

The surface of the cerebrum consists of folds called gyri separated by fissures called sulci. The lateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian Fissure, is present on the infero-lateral surface of each cerebral hemisphere and separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. The lateral sulcus consists of a stem which divides into three rami, which are, the anterior horizontal, anterior ascending, and the posterior rami.

The structures lying deep to the pterion are:

• The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery
• The middle meningeal vein
• The stem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure)

The bone in this area is thin and an injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with chronic liver disease presents with hepatomegaly, ascites, and jaundice, and is diagnosed with hepatocellular carcinoma. Which factor is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.explanation: Aflatoxin, specifically Aflatoxin B1, is a potent hepatic carcinogen produced by the molds Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus which contaminate stored crops like peanuts and grains. It is strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), particularly in tropical regions. Mechanistically, aflatoxin causes a specific mutation in the p53 tumor suppressor gene (a G to T transversion at codon 249), which leads to uncontrolled cellular proliferation. Benzol (Option A, Benzene) is primarily associated with acute myeloid leukemia. Arsenic (Option B) is linked to skin cancer and hepatic angiosarcoma. Vinyl chloride (Option D) is the classic risk factor for angiosarcoma of the liver, a rare vascular tumor, rather than HCC. In many cases, aflatoxin exposure acts synergistically with chronic Hepatitis B infection to drastically increase the risk of developing HCC. Clinical prevention focuses on improving food storage practices to prevent mold growth and universal Hepatitis B vaccination. HCC carries a high mortality rate and requires management via surgical resection, ablation, or liver transplantation
questions.learning: Aflatoxin, specifically Aflatoxin B1, is a potent hepatic carcinogen produced by the molds Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus which contaminate stored crops like peanuts and grains.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-year-old child with a history of repeated, multiple, long bone fractures is diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta. Which of the following structures contains the type of collagen that is defective in this disease? * Tendon * Basement membrane * Elastic cartilage * Skin * Sclera
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 4, 5

Osteogenesis imperfecta(OI) is a connective tissue disorder that occurs due to abnormal type 1 collagen production. Type 1 collagen is also present in the skin, tendons, and sclera (1, 4, 5) apart from bones.

OI also called brittle bone disease, is an autosomal dominant disorder. There are 8 types of osteogenesis imperfecta. It occurs most commonly due to mutation in the COL1A and COL2A genes. These mutations lead to the replacement of glycine amino acid with another amino acid resulting in an abnormal triple helix of collagen. This results in the abnormal formation of type 1 collagen.

The defining clinical features of OI include:

* Osteopenia

* Recurrent Fractures

* Laxity of Ligaments

* Bluish Discoloration of The Sclerae

* Dentinogenesis Imperfecta ("Crumbling Teeth")

Note:

* Type I collagen is seen in the bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, fibrocartilage, and sclera of the eyeball.

* Type II collagen is seen in hyaline and elastic cartilage (Option 3) and the vitreous body of the eye.

* Type III collagen is seen in reticulin fibers, smooth muscle, endoneurium, arteries, uterus, kidney, spleen, and liver.

* Type IV collagen is seen in epithelial and endothelial basal laminae and basement membranes. (Option 2)
