questions.learning: 1, 4, 5 Osteogenesis imperfecta(OI) is a connective tissue disorder that occurs due to abnormal type 1 collagen production. Type 1 collagen is also present in the skin, tendons, and sclera (1, 4, 5) apart from bones.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A person has suffered from chest trauma resulting in fracture of 2-6th ribs. He is being given pain relief by IV analgesic agents. Which of these blocks will be helpful in pain relief?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thoracic epidural

Rib fractures from T2–T6 produce severe chest wall pain best relieved by thoracic epidural, which provides segmental analgesia to the corresponding dermatomes. Cervical and supraclavicular blocks do not cover thoracic levels, and lumbar epidural is too low to provide effective analgesia for upper thoracic ribs.
questions.learning: Thoracic epidural Rib fractures from T2–T6 produce severe chest wall pain best relieved by thoracic epidural, which provides segmental analgesia to the corresponding dermatomes.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 60 year old woman presents with low backache and on a lumbar CT the following is seen. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteoporosis

The given image depicts the ballooning of the intervertebral disc into the adjacent vertebrae leading to biconcave shape of vertebral body and biconvex shape of the disc which is known as the ‘codfish appearance’. This is classically seen in osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is a metabolic disease of the bone that is caused due to an equivalent decrease in both bone matrix and its mineralization, resulting in a diffuse decrease in both, bone density and bone mass. It is seen in various conditions namely in postmenopausal females, Cushing's disease, and long-term steroid therapy.

The various complications seen in osteoporosis are due to decreased bone mass which contributes to bone pains and increased frequency of pathological fractures such as Colle's fracture and neck of femur fractures. In the vertebrae, the dorso-lumbar spine is the most frequent site to be involved and can present as increased kyphosis due to compression of the anterior part of the vertebral bodies.

Other radiological features of osteoporosis:

• Loss of vertical height of vertebra due to collapse
• Ground glass appearance of bones especially in the bones like pelvis
• Loss of cortical bone (picture frame vertebrae) and trabecular bone (ghost vertebrae)
• Loss of trabeculae in proximal femur area.

DEXA scan is the gold standard for quantifying bone mass in osteoporotic patients. A T-score of less than -2.5 is diagnostic of osteoporosis.

The X-ray given below is of a post-menopausal female with Colle's fracture after trivial trauma, caused secondary to osteoporosis.

Option A: Spondylolisthesis is the anterior translation of one vertebra over another. It commonly occurs between L5-S1 followed by L4-L5. On examination, often there is a visible or palpable 'step'.

A lateral X-ray of the spine shows anterior displacement of one vertebra over another. The oblique view in severe spondylolisthesis shows the 'beheaded Scottish terrier sign' (due to a break in pars interarticularis).

The below-given images depict spondylolisthesis as seen on X-ray:

Option D: Pott's spine also known as TB spine occurs secondary to a pulmonary or gastrointestinal primary and spreads through the Batson's plexus of veins (paravertebral plexus). It most commonly involves the dorso-lumbar region.

On X-ray and CT imaging:

• A reduction in disc space is seen between the vertebrae and it is one of the earlieast signs of TB spine
• Vertebral body destruction can also be seen- based on the number of vertebrae involved they are called by different names. An involvement of 3-4 vertebrae is called as kyphosis
• Cold abscesses such as paravertebral abscess can be visible as a soft tissue shadow
• Advanced destruction and wedging of vertebrae
questions.learning: Osteoporosis — The given image depicts the ballooning of the intervertebral disc into the adjacent vertebrae leading to biconcave shape of vertebral body and biconvex shape of the disc which is known as the ‘codfish appearance’.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented to the OPD with an abnormal gait. On examination, when the patient was asked to stand on the left foot, a right-sided hip drop was observed. Which of the following muscles are paralyzed in this patient?
options: Right gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
Left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus

The examination of the patient indicates a positive Trendelenburg's sign (Trendelenburg's gait), with sagging on the right side. It is seen in paralysis of the left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles which are supplied by the left superior gluteal nerve.

The superior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus.

Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus:

* When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, on the opposite supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in the slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.

* When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis sinks down on the unsupported (normal) side, when the patient tries to stand on the affected limb.

Inferior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus maximus muscle.

The below GIF shows a positive Trendelenburg's sign (Trendelenburg's gait) with a left superior gluteal nerve injury.

In the GIF, when the person lifts up his right leg and tries to stand on the left leg, the right pelvis tilts down. This shows that the left side abduction mechanism is paralyzed and the right side is normal. The left superior gluteal nerve is injured in this case since it supplies the left gluteus medius and minimus.

Note: These patients can also have a characteristic lurching gait.
questions.learning: Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus — The examination of the patient indicates a positive Trendelenburg's sign (Trendelenburg's gait), with sagging on the right side.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following poison can be found even in skeletonised remains of the body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arsenic

Arsenic can be found even in skeletonized remains of the body.

It becomes fixed in the cancellous tissues of the long bones by the conversion of phosphates to arsenates. The elimination of arsenic in this form is much slower and can be detected in the bones for several years after death.

Heavy metals such as lead, copper, mercury, including metalloids like arsenic and antimony, may be found in bones for a prolonged period in cases of chronic poisoning. They are also deposited in hair, nails, etc. For these reasons, when heavy metal poisoning is suspected, these specimens are collected in addition to the routine viscera and body fluids.
questions.learning: Arsenic Arsenic can be found even in skeletonized remains of the body. It becomes fixed in the cancellous tissues of the long bones by the conversion of phosphates to arsenates.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman visits the clinic for a routine check-up. She has a history of epilepsy and has been taking anti-epileptic medication for the past five years. Which of the following statements about folic acid supplementation in patients on anti-epileptic drugs is most accurate?
options: The daily requirement of folic acid is .
The daily requirement of folic acid is .
The daily requirement of folic acid is .
The daily requirement of folic acid is .
questions.explanation: Women on anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs), such as valproate or carbamazepine, are at a significantly increased risk of having a baby with neural tube defects (NTDs). This is because many AEDs interfere with folate metabolism. Therefore, for these high-risk patients, the recommended dose of folic acid is (or depending on the local guideline), which is ten times the standard dose of (Option A) given to low-risk women. Options C and D are also insufficient for this high-risk population. Ideally, this high-dose supplementation should begin at least one to three months before conception and continue through the first trimester. Clinicians must also review and optimize the epilepsy treatment, aiming for the lowest effective dose of the safest possible AED (e.g., lamotrigine or levetiracetam) before the patient becomes pregnant. This targeted nutritional intervention is vital for preventing life-altering congenital malformations
questions.learning: Women on anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs), such as valproate or carbamazepine, are at a significantly increased risk of having a baby with neural tube defects (NTDs).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
Which of the following has familial inheritance?

1. Retinoblastoma
2. Retinitis pigmentosa
3. Myopia
4. Primary open angle glaucoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

All the above conditions (1, 2, 3, 4) have a familial inheritance.

Retinoblastoma is a malignancy arising from the retina more commonly seen in children. 10% of the cases are familial. These cases have an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. The remaining 90% occurs sporadically. The clinical presentation includes leucocoria, strabismus, and painful red eye.

Retinitis pigmentosa is a pigmental retinal dystrophy where the photoreceptors, especially rods are affected. Around 50 - 60% of the cases have a familial inheritance. It has multiple modes of inheritance, autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked recessive. Night blindness is a characteristic feature. Tubular vision is seen in advanced cases.

Myopia (shortsightedness) is a refractive error in which the light rays from infinity are focused in front of the retina. It is proven to have familial inheritance. Features include defective vision, impaired night vision, and muscae volitantes.

Primary open-angle glaucoma has a normal anterior chamber angle. Family history is a risk factor implicated in the condition. Symptoms include headache, scotoma, and delayed dark adaptation.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4 All the above conditions (1, 2, 3, 4) have a familial inheritance. Retinoblastoma is a malignancy arising from the retina more commonly seen in children.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the mutation seen in Sickle cell anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glu---> Val(6)

Glu---> Val(6) mutation is seen in Sickle cell anemia.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to a missense mutation (a type of point mutation) in the β-globin gene of HbS, which results in the replacement of polar glutamate residue with non-polar valine at the 6th position, generating a hydrophobic “sticky patch” on the surface of the β subunit of deoxygenated HbS.

Both HbA and HbS contain a complementary sticky patch on their surfaces that is exposed only in the deoxygenated state. Thus, at low Po2, deoxyHbS polymerizes to form long, twisted helical fibers. This distorts the biconcave RBC into a sickle shape. The precipitated HbS also damages the RBC membrane, so the cells become highly fragile and get easily hemolyzed leading to anemia.

The major pathophysiology involves chronic hemolysis and microvascular occlusion. Hypoxia  increases the concentration of deoxygenated HbS promoting RBC sickling. These sickle cells can disrupt circulation causing vascular occlusion and tissue infarction. Vaso-occlusive crises, also known as pain crises, are a result of this hypoxic injury and infarction. These crises predominantly affect the bones, lungs, liver, brain, spleen, and penis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A nurse keeps the bins as shown in the image in the hospital ward. Which of the following items would go into the black bin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glove paper cover

Glove paper cover is a general solid waste that is to be collected in the black bin.

All non-infectious general wastes like food waste, paper waste, and mineral water bottles should be discarded in black bins.

Soiled linen bedsheets contaminated by blood or body fluids should be disposed in the yellow bin. All plastic recyclable wastes are discarded in red bins (gloves and contaminated gloves).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is altered in thyroid profile throughout pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Total T3 level

Total T3 levels are altered throughout pregnancy.

Total T3 and total T4 increase due to stimulation of thyroid tissue by hCG (α-subunit of hCG is similar to TSH) during the early period of gestation. However, there is no change in free T3 and T4 due to an increase in thyroid-binding globulin (TBG).

This leads to a transient fall in TSH (but remains in the normal range) during the early weeks of gestation. The level of TSH becomes normal during the second and third trimesters.

The hormonal changes during pregnancy are as follows:

Increased
Decreased
Unchanged

Growth Hormone
LH (Luteinizing hormone)
Free T3, T4

Insulin (due to insulin resistance)
FSH (Follicle-stimulating hormone)
TSH

Prolactin
DHEAS (Di-hydro epiandrosterone)
ADH (Anti-  diuretic hormone)

Total T3, T4

Aldosterone

Testosterone, Androstenedione, and cortisol
questions.learning: Total T3 level Total T3 levels are altered throughout pregnancy. Total T3 and total T4 increase due to stimulation of thyroid tissue by hCG (α-subunit of hCG is similar to TSH) during the early period of gestation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Contralateral homonymous upper quadrantanopia is the type of visual loss seen when the lesion is located at which one of the following anatomical locations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Temporal lobe

A lesion involving the temporal lobe, specifically the Meyer’s loop (inferior optic radiations), produces a contralateral homonymous superior (upper) quadrantanopia, classically described as “pie in the sky” visual field defect.

The inferior retinal fibers, which carry information from the superior visual field, pass anteriorly through the temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop) before reaching the occipital cortex. Damage to these fibers results in loss of the contralateral upper visual field in both eyes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Frontal lobe: Does not contain the visual pathway responsible for quadrantanopia.
• C. Parietal lobe: Contains the superior optic radiations, and lesions produce contralateral homonymous lower quadrantanopia (“pie on the floor”).
• D. Occipital lobe: Lesions usually cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing if due to posterior cerebral artery infarction.
questions.learning: Temporal lobe — A lesion involving the temporal lobe, specifically the Meyer’s loop (inferior optic radiations), produces a contralateral homonymous superior (upper) quadrantanopia, classically described as “pie in the sky” visual field defect.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A child is having fecal discharge from the umbilicus. What is the abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Patent vitello-intestinal duct

Patent Vitellointestinal Duct (Omphalomesenteric Fistula)

• Connection: Ileum to Umbilicus
• Presentation:

• Fecal discharge from umbilicus
• May see mucosal prolapse

• Complete patency of duct

Omphalomesenteric (Vitellointestinal) Cyst

• Connection: Both ends closed, cyst in between
• Presentation:

• Umbilical swelling
• May get infected → painful mass

• No external discharge unless ruptured

Urachal Anomalies (Allantoic Remnant)

A. Patent Urachus

• Connection: Bladder to Umbilicus
• Presentation:

• Urine discharge from umbilicus

B. Urachal Cyst

• Connection: Both ends closed, cyst in midline
• Presentation:

• Infraumbilical swelling
• Infection → tender mass

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with both cutaneous lesions and joint involvement, as shown in the image, and later develops arthritis. What is the treatment of choice for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—featuring cutaneous silvery plaques (psoriasis) and concurrent inflammatory arthritis with dactylitis ("sausage digit")—is diagnostic of Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) . For a patient exhibiting both cutaneous and joint disease, the standard first-line disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) of choice is Methotrexate (Option C). Methotrexate is highly effective at managing both the skin manifestations and the underlying synovial inflammation. PUVA (Option A) is a specialized phototherapy for skin psoriasis but does not treat the inflammatory joint disease. Steroids (Option B) are used with extreme caution in psoriasis as their withdrawal can trigger life-threatening pustular flares. Infliximab (Option D), a TNF-inhibitor, is a highly effective "second-line" biological therapy used when DMARDs like methotrexate fail. Therefore, as the primary systemic treatment addressing both organ systems, Methotrexate is the definitive clinical choice
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation—featuring cutaneous silvery plaques (psoriasis) and concurrent inflammatory arthritis with dactylitis ("sausage digit")—is diagnostic of Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) .

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A group of individuals travel to a high-altitude mountainous region, and a girl develops symptoms suggestive of acute mountain sickness. Which drug is the treatment of choice in this situation?
questions.explanation: Acetazolamide is the drug of choice for both the prevention and treatment of Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS). It is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that works by promoting the renal excretion of bicarbonate, leading to a mild metabolic acidosis. This acidosis stimulates the respiratory centers in the brain, increasing the ventilation rate and helping the body acclimatize to lower oxygen levels at high altitudes. Promethazine (Option A) and Dimenhydrinate (Option C) are antihistamines used primarily for motion sickness and nausea, but they do not address the underlying physiological cause of mountain sickness. Thiazides (Option D) are diuretics used for hypertension and do not play a role in altitude medicine. Patients with severe AMS or high-altitude pulmonary edema require immediate descent and supplemental oxygen. Acetazolamide is a vital pharmacological tool for trekkers and climbers to facilitate safe ascent and manage mild symptoms like headache and fatigue
questions.learning: Acetazolamide is the drug of choice for both the prevention and treatment of Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS). It is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that works by promoting the renal excretion of bicarbonate, leading to a mild metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the cranial nerve passing through the given structure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. IV

In the given image, the dorsal aspect of the brainstem is marked and the cranial nerve that is passing there is the trochlear nerve (CN IV).

The trochlear nerve is the fourth cranial nerve that originates from the trochlear nuclei within the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. It is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal surface of the brainstem and has the longest intracranial course. It passes on to the lateral surface of the crus of cerebellar peduncle and lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. The nerve then crosses the oculomotor nerve to enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure to exclusively supply the contralateral superior oblique muscle.

The main actions of superior oblique are

• Depression in adducted position- The muscle elevates the posterior of the eye causing the front of the eye to be depressed. Patients with trochlear nerve palsy have difficulty in looking downwards when eyes are in the adducted position.
• Abduction
• Intortion of the eyeball.

Other options- Oculomotor (CN III), trigeminal (CN V) and abducens (CN VI) nerves exit ventrally from the brainstem.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida presents with labor pains, and per vaginal examination reveals that the cervix is 7 cm dilated and fully effaced. Which stage of labor is she currently in?
questions.explanation: The first stage of labor is divided into the latent and active phases . Friedman’s curve further subdivides the active phase into the acceleration phase, the phase of maximum slope, and the deceleration phase . The latent phase ends and the active phase begins around 4 cm of cervical dilation. Between 4 cm and 9 cm of dilation, particularly at 7 cm, the patient is in the phase of maximum slope. This is when cervical dilation occurs at its fastest rate. The acceleration phase (Option A) occurs just before this, usually between 3–4 cm. The deceleration phase (Option C) occurs after 9 cm, when dilation slows down before full dilation (10 cm). The latent phase (Option B) is the early part of labor with slow cervical change. Because the patient is 7 cm dilated and fully effaced, she has progressed well into the most rapid portion of the active stage, identifying this as the phase of maximum slope
questions.learning: The first stage of labor is divided into the latent and active phases . Friedman’s curve further subdivides the active phase into the acceleration phase, the phase of maximum slope, and the deceleration phase .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Pulsus paradoxus is seen in______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute severe asthma

Pulsus paradoxus is seen in acute severe asthma.

Features of Acute severe attack of asthma include:

* Inability to speak a complete sentence in one breath

* Pulse >120/min

* Respiratory rate >25/min

* FEV1 between 33 to 50% of predicted

* Pulsus paradoxus of >10 mmHg

Pearl PF1591: Causes of Pulsus Paradoxus

Physiological causes

Obesity

Pregnancy

Cardiovascular causes

Cardiac tamponade – most common cause

Constrictive pericarditis ( in 1/3rd cases )

Massive pulmonary embolism

Severe CCF

Hypovolemic shock

Respiratory causes

Severe obstructive lung disease

Acute severe asthma

Severe emphysema

Tension pneumothorax

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Allelic exclusion during B-cell maturation is ensured by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. V(D)J rearrangements

Allelic exclusion ensures that each B cell expresses a single antigen receptor specificity by allowing productive rearrangement of only one immunoglobulin heavy-chain allele and one light-chain allele.

• During B-cell development in the bone marrow, V(D)J recombination rearranges variable (V), diversity (D), and joining (J) gene segments.
• Once a functional Ig heavy chain is produced, further rearrangement of the other allele is inhibited, ensuring single antibody specificity.

Why not other options:

B) Alternative splicing: Produces different forms of Ig (IgM vs IgD) from the same transcript. Does not ensure single allele expression.

C) Alternative polyadenylation: Determines membrane-bound vs secreted antibody forms. Not related to allelic exclusion.

D) Somatic hypermutation: Occurs after antigen stimulation in germinal centers to increase antibody affinity. Not involved in initial allele selection.
questions.learning: V(D)J rearrangements Allelic exclusion ensures that each B cell expresses a single antigen receptor specificity by allowing productive rearrangement of only one immunoglobulin heavy-chain allele and one light-chain allele. • During B-cell development in…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During exercise, skeletal muscle blood flow increases primarily due to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Local metabolic vasodilation

During exercise, skeletal muscle blood flow increases mainly due to local metabolic vasodilation in active muscles.

• Contracting muscles produce metabolic by-products such as:
• CO₂
• H⁺ (lactic acid)
• K⁺
• Adenosine
• ↓ O₂
• These metabolites cause local arteriolar dilation, greatly increasing muscle perfusion.

Although sympathetic activity increases during exercise, the local metabolic effects override sympathetic vasoconstriction in active muscles.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are the risk factors for the acquisition of hepatitis C infection? 1. Faeco-oral transmission 2. Intravenous drug abuse 3. Vertical transmission 4. Sharing toothbrush and razors Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is transmitted primarily through blood exposure. The major risk factors include intravenous drug use, vertical (mother-to-child) transmission, and sharing blood-contaminated personal items such as razors and toothbrushes.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Faeco-oral transmission ❌: Incorrect. This is the route for Hepatitis A and E, not HCV.
• 2. Intravenous drug abuse ✔️: Major risk factor.
• 3. Vertical transmission ✔️: Occurs, especially if the mother has a high viral load or HIV coinfection.
• 4. Sharing toothbrush and razors ✔️: Can transmit HCV through blood contamination.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is transmitted primarily through blood exposure. The major risk factors include intravenous drug use, vertical (mother-to-child) transmission, and sharing blood-contaminated personal items such as razors and toothbrushes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a marker of the heat stability of vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. VVM

Vaccine Vial Monitors (VVM) are heat-sensitive indicators that are routinely used to monitor vaccine viability as the vaccine vial moves across the supply chain.

VVM records cumulative heat exposure through a gradual change in color. If the color of the inner square is the same or is darker than the outer circle, the vaccine has been exposed to too much temperature and should be discarded.
questions.learning: VVM Vaccine Vial Monitors (VVM) are heat-sensitive indicators that are routinely used to monitor vaccine viability as the vaccine vial moves across the supply chain.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During the management of labor, oxytocin may be administered as an intravenous bolus. What adverse effect is commonly associated with giving oxytocin by this route?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is a potent uterotonic agent used for labor induction and the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage. While it is vital for obstetric care, rapid intravenous bolus administration can lead to significant hemodynamic changes. Specifically, oxytocin has a direct relaxant effect on vascular smooth muscle, which can cause sudden, transient peripheral vasodilation. This results in acute maternal hypotension, often accompanied by tachycardia and increased cardiac output. Hypertension (Option B) is more commonly associated with other uterotonics like ergometrine. Neither hyperglycemia (Option C) nor hypoglycemia (Option D) are recognized side effects of oxytocin administration. To minimize the risk of cardiovascular collapse or profound hypotension, oxytocin is standardly administered as a slow intravenous infusion rather than a rapid bolus. Clinicians must be particularly cautious in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease or hypovolemia, as the rapid drop in blood pressure can compromise maternal safety and fetal perfusion. Monitoring of maternal vitals is essential during any oxytocin administration in the peripartum period
questions.learning: Oxytocin is a potent uterotonic agent used for labor induction and the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage. While it is vital for obstetric care, rapid intravenous bolus administration can lead to significant hemodynamic changes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on the lateral aspect of the nasal fold, below the eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Squamous Cell Carcinoma

The clinical description of a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on a sun-exposed site like the lateral nasal fold is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma(SCC).

SCC is a malignant tumour of keratinising cells of the epidermis or its appendages. It arises from the stratum basalis of the epidermis and is the second most common skin cancer. The primary risk factor and driving force for the development of this common cancer is UV exposure. Variants of SCC include, Bowen's disease and Erythroplasia of Queyrat.

It initially presents as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous lesions. All these lesions later ulcerate and have a characteristic everted edge and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin. When a SCC appears in a scar it is known as a Marjolin’s ulcer.

Surgical excision is the treatment of choice SCC. It provides both histological confirmation and complete clearance. The excision margins depend on tumor size:

* lesions <2 cm require a 4-mm margin,

* while those >2 cm need a 1-cm margin.

Other options:

Option B: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumor that originates from pluripotential epithelial cells of the basal epidermis and hair follicles, typically involving pilosebaceous skin.

Option C: Malignant Melanoma is a malignancy of melanocytes and may develop in the skin, mucous membranes, retina, or leptomeninges. There are four common macroscopic variants of malignant melanoma. It doesn’t present as an edged-out ulcer.

Option D: Keratoacanthoma presents with a reddish papule with a horny crust in the centre. It is a rapidly evolving tumour of the skin considered as a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.learning: Squamous Cell Carcinoma — The clinical description of a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on a sun-exposed site like the lateral nasal fold is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma(SCC).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An adult patient presents with a pulsatile swelling in the neck just below the angle of the jaw, exhibiting an outward expansile impulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A pulsatile neck swelling located at the carotid bifurcation (below the angle of the jaw) that exhibits an expansile impulse is classic for a Carotid Body Tumor (Option D). This is a highly vascular paraganglioma. A hallmark sign is that the swelling can be moved side-to-side but not up and down (Fontaine's sign), as it is fixed to the carotid artery. The provided angiography (Option DSA) demonstrates the pathognomonic "Lyre sign", where the tumor physically splays the internal and external carotid arteries apart. Grave's disease (Option A) involves generalized thyroid enlargement. Branchial cysts (Option B) and thymic cysts (Option C) are soft, non-pulsatile masses . Because the tumor is intensely vascular and intimately associated with the major neck arteries, it pulsates with the arterial pressure. Surgical excision is the treatment but carries a high risk of vascular or nerve injury
questions.learning: A pulsatile neck swelling located at the carotid bifurcation (below the angle of the jaw) that exhibits an expansile impulse is classic for a Carotid Body Tumor (Option D).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mechanism of carcinogenesis of UV radiation is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Formation of pyrimidine dimers

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation, particularly UV-B (280– 320 nm), causes DNA damage by inducing the formation of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers between adjacent pyrimidine bases. These dimers distort the DNA helix and interfere with DNA replication and transcription. If not repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway, they can result in mutations that promote skin carcinogenesis.

• Formation of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers is the primary mechanism by which UV radiation causes carcinogenesis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Activation of cyclins: Promotes cell cycle progression but is not the direct mechanism of UV-induced DNA damage.
• B. Degradation of TP53: Occurs with oncogenic viruses such as HPV (E6 protein), not UV radiation.
• D. Inhibition of NF-Κb: Not the primary mechanism of UV-induced carcinogenesis.
questions.learning: Formation of pyrimidine dimers Ultraviolet (UV) radiation, particularly UV-B (280– 320 nm), causes DNA damage by inducing the formation of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers between adjacent pyrimidine bases.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Anencephaly occurs due to failure of neural tube closure during which week of intrauterine development?
questions.explanation: Neural tube defects (NTDs) result from the failure of the neural tube to close properly during early embryogenesis. Anencephaly specifically occurs when the anterior (cranial) neuropore fails to close. This critical developmental event typically occurs between days 23 and 26 of gestation, which is during the 4th week of intrauterine life. The posterior neuropore closes slightly later, around day 28; its failure results in spina bifida. The 2nd week (Option D) involves implantation and the formation of the bilaminar disc. The 3rd week (Option A) is the period of gastrulation and the beginning of neurulation. The 5th week (Option C) is when organogenesis is already well underway. Because the neural tube closes so early—often before a woman even knows she is pregnant—folic acid supplementation must be started periconceptionally to be effective. Anencephaly is a lethal condition characterized by the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp
questions.learning: Neural tube defects (NTDs) result from the failure of the neural tube to close properly during early embryogenesis. Anencephaly specifically occurs when the anterior (cranial) neuropore fails to close.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A diabetic patient is diagnosed with proliferative diabetic retinopathy during routine screening. Laser photocoagulation is performed immediately to preserve vision and prevent blindness. This intervention is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Secondary prevention

Prompt treatment of an early diagnosed disease to prevent disability is secondary prevention.

Exam pearl:

• Treatment before disability → Secondary prevention.
• Rehabilitation after disability → Tertiary prevention.
questions.learning: Secondary prevention Prompt treatment of an early diagnosed disease to prevent disability is secondary prevention. Exam pearl: • Treatment before disability → Secondary prevention. • Rehabilitation after disability → Tertiary prevention.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, reducible swelling in the left inguinal region that appears on standing and disappears on lying down, with a positive cough impulse. Imaging confirms a left inguinal hernia. What is the most appropriate surgical treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: In an adult male with a reducible inguinal hernia, the standard surgical treatment is hernioplasty. This procedure involves the reduction of the hernia sac followed by a tension-free repair using a prosthetic mesh (like the Lichtenstein repair). Mesh repairs significantly reduce the risk of hernia recurrence compared to older suture-only techniques. Herniotomy (Option A), which is the simple excision of the hernia sac without strengthening the abdominal wall, is the standard treatment for congenital hernias in children but is insufficient for adults. "Wait and watch" (Option C) might be considered for completely asymptomatic patients, but surgical repair is generally recommended for fit young adults to prevent future complications like strangulation. Emergency laparotomy (Option D) is only indicated if the hernia is strangulated and there is evidence of bowel necrosis, which is not the case for this reducible, painless bulge. Therefore, scheduled mesh hernioplasty is the most appropriate definitive management
questions.learning: In an adult male with a reducible inguinal hernia, the standard surgical treatment is hernioplasty. This procedure involves the reduction of the hernia sac followed by a tension-free repair using a prosthetic mesh (like the Lichtenstein repair).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a normal distribution, the mean value is 82 and SD is 1.5. Calculate the range of 2 SD. SD-Standard deviation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 79 to 85

The range of 2 standard deviations for the given mean value is 79 to 85.

To determine the range within two standard deviations in a normal distribution, we use the formula:

Range= Mean ±2 × Standard Deviation (SD)

Given data: Mean = 82, Standard Deviation = 1.5.

2 SD = mean +/- 2 SD.

Calculation:
Lower limit=82−(2×1.5)=82−3=79.

Upper limit=82+(2×1.5)=82+3=85.

The range within two standard deviations is 79 to 85. This means approximately 95.4% of the values in a normal distribution fall within this range.

Pearl PF0301: Normal Distribution

* Normal distribution is the most widely used continuous distribution.

* It is also called bell curve (bell shaped) or Gaussian distribution after a mathematician named Karl Friedrich Gauss.

* The following is an image of three different types of normal distributions.

* Normal distributions are defined by two parameters: the mean and the standard deviation.

* The mean, median and mode are all equal in a normal distribution.

* All normal distributions are symmetric and have bell-shaped density curves with a single peak.

* Exactly half of the values are to the left of the centre and the other half to the right.

* The total area under the curve is 1.

* The density of a normal distribution is more around the centre and less around the tails.

* There is no skew in the curve.

* Looking at the figure below, we can understand the empirical rule of a normal distribution which states that:

* Approximately 68% of the distribution falls within one standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 1 SD).

* Approximately 95% of the distribution falls within two standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 2 SD).

* Approximately 99.7% of the distribution falls within three standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 3 SD).

* Many data like blood pressure, heights, IQ scores, etc. form a normal distribution.

* A standard normal distribution is a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: In patients with renal failure, which imaging technique is appropriate for visualizing vessels without causing further renal impairment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Time-of-flight MRI angiography

In patients with renal failure, non-contrast vascular imaging is preferred to avoid contrast-induced nephropathy (iodinated contrast in CT/DSA) and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (gadolinium in contrast MRI). Time-of-flight (TOF) MR angiography is a non-contrast technique that visualizes blood vessels using flow-related enhancement and is safest for evaluating vasculature in renal impairment.

Key Points:

• CT angiography & DSA: Use iodinated contrast → risk of contrast-induced nephropathy
• Contrast MRI angiography: Uses gadolinium → risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in renal failure
• TOF MR angiography: No contrast required → safest option
questions.learning: Time-of-flight MRI angiography — In patients with renal failure, non-contrast vascular imaging is preferred to avoid contrast-induced nephropathy (iodinated contrast in CT/DSA) and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (gadolinium in contrast MRI).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, neck rigidity and altered sensorium. The resident was instructed to perform a lumbar puncture on this patient. What is the correct order of managing this patient? 1. Place IV cannula and give fluids at 40 mL/h 2. Start injection ceftriaxone 3. Fundoscopy 4. Perform guarded lumbar puncture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3, 4, 2

In suspected acute bacterial meningitis, lumbar puncture must be performed safely after ruling out raised intracranial pressure to prevent brain herniation.

Correct sequence of management:

• Stabilize patient first → secure IV access and start fluids
• Fundoscopy → check for papilledema (sign of raised ICP)
• Guarded lumbar puncture → if no signs of raised ICP
• Start antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) immediately after CSF collection

Always rule out raised intracranial pressure before LP to avoid herniation.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4, 2 In suspected acute bacterial meningitis, lumbar puncture must be performed safely after ruling out raised intracranial pressure to prevent brain herniation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All are true about patients with trigeminal neuralgia except:
options: Pain along V2 and V3 division of trigeminal nerve
No objective signs of sensory loss
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deep seated pain

Trigeminal neuralgia is associated with superficial pain and not deep-seated pain.

It is more common (~ 60% of cases) in females (Option A) over 50 years and is characterized by unilateral lancinating facial pain. This most commonly involves the second and/or third divisions (Option B) of the trigeminal nerve territory. Bilateral or early-onset pain is associated with multiple sclerosis. Unilateral trigeminal nerve compression can be due to the superior cerebellar artery.

Pain is repetitive, severe, and brief and can be triggered by touch, cold, wind, or eating. Physical signs are usually absent, although the spasms may make the patient wince and sit silently (tic douloureux). No signs of sensory loss are present (Option D)

The drug of choice is carbamazepine.

Note: It is important to note that trigeminal neuralgia and trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia (TAC) are different entities. TAC is a group of primary headaches that include - cluster headaches, paroxysmal hemicrania, short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with conjunctival injection and tearing (SUNCT)/short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with cranial autonomic symptoms (SUNA), and hemicrania continua.
questions.learning: Deep seated pain Trigeminal neuralgia is associated with superficial pain and not deep-seated pain. It is more common (~ 60% of cases) in females (Option A) over 50 years and is characterized by unilateral lancinating facial pain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a post-transcriptional modification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glycosylation

Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification; it is a post-translational modification.

A primary transcript is the initial, linear, RNA copy of a transcription unit. The collection of all the primary transcripts synthesized in the nucleus by RNA polymerase II is known as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA). The pre-mRNA components of hnRNA undergo extensive co- and posttranscriptional modification in the nucleus and become mature mRNA. These modifications usually include the following :

• Addition of a 5′ cap - This is the first of the processing reactions for pre-mRNA. The cap is a 7-methylguanosine attached to the 5′ terminal end of the mRNA and is resistant to most nucleases. Creation of the cap requires the removal of the γ-phosphoryl group from the 5′ triphosphate of the pre-mRNA, followed by the addition of guanosine monophosphate. Methylation of this terminal G occurs in the cytosol and is catalyzed by guanine- 7-methyltransferase. Additional methylation steps may occur (options A and B).
• Addition of a 3′-poly-A tail - Most eukaryotic mRNA have a chain of 40 to 250 adenylates (adenosine monophosphates) attached to the 3′ end. This poly-A tail is added by the nuclear enzyme, polyadenylate polymerase. The poly-A tail terminates eukaryotic transcription. In addition, it helps stabilize the mRNA, facilitates its exit from the nucleus, and aids in translation.
• Splicing - Maturation of eukaryotic mRNA usually involves removal from the primary transcript of RNA sequences (introns) that do not code for protein (endonuclease cleavage). The remaining coding (expressed) sequences, the exons, are joined together to form the mature mRNA. The process of removing introns and joining exons is called splicing. The molecular complex that accomplishes these tasks is known as the spliceosome (option D).
questions.learning: Glycosylation Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification; it is a post-translational modification. A primary transcript is the initial, linear, RNA copy of a transcription unit.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents to the emergency department with a burn on his upper thigh extending to his leg. On examination, there is soddening of the skin. There is erythema, vesicles, and a line of demarcation. What type of burn is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Moist heat burn

Moist heat burns (scalds) are caused by hot liquids or steam

Characterised by : sodden (water-soaked) skin, erythema, vesicle (blister) formation, and well-defined margins.

Mechanism: Heat transfer via liquid → greater penetration → superficial to partial-thickness burns

• Skin appears soft, moist, and sodden (not dry or charred)
• Common sites: thighs, legs, trunk (due to accidental spillage)

Why this diagnosis:

• Sodden skin is the most distinguishing feature
• Presence of vesicles and erythema indicates partial-thickness injury
• Clear line of demarcation seen in scald injuries
questions.learning: Moist heat burn Moist heat burns (scalds) are caused by hot liquids or steam Characterised by : sodden (water-soaked) skin, erythema, vesicle (blister) formation, and well-defined margins.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. S phase

S phase is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle.

The replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time period during the cell cycle. This period is referred to as the synthetic or S phase. The S phase is separated from the mitotic, or M phase, by nonsynthetic periods referred to as gap 1 (G1) and gap 2 (G2) phases, occurring before and after the S phase, respectively. The cell prepares for DNA synthesis in G1, and for mitosis in G2.

The most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle is the G2-M phase. Cells in the G2 or M phase do not have time to repair DNA damage that occurs before they start to divide. This affects mitosis, leading to catastrophe.

Cells become gradually less sensitive to radiation in the G1 phase to the early S phase and are least sensitive in the late S phase.
questions.learning: S phase S phase is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle. The replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time period during the cell cycle.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient presented with headache, vomiting, and fever. Meningitis was suspected. While performing a lumbar puncture, which is the last structure you will pierce just before entering the lumbar cistern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arachnoid membrane

The arachnoid membrane is the last structure you will pierce while performing a lumbar puncture, just before entering the lumbar cistern.

Lumbar puncture is a diagnostic procedure done to obtain a sample of cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space. During the procedure, the following structures are pierced to reach the subarachnoid space, in the given order:

• Skin
• Subcutaneous tissue
• Supraspinous ligament
• Interspinous ligament
• Ligamentum flavum
• Dura mater
• Arachnoid membrane

Indications:

• Diagnosis of suspected meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage
• Spinal anesthesia and intrathecal administration of antibiotics/chemotherapy
• Therapeutic relief of pseudotumor cerebri, less frequently

Contraindications for lumbar puncture include:

• Thrombocytopenia or other bleeding diatheses (including anticoagulant therapy)
• Raised intracranial pressure
• Spinal epidural abscess
• Infection over the site

Site of the procedure:

In adults, the spinal cord ends at the level of the lower border of the L1 vertebra. Lumbar puncture is usually performed at L3-L4 space (below L1 vertebra) to avoid potential needle trauma to the spinal cord.

Technique:

The patient is usually placed in the lateral recumbent position. An alternative position is the sitting position, useful in obese patients to determine the midline. L3-L4 space is located by palpating the right and left posterior superior iliac crests and moving the fingers medially toward the spine at the same level.

A local anesthetic like 1% lidocaine is administered. A 22-gauge needle is advanced through the skin. In the lateral recumbent position, the bevel should face up, and in the sitting position, it should face to one side or the other, to avoid injury to the dural fibers. There is a loss of resistance as the needle enters the epidural space. Dura and then arachnoid are next pierced, to release CSF.
Complications following lumbar puncture:

Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a common post-procedure symptom. It occurs due to loss of CSF through the dura which causes traction on the pain-sensitive intracranial structures. The headache in PDPH is typically frontal or occipital. The smaller the needle used, the lesser the risk of PDPH.

Other complications include infections, bleeding, cerebral herniation, and radicular pain.

questions.learning: Arachnoid membrane — The arachnoid membrane is the last structure you will pierce while performing a lumbar puncture, just before entering the lumbar cistern.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: CSF shows abundant PMNs with low sugar and elevated proteins. Diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: Acute bacterial meningitis (ABM) is characterized by a specific set of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings: a predominance of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs), low glucose levels (due to consumption by bacteria and impaired transport), and significantly elevated protein levels (resulting from blood-brain barrier damage). Tubercular meningitis (Option B) typically presents with a lymphocytic predominance and very high protein levels, although PMNs may be seen early in the disease. Viral meningitis and encephalitis (Options C and D) generally show a lymphocytic predominance with normal or only slightly reduced glucose levels and mild protein elevation. The gross appearance of the CSF in ABM is often turbid or purulent, reflecting the high neutrophil count. Therefore, the provided laboratory values are the classic diagnostic signature for an acute bacterial etiology

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: IUCD can be inserted after delivery till?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 48 hrs

Postpartum IUCD insertion is safe within 10 minutes up to 48 hours after delivery. The period between 48 hours–6 weeks should be avoided due to highest expulsion risk. Insertion after 6 weeks is classified as interval IUCD placement.
questions.learning: 48 hrs Postpartum IUCD insertion is safe within 10 minutes up to 48 hours after delivery. The period between 48 hours–6 weeks should be avoided due to highest expulsion risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Melanosis coli, which occurs due to long-term consumption of stimulant laxatives, presents as brown discoloration of colonic mucosa due to deposition of which one of the following pigments?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lipofuscin

Melanosis coli is a benign, reversible pigmentation of the colonic mucosa caused by chronic use of stimulant laxatives, particularly anthraquinone-containing laxatives such as senna, cascara, and aloe.

Despite its name, the brown-black discoloration is not due to melanin. It results from accumulation of lipofuscin pigment within macrophages in the lamina propria following apoptosis of colonic epithelial cells induced by stimulant laxatives.

Why not the other options?

• A. Melanin: Incorrect. Despite the name melanosis coli, melanin is not deposited.
• B. Hemosiderin: Incorrect. Iron storage pigment seen after hemorrhage or iron overload, not in melanosis coli.
• D. Hemoglobin: Incorrect. Does not accumulate as a pigment in the colonic mucosa.
questions.learning: Lipofuscin Melanosis coli is a benign, reversible pigmentation of the colonic mucosa caused by chronic use of stimulant laxatives, particularly anthraquinone-containing laxatives such as senna, cascara, and aloe.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with diabetes undergoes stress testing. He walks for 7 minutes without chest pain. Peak heart rate is 132/min, BP increases from 95 to 112 mmHg. Which of the following parameters was most likely decreased during peak stress?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Total systemic vascular resistance

During exercise or stress testing, increased metabolic activity in skeletal muscles causes local vasodilation due to accumulation of metabolites (adenosine, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺).

Physiological changes during exercise:

• ↑ Heart rate
• ↑ Cardiac output
• ↑ Systolic blood pressure
• ↑ Venous return
• ↓ Total systemic vascular resistance (SVR) due to vasodilation in active muscles

Even though sympathetic tone increases, the metabolic vasodilation in skeletal muscles predominates, causing an overall decrease in SVR.
questions.learning: Total systemic vascular resistance During exercise or stress testing, increased metabolic activity in skeletal muscles causes local vasodilation due to accumulation of metabolites (adenosine, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic small bowel diarrhea and says that he is allergic to wheat. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy. Anti-endomysial antibodies and tTG IgA antibodies are positive. What is the diagnosis? tTG - tissue transglutaminase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Celiac sprue

Villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy together with a positive serological test for anti-endomysial antibodies and IgA anti-TTG antibodies suggests the diagnosis of celiac sprue.

Celiac disease is triggered by the ingestion of gluten, which is the major storage protein of wheat and similar grains. It usually affects the second portion of the duodenum or proximal jejunum. Antibodies associated with celiac disease are anti-gliadin antibodies, anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, and anti-endomysial antibodies.

The histopathology is characterized by villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial CD8+T lymphocytes. An increase in the number of intraepithelial lymphocytes is a sensitive marker of celiac disease, even in the absence of epithelial damage and villous atrophy. MARSH's Score is used to assess celiac disease histologically.

Dermatitis herpetiformis can occur in as many as 10% of patients.

The main stay of treatment is a gluten-free diet.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of prospective screening?
options: Cervical Pap smear in a 40 year old patient
Neonatal screening of a new-born baby for hypothyroidism
Screening of immigrants to a country
Urine for sugar screening in a 40 year old man
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Screening of immigrants to a country

Screening of immigrants to a country is an example of prospective screening.

Screening of disease is done to detect unrecognized disease or defect, in apparently healthy individuals, by means of rapidly applied tests, examinations, or other procedures.

The difference between prospective and prescriptive screening is given below:

Prospective screening
Prescriptive screening

Definition
People screened for others benefit
People screened solely for their own benefit

Essential purpose
Disease control
Case detection

Request for screening
Specific request from the authority
Request from physician

Example

• Immigrants for infectious diseases like tuberculosis syphilis, yellow fever, etc;
• HIV screening during antenatal visits, sex workers.
• Screening of blood donors.

• Neonatal screening for hypothyroidism.
• Pap smear for detection of cervical cancer.
• Testing of urine sugar for diabetes mellitus.

Note: Most common neonatal disease to be screened for is neonatal hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient has been brought with severe bleeding to your ER. His blood group is unknown. Fresh frozen plasma from which of the following blood groups can be given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. AB

Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) from AB blood group can be given to this patient as it is the universal plasma donor. AB plasma does not contain antibodies against antigens on RBCs of AB blood group.

O Rh-negative blood is the universal blood donor. It is used during emergency packed cell blood transfusion with an unknown blood group. It is preferred because it lacks the A and B and Rh antigens. Hence, it cannot be hemolyzed by anti-A, anti-B or anti-D antibodies in the recipient’s blood.
questions.learning: AB Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) from AB blood group can be given to this patient as it is the universal plasma donor. AB plasma does not contain antibodies against antigens on RBCs of AB blood group.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to pulmonary embolism: 1. Unexplained breathlessness is the most common symptom. 2. When congestive heart failure or pneumonia fail to improve despite standard medical treatment, occult pulmonary embolism should be considered. 3. Patients with high clinical likelihood of venous thromboembolism should first undergo D-dimer testing alone without obligatory imaging tests. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2 only

Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by obstruction of the pulmonary arteries, most commonly by thrombi originating from the deep veins of the lower limbs.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Unexplained breathlessness is the most common symptom: Correct. Unexplained dyspnoea (breathlessness) is the most common presenting symptom of pulmonary embolism.
• Statement 2. When congestive heart failure or pneumonia fail to improve despite standard medical treatment, occult pulmonary embolism should be considered: Correct. If congestive heart failure or pneumonia fails to improve despite appropriate treatment, occult pulmonary embolism should be suspected, especially in patients with risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
• Statement 3. Patients with high clinical likelihood of venous thromboembolism should first undergo D-dimer testing alone without obligatory imaging tests: Incorrect. In patients with a high clinical probability of PE, imaging (usually CT pulmonary angiography) should be performed promptly. D-dimer testing alone is not recommended, as a negative D-dimer cannot reliably exclude PE in high-risk patients.
questions.learning: 1 and 2 only Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by obstruction of the pulmonary arteries, most commonly by thrombi originating from the deep veins of the lower limbs.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 4-year- old boy presenting with a red rash on the cheeks that spreads to the trunk and limbs, accompanied by low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory symptoms, caused by a single-stranded DNA virus?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a "slapped-cheek" red rash followed by a generalized spread is the classic description of Erythema Infectiosum (also known as Fifth Disease). This condition is caused by Parvovirus B19. The question provides a definitive virological clue: the causative organism is a single-stranded DNA virus, which is the unique genomic classification of Parvoviruses. Scarlet fever (Option A) is caused by bacteria and presents with a "sandpaper" rash and strawberry tongue. Exanthema subitum (Option C), or Roseola, is caused by HHV-6 (double-stranded DNA) and features a high fever followed by a rash after the fever drops. Rubeola (Option D), or Measles, is an RNA virus presenting with Koplik spots and a more severe prodrome. Therefore, the specific genomic type and pathognomonic cheek rash confirm Erythema Infectiosum
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a "slapped-cheek" red rash followed by a generalized spread is the classic description of Erythema Infectiosum (also known as Fifth Disease).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions shown below has a false positive Barr body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Klinefelter's syndrome

A person with Klinefelter syndrome has an extra X chromosome and thus there is a false positive Barr body in this patient.

Barr body is the inactivated X chromosome in the cell which is peripherally situated as a darkly stained nodule, chromatin positive, and better seen in the epithelial cell nuclei. Male cells have only one X chromosome and are called chromatin negative as they do not have a Barr body. The total number of Barr bodies is given by the formula (X-1) as the inactivated X chromosome is seen as the Barr body.

Barr bodies are seen in 0-4% of genetic males (46XY) and 20-80% of genetic females (46XX and the most common sites for sampling for sex chromatin are Buccal mucosa, tooth pulp, and hair bulb.

In a normal male, there are no Barr bodies as the genotype is XY. Females are XX and thus have a Barr body in them.

Males with Klinefelter syndrome have XXY genotype and thus have a false positive Barr body while a female with Turner syndrome has XO and has no Barr body usually. Only in rare cases of mosaicism will Turner syndrome patients have a Barr body.

The image of a Barr body in a confocal microscope is shown below and is indicated by the arrow as the inactive X (Xi).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which adverse effect of Bleomycin is exacerbated by radiation exposure?
questions.explanation: Bleomycin is an antitumor antibiotic known for its dose-limiting pulmonary toxicity, which can manifest as interstitial pneumonitis or progressive pulmonary fibrosis. This risk is significantly exacerbated by concurrent or prior radiation exposure, a phenomenon sometimes called "radiation recall pneumonitis". The lung tissue is particularly vulnerable because it lacks significant levels of bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme responsible for inactivating the drug. Regarding other options, bleomycin has minimal impact on the gastrointestinal tract (Option B) and is not associated with significant neurotoxicity (Option C), unlike drugs like vincristine. It also lacks the significant hepatotoxicity (Option D) seen with many other chemotherapeutic agents. Cumulative doses exceeding 400 units and supplemental oxygen therapy also increase the risk of lung damage. Therefore, monitoring pulmonary function via is essential when combining bleomycin with radiation
questions.learning: Bleomycin is an antitumor antibiotic known for its dose-limiting pulmonary toxicity, which can manifest as interstitial pneumonitis or progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden onset of chest pain shooting to the neck and interscapular region. X-ray shows widened mediastinum. BP is 110/90 mmHg in the right upper limb and 160/100 mmHg in the left upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute aortic dissection

Sudden-onset severe chest pain, with a wide discrepancy in blood pressure between the two limbs, and a widened mediastinum on x-ray point towards a diagnosis of aortic dissection.

It is initiated by an intimal tear, which allows blood to penetrate into the medial layer, producing a cleavage plane (false lumen) between the inner two-thirds and outer one-third of the media. The true lumen is separated from the false lumen by an intimomedial flap.

Classification of aortic dissection:

Acute aortic dissection can be classified by the original DeBakey system, which is based on the location of the proximal tear and distal extent of the dissection flap, or the Stanford system, which is based only on the location of the proximal tear.

DeBakey
Stanford

Clinically, patients present with tearing chest/back pain associated with diaphoresis, syncope, weakness, and dyspnea or neurological manifestations.

On examination, unequal pulses or blood pressure in the extremities may be seen due to changes of flow in the true and false lumens. There can be hypertension or hypotension, loss of pulses, findings of aortic regurgitation, and pulmonary edema.

Imaging:

Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is the investigation of choice in a hemodynamically unstable patient. In hemodynamically stable patients, the diagnosis is established with a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The characteristic diagnostic finding is a double-lumen aorta. The image below shows aortic dissection in the thoracic aorta with the true lumen, as well as the false lumen. The true lumen is often the smaller of the two because of being compressed by the false lumen.

Acute coronary syndrome and acute pulmonary embolism may both present with sudden onset chest pain but widened mediastinum and blood pressure discrepancy make aortic dissection more likely. (Options A and B)

Both sudden onset chest pain and widened mediastinum may be seen in esophageal rupture but blood pressure discrepancy between the upper limbs makes aortic dissection more likely. (Option D)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 45-year-old man with a 2-year history of prediabetes presents for routine evaluation. He has gained weight over the past year and has a strong family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. His BMI is 32 kg/m², and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Laboratory evaluation shows fasting plasma glucose of 157 mg/dL and HbA1c of 7.4%. Serum creatinine is normal, and urine testing shows no detectable albuminuria. Which of the following renal changes is most likely present at this stage of disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased glomerular filtration rate

The earliest functional change in diabetic nephropathy is glomerular hyperfiltration, characterized by an increased GFR despite normal serum creatinine and absence of albuminuria. This occurs due to afferent arteriolar dilation mediated by altered tubuloglomerular feedback: increased proximal glucose and sodium reabsorption reduces sodium delivery to the macula densa, leading to decreased afferent arteriolar resistance and increased intraglomerular capillary pressure.

This phase precedes structural damage and is potentially reversible. Persistent hyperfiltration, however, leads to glomerular injury, basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and eventual microalbuminuria, marking progression of disease.

Why not other options?

A. Decreased intraglomerular capillary pressure → Incorrect; early diabetic nephropathy involves increased, not decreased pressure

B. Decreased peritubular capillary oncotic pressure → Not a defining feature of early diabetic kidney disease

C. Glomerular atrophy → Occurs in late-stage CKD, not early disease

D. Increased oncotic pressure in Bowman space → Seen when significant protein leaks into filtrate (i.e., later stages with proteinuria)
questions.learning: Increased glomerular filtration rate — The earliest functional change in diabetic nephropathy is glomerular hyperfiltration, characterized by an increased GFR despite normal serum creatinine and absence of albuminuria.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the narrowest part of the airway in the adult larynx?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glottis

In adults, the glottis (rima glottidis) is the narrowest part of the airway, formed by the space between the true vocal cords.

·    The glottis is the most critical site for airway resistance in adults.

·    It is the narrowest functional segment during normal respiration and phonation.

·    Any pathology at this level (edema, tumor, vocal cord paralysis) can significantly compromise the airway.

Clinical importance:

·   In intubation, the endotracheal tube size is determined based on the glottic opening.

·    Conditions like laryngeal edema or vocal cord lesions can rapidly lead to airway obstruction.

Contrast with pediatrics:

·    In children, the narrowest part is the subglottis (cricoid cartilage level), not the glottis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following tests is based on the principle that prior knowledge of the events/activity will influence the suspect’s reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Brain Mapping

Brain Mapping is based on the principle that if the suspect has prior knowledge of the event/activity being described it will reflect in the suspect’s brain wave responses.

It is a technique that measures recognition of familiar stimuli by measuring electrical brain wave responses(P300) to words, phrases, or pictures that are presented on a computer screen.

Truth serum : This is based on the principle, that at a point very close to unconsciousness, the subject will be mentally incapable of resisting questioning and will be incapable of lying.

Polygraph : It is based on the theory, that when a person lies in the answer to a question, if he/she experiences fear, the emotion of fear will result in certain physiological changes.

The physiological changes are commonly observed are :

1. Relative rise in blood pressure
2. Pulse rate increases
3. Slowing down of breathing/erratic breathing
4. Suppression of involuntary muscular movements
5. Increased activity of sweat glands
questions.learning: Brain Mapping Brain Mapping is based on the principle that if the suspect has prior knowledge of the event/activity being described it will reflect in the suspect’s brain wave responses.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to an ESI hospital for treatment. Under the ESI Act, he/she is treated under which benefit ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medical benefit

Under the ESI Act, medical benefit is not given as a cash benefit. It is provided in the form of consultations, investigations and treatment by means of the ESI hospitals or ESI dispensaries.

Pearl PF0292: ESI ACT, 1948

Employees State Insurance Act, 1948 (Revised)

Scope: It is applicable to all factories in India excluding

* Defense

* Railway

* Mines

Finance Contribution

* Employee – 0.75% of his daily wage

* Employer – 3.25% of the employees' daily wage

* Medical benefit – 1/8th by the state government and 7/8th by the ESI Corporation.

To the Employees

* Medical Benefit- no cash benefit, full medical care is provided.

* Sickness Benefit- is given at 70% of daily wage for a duration of 91 days in one year

* Extended sickness benefit – 80% of the daily wages for a duration of 2 years for 34 specified diseases

* Enhanced sickness benefit – at full wages for sterilization procedure for a duration of 7 days post-vasectomy and 14 days post tubectomy.

* Maternity Benefit – Benefit is payable at full wages for 26 weeks (6.5 months) for pregnancy, 6 weeks following a miscarriage, and 30 days for sickness arising out of pregnancy

* Dependance Benefit– is at 90% daily wages, lifelong for the spouse and parents and till the age of 18 years for any dependant's child, however, the benefit is withdrawn if the daughter is married earlier.

* Disablement Benefits – temporary disability – is as long as the person is disabled at 90% daily wages. Permanent disability – the lifetime pension

* Funeral Benefit – Rs.15,000/-

* Rehabilitation Benefit- on payment of Rs. 10, the insured person and his/her family continue to get medical treatment after permanent disablement or retirement.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which among the following is most radiosensitive?
options: Muscle AAns (A)Testis Radiosensitivity refers to the susceptibility of cells and tissues to the damaging effects of ionizing radiation. According to the Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau, cells that are rapidly dividing and poorly differentiated are the most radiosensitive. The testis, specifically the germinal epithelium responsible for spermatogenesis, is one of the most radiosensitive tissues in the body. Even low doses of radiation can cause temporary or permanent infertility. Bone (Option B) and muscle (Option D) are much more radio-resistant because their cells are highly differentiated and divide very slowly. Nerve tissue (Option C) is also highly radio-resistant, as neurons are non-dividing (post-mitotic) cells. Other highly radiosensitive tissues include the bone marrow, the lining of the gastrointestinal tract, and the ovaries. Understanding these differences is critical for planning radiotherapy treatments to ensure tumor control while minimizing long-term damage to vital, sensitive organs.
