questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A prokaryotic mRNA has a mutation in a specific sequence required for ribosomal binding, located upstream of the start codon. Translation initiation fails despite a normal AUG start codon. Which sequence is mutated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Shine-Dalgarno sequence

Shine-Dalgarno sequence is the prokaryotic ribosomal binding site, recognized by 16S rRNA of the small subunit — aligns the ribosome with the start codon for correct reading frame initiation. Kozak sequence is the eukaryotic equivalent.

| Feature | Prokaryotes | Eukaryotes

| ------- | ----------- | ----------

| Ribosome-binding sequence | Shine-Dalgarno | Kozak

| Recognized by | 16S rRNA | Small ribosomal subunit (40S) scanning

| Location | Upstream of start codon | Around start codon
questions.learning: Shine-Dalgarno sequence Shine-Dalgarno sequence is the prokaryotic ribosomal binding site, recognized by 16S rRNA of the small subunit — aligns the ribosome with the start codon for correct reading frame initiation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During his posting in the surgery department, an intern noticed that after a surgical procedure, the nursing staff placed used syringes (without needles) and IV fluid bottles in a separate tray. The tray was marked with a distinct logo that indicated the waste collected could be recycled. Which among the following logos will be seen on a trolley designated for this type of waste?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The logo seen on a trolley containing used syringes (without needles) and IV fluid bottles should be the recyclable logo, which is represented by “2” in the given image. This symbol indicates that the waste materials collected are suitable for reprocessing and recycling after appropriate disinfection and treatment.

Recyclable waste in healthcare, according to biomedical waste guidelines, includes items like IV fluid bottles, syringes without needles, plastic tubing, catheters, urine bag, vacutainers(needles removed) and gloves.

Other options:

Option A: Image 1 represents the Bio-hazard and is used for infectious and contaminated biomedical waste

Option C: Image 3 represents the Radiation hazard and is used for radioactive waste

Option D: Image 4 represents the Electrical hazard
questions.learning: 2 The logo seen on a trolley containing used syringes (without needles) and IV fluid bottles should be the recyclable logo, which is represented by “2” in the given image.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy undergoing combination chemotherapy for non-Hodgkin lymphoma presents on day 7 of his treatment cycle with dysuria, suprapubic pain, and frank hematuria. Urinalysis reveals numerous red blood cells with no evidence of infection. He is diagnosed with hemorrhagic cystitis. His current chemotherapy regimen includes the following agents. Which of the following drug is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ifosfamide

Hemorrhagic cystitis is a characteristic dose-limiting toxicity of ifosfamide (and cyclophosphamide), caused by the toxic metabolite acrolein, which directly injures the bladder urothelium. This complication is preventable with mesna, which binds and detoxifies acrolein in the urine, along with adequate hydration.

Why not the other options?

• B. Vincristine: Causes peripheral neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction (constipation), and SIADH; it is not associated with hemorrhagic cystitis.
• C. Methotrexate: Causes myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and nephrotoxicity (high doses); hemorrhagic cystitis is not a typical adverse effect.
• D. Doxorubicin: Causes dose-dependent cardiomyopathy, myelosuppression, and alopecia; cardiotoxicity is prevented with dexrazoxane, not mesna.
•
questions.learning: Ifosfamide Hemorrhagic cystitis is a characteristic dose-limiting toxicity of ifosfamide (and cyclophosphamide), caused by the toxic metabolite acrolein, which directly injures the bladder urothelium.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 50 year old male who was working in the dye industry with exposure to aniline dyes presented with bladder problems. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transitional cell carcinoma

Since the person has chronic exposure to dyes , especially aniline dyes the most probable cancer in this patient is transitional cell carcinoma or bladder cancer.

Bladder cancer is caused by aromatic amines, which are metabolised in the body and excreted in the urine. Bladder carcinoma is associated with aniline dye exposure – benzidine , b-naphthylamine ,auramine, magenta.

Risk factors for carcinoma bladder are:

* Transitional cell carcinoma:

* Cigarette smoking is the main etiological factor

* Occupational exposure to chemicals: Naphthyline, benzidine, acrolein, aniline dyes, hydrocarbons

* Dye, petroleum, rubber, leather and printing industry workers

* Schistosoma hematobium

* Drugs: phenacetin, chlornaphazine, cyclophosphamide

* Pelvic irradiation

* Squamous cell carcinoma:

* Bladder diverticula

* Chronic irritation: chronic UTI, long term indwelling catheters, urinary calculi

* Schistosoma hematobium

Pearl PF0897: Etiological Factors for Bladder Carcinoma

Cigarette smoking

Exposure to aryl amines, particularly 2-
naphthylamine and related compounds (e.g., in diesel exhaust, in paint products)

Schistosoma haematobium infestation

Long-term use of analgesics (phenacetin)

Heavy-dose long-term use of cyclophosphamide

Radiotherapy

Congenital bladder exstrophy

Inherited cancer syndromes:

• Lynch syndrome
• Heriditary retinoblastoma
• Costello syndrome

Acquired genetic mutations in FGFR3, HRAS, P53, RB genes.
questions.learning: Transitional cell carcinoma Since the person has chronic exposure to dyes , especially aniline dyes the most probable cancer in this patient is transitional cell carcinoma or bladder cancer.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Mutism and akinesis in a person who is aware of his surroundings and somewhat alert is best described as a feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stupor

Akinetic mutism is a feature of Stupor.

• In this condition , the patient is unable to initiate action and speech but appears awake and alert.
• There is severe reduction of relational function – speech and action.

Akinetic mutism is also seen in Schizophrenia with affective psychosis and dissociative states.

Stupor :

• Lesion at :

• Diencephalon
• Upper brain stem
• Frontal lobes
• Basal ganglia

• Locked In syndrome

Option A, Oneroid state

• Impaired consciousness.
• Marked emotional changes in response to visual hallucination.
• Patient lives as if in a dream state – occupational delirium.

Option B, Twilight state

• Abrupt onset of abnormal violent behavior
• Occurs in

• Epilepsy
• Alcoholism
• Brain trauma

Option D, Delirium

• Global impairment of consciousness and cognition.
questions.learning: Stupor Akinetic mutism is a feature of Stupor. • In this condition , the patient is unable to initiate action and speech but appears awake and alert. • There is severe reduction of relational function – speech and action.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Horrocks’ apparatus was used to find out the dose of bleaching powder required to disinfect the water in a well. The 3rd cup in the Horrocks’ apparatus showed the distinct blue colour. How much bleaching powder (good quality) will be required to disinfect the well, for every 455 litres of water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6 grams

The Horrocks apparatus is used to determine the approximate amount of bleaching powder required to disinfect a well.

• The 3rd cup showing a distinct blue colour indicates that the required dose corresponds to 3 g of bleaching powder per 455 L (100 gallons) of water in the standard Horrocks calculation.
• For good-quality bleaching powder, the calculated quantity is multiplied by 2.

Therefore:

3 g × 2 = 6 g per 455 L

Hence, the correct answer is (d) 6 grams.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The true statement among the following is _____
options: The dose of telmisartan should be reduced in renal failure but not in hepatic failure.
The dose of irbesartan should be reduced in case of mild-moderate hepatic failure and renal failure.
The dose of candesartan should be reduced in mild-moderate liver failure but not in renal failure.
Losartan acts as thromboxane A2 antagonist and inhibits platelet aggregation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Losartan acts as thromboxane A2 antagonist and inhibits platelet aggregation.

The true statement is losartan acts as a thromboxane A2 antagonist and inhibits platelet aggregation.

Losartan is a competitive angiotensin receptor antagonist. It binds to the AT1 receptor with high affinity. It is also a competitive antagonist of the thromboxane A2 receptor and attenuates platelet aggregation.

Losartan is the angiotensin receptor blocker used in the treatment of hypertension. Hyperkalemia is an important side effect of ARBs. It appears to be a safe and efficacious agent to lower serum uric acid levels in patients with hyperuricemia.

Other options:

Option A: The clearance of telmisartan is mainly by biliary secretion. The clearance is affected by hepatic insufficiency. The dose of telmisartan should be reduced in hepatic failure but not in renal failure.

Option B: Irbesartan is metabolized to glucuronide conjugate, and is cleared mainly by biliary excretion. The plasma clearance is unaffected by either renal or mild-to-moderate hepatic insufficiency. Hence, the dose need not be reduced in either of the cases.

Option C: The plasma clearance of candesartan is by biliary excretion and renal elimination. The clearance is affected by renal insufficiency. Hence, the dose should be reduced in case of renal failure and not in mild-moderate liver failure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following features is associated with vitamin A deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bitot spots

Bitot spots are triangular, pearly-white or yellowish, and foamy spots on the bulbar conjunctiva on either side of the cornea are associated with Vitamin A deficiency.

Option A: Pinguecula is a degenerative condition of the conjunctiva, characterized by the formation of a yellowish-white patch on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus. It usually presents as a triangular patch on the nasal side, with the triangle's apex commonly pointed away from the cornea.

Option C: Pterygium is a degenerative condition of the sub-conjunctival tissue. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory.  It is made up of three parts: a "cap" (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge), a head, and a body. It occurs due to exposure to radiation: UV-B. The most common site is nasal.

Option D: Stocker's line - deposition of iron on the advancing edge is seen in Pterygium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
An 18-year-old girl with short stature has primary amenorrhea and has not attained puberty yet. Identify the chromosomal defect as shown in the image.

AIS - Androgen insensitivity syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Turner's syndrome

The given karyotyping image shows a “45 XO” abnormality, which is seen in Turner's syndrome.

Clinical features of Turner's syndrome include short stature, low posterior hairline, broad chest, widely spaced nipples, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, cubitus valgus, and pigmented nevi.

Turner's syndrome is the most common sex chromosome abnormality in females. The classical karyotype is 45, XO. Other variants have structural abnormalities of X chromosomes or mosaic patterns. Some patients may present during infancy. They mainly present with oedema of the dorsum of the hand and foot due to lymphatic stasis. The most important cause of increased mortality in children with Turner's syndrome is cardiac abnormalities.

Turner's syndrome is a common cause of primary amenorrhea. During embryogenesis, fetal ovaries develop normally and the absence of a second X chromosome leads to accelerated loss of normally formed oocytes. This gets completed by the age of 2. The ovaries are reduced to atrophic fibrous bands without ova and follicles. These are called streak ovaries.

At puberty, they fail to develop secondary sexual characteristics.

Other options:

Option B: Eunuchoid body habitus with abnormally long legs is usually seen in Klinefelter Syndrome (47, XXY). The image below shows the clinical features and karyotyping of Klinefelter Syndrome respectively. Note the two X and one Y chromosomes.

Option C : Kallman's syndrome is a hypothalamic disorder that occurs due to defective gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).

It is mainly associated with anosmia or hyposmia or hypoplasia. Other associated features such as colour blindness, optic atrophy, deafness, cleft palate, renal abnormalities, and cryptorchidism may be present.

Option D : Androgen insensitivity syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder in which the androgen receptors are absent, scanty, or fail to respond to testosterone. In complete AIS, the individual is born as a phenotypically normal female but generally presents with primary amenorrhea.

The external genitalia appears normal, with absent or scant pubic and axillary hair. The vagina is shortened and blind-ending with an absent uterus and ovaries. These patients may also present with a history of childhood inguinal hernias, due to the presence of undescended testis in the abdomen or in the inguinal canal. Due to the constant conversion of testosterone into estrogen, these individuals have normal breast development.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 7 year old child is brought to the clinic with complaints of fatigue and poor concentration. The mother reports that the child has been eating non-food items such as soil and paint chips for the past few months. A peripheral blood smear image shows microcytic, hypochromatic red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iron deficiency anemia

The above clinical scenario of a child with fatigue, poor concentration, and a history of pica (eating soil and paint chips) presents with a peripheral smear showing small RBC with increased central pallor with no basophilic stippling( helps rule out lead poisoning) demonstrates classical features of Iron deficiency anemia(IDA).

The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement, and increased blood loss.

The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorption and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials)

Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA.

Laboratory findings of IDA are:

* Reduced hemoglobin and hematocrit values. hypochromia, microcytosis, and poikilocytosis.

* Serum iron and ferritin levels are low.

* The total plasma iron-binding capacity, which reflects the elevated transferrin level, is high.

* Low serum iron with increased iron-binding capacity results in a reduction of transferrin saturation to below 15%.

* RBC protoporphyrin levels are increased.

* Bone marrow reveals a mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. The absence of stainable iron in macrophages is a diagnostically significant finding

Option A: In Vitamin B12 deficiency, patients usually present with larger than normal RBC, no history of Pica, hypersegmented neutrophils (image below) and Macrocytes on PBS.

Option B: Thalassemia Major generally presents in infancy, with Microcytic hypochromic anemia as well, requiring multiple blood transfusions, it is a hereditary hemoglobinopathy resulting from deficient synthesis of one or more globin chains. Differentiating IDA and Thalassemia: Both conditions present with microcytosis and anisocytosis, with the Mentzer index being less than 13 (MCV/RBC).

Option C: Lead poisoning causes dry throat, burning abdominal pain, peripheral circulatory collapse, insomnia, paraesthesias, depression, coma, and death. Cerebellar ataxia is common in children with acute lead poisoning. A screening test for lead poisoning is the presence of porphyrinuria, mainly due to coproporphyrin III. Peripheral smear shows basophilic stippling. A Burtonian line may be visible on the gums.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with dyspnoea on exertion has been found to have a single second heart sound and a loud diamond-shaped, rough quality systolic murmur best heard at the right 2nd intercostal space, radiating to the right carotid artery. Which one of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aortic stenosis

Key clinical features of aortic stenosis:

• Murmur: Harsh, crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur (diamond-shaped)
• Best heard: Right 2nd intercostal space.
• Radiation: Carotid arteries.
• S2: Soft or single in severe disease.
• Symptoms (classic triad):

• Angina
• Syncope (especially on exertion)
• Dyspnoea/heart failure

• Pulse: Slow-rising, low-volume pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus).

Why not the other options?

• A. Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA): Continuous “machinery” murmur in the left infraclavicular area.
• B. Ventricular septal defect (VSD): Harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
• D. Pulmonary stenosis: Ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, radiating to the left shoulder/back.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common location of implantation in ectopic pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A

The most common location of implantation in ectopic pregnancy is the tubal ampulla, which is labelled as A in the image.

In the given image-

B-Isthmus

C- Fimbrae

D- Infundibulum

Almost 95% of ectopic pregnancies implant within the fallopian tube. Within the fallopian tube, the ampulla is the most commonly affected location in 70% of the cases. The remaining implant is in the isthmus (12%), fimbria (11%), and interstitial tube (2%).

The other implantation sites are the ovary, peritoneal cavity, cervix, or prior cesarean scar.

Patients usually present with rupture of ectopic pregnancy with the triad of the delayed menstrual cycle, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding.

The examination may reveal abdominal tenderness, pain in cervical motion, a bulging posterior vaginal fornix, boggy mass next to the uterus. Vaginal bleeding or spotting may be present. Ruptured ectopic will lead to intraabdominal hemorrhage leading to reciprocal changes in vital signs.

Investigations used to diagnose ectopic pregnancy include a positive beta-human chorionic gonadotropin to diagnose a pregnancy. Transvaginal ultrasound can be used to identify the gestational sac or determine if the case is a pregnancy of an unknown location. In an ectopic pregnancy, the endometrial stripe will appear as a trilaminar pattern and anechoic fluid collections may be present.

Medical management of ectopic pregnancy involves the use of methotrexate. Surgical management depends on whether the patient is hemodynamically stable, and whether she desires future fertility (salpingectomy versus salpingostomy). For a ruptured ectopic, only salpingectomy can be done.

* Hemodynamically stable - laparoscopically done

* Hemodynamically unstable - laparotomy is done

Pearl PF1615: Fallopian tube

Gross anatomy:

The fallopian tube is divided into the following parts:

* Intramural/Interstitial portion:

* Intrauterine

* The narrowest and shortest part

* Isthmus:

* The most common site for tubectomy

* Ampulla:

* The longest part

* The most common site for - fertilization and ectopic pregnancy

* Infundibulum:

* The widest part

Histology:

The ampulla, isthmus and infundibulum are extrauterine. They're covered by three layers:

* Mesosalpinx - It is the peritoneal layer. Also called serosa.

* Myosalpinx - It contains smooth muscle and has 2 layers:

* Inner circular

* Outer longitudinal

* Endosalpinx - It is the mucosal layer. It has the following features:

* Numerous branching folds, filling the entire lumen

* Basement membrane

* Ciliated, columnar epithelium

* Peg cells - non-ciliated epithelium. They help in the capacitation of sperms.

questions.text: A drug solution containing 500 mg/5 ml of the drug is given to you. You are provided with a 2 ml syringe (having 10 divisions for each ml). How many divisions of the 2 ml syringe need to be administered to deliver 180 mg of the drug to a patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 18

Concentration of drug solution given = 500/5 ml or 100 mg/ml

-> 100 mg of drug in 1ml

i.e 180 mg of drug in "X" ml

-> X = 180/100 = 1.8 ml

So, 1.8 ml of the drug with 180 mg of the drug is to be given to the patient.

In the 2 ml syringe provided, each ml has 10 divisions i.e. each division corresponds to 0.1 ml.

So, for delivering 1.8 ml, 1.8/0.1= 18 divisions need to be administered.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident and is diagnosed with an injury to the bulbar urethra. Where is urine most likely to collect as a result of this injury?
questions.explanation: In cases of a traumatic rupture of the bulbar urethra, particularly when Buck's fascia is also torn, urine extravasates into the superficial perineal pouch. Due to the anatomical attachments of Colles' fascia, the extravasated urine is restricted posteriorly by its attachment to the perineal membrane and laterally by its attachment to the ischiopubic rami. However, Colles' fascia is continuous anteriorly with Scarpa's fascia of the abdominal wall. This allows the urine to track upward into the scrotum, penis, and eventually the anterior abdominal wall. Urine cannot enter the ischiorectal fossa (Option C) because it is a separate anatomical compartment. It does not enter the peritoneal cavity (Option B) as the injury is extraperitoneal. The inguinal pouch (Option A) is not a standard site for extravasation in this specific urethral injury pattern. Thus, the characteristic clinical sign of bulbar urethral trauma is swelling that spreads from the perineum toward the abdomen
questions.learning: In cases of a traumatic rupture of the bulbar urethra, particularly when Buck's fascia is also torn, urine extravasates into the superficial perineal pouch.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is brought after a road traffic accident and imaging reveals the fracture shown. What type of fracture is this?
questions.explanation: The X-ray depicts a fracture occurring in the region between the greater and lesser trochanters of the proximal femur. This is an intertrochanteric fracture, which is extra-capsular in nature. Because it is outside the hip joint capsule, the blood supply to the femoral head remains relatively well-preserved, leading to a much lower risk of avascular necrosis compared to neck fractures. Subtrochanteric fractures (Option A) occur below the lesser trochanter in the femoral shaft. Femoral neck fractures (Option C) occur superior to the trochanters and within the joint capsule (intracapsular). Pubic rami fractures (Option D) involve the pelvic ring and not the femur itself. Intertrochanteric fractures are often comminuted and result from high-energy trauma in young patients or simple falls in the elderly. Based on the specific bony landmarks, the diagnosis is confirmed

options: Causes the enzyme to work faster only.

Correct answer: D. Participates in feedback regulation

An allosteric modifier of an enzyme usually participates in feedback regulation.

Allosteric regulations are a natural example of control loops, such as feedback from downstream products or feedforward from upstream substrates. Allosteric regulation is also particularly important in the cell's ability to adjust enzyme activity.

An allosteric modifier or effector binds to the allosteric site to induce a conformational change in the catalytic or active site. Those modifiers or effectors that enhance the protein's activity are referred to as allosteric activators, whereas those that decrease the protein's activity are called allosteric inhibitors.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: You are in the operating room and notice the tracing in yellow color on this device. What does it indicate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Capnography

The reading marked as X in the monitor is the capnography.

Waveform capnography is a continuous non-invasive measurement and graphical display of the EtCO2.

It is a direct measure of lung ventilation and an indirect measure of circulation and metabolism.

The normal capnograph displays the exhaled CO2 in both inspiratory and expiratory phases. The expiratory phase is divided into three distinct components:

• Phase I: exhalation of dead space gas (i.e., partial pressure of CO2, pCO2 ∼0).
• Phase II: A sharp rise in pCO2 to a plateauindicates the sampling of transitional gas between the airways and alveoli.
• Phase III: The plateau region of the capnograph, corresponds to the pCO2 in the alveolar compartment.
• Following phase III, a sharp inspiratory downstroke occurs, which is referred to as the beginning of phase 0 or phase IV by some.
questions.learning: Capnography — The reading marked as X in the monitor is the capnography. Waveform capnography is a continuous non-invasive measurement and graphical display of the EtCO2.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 20-year-old boy complains of swelling and severe pain in his right ear associated with high-grade fever and profuse ear discharge. Clinical examination shows mastoid tenderness and perforation of the tympanic membrane. On examination, the swelling extends anteriorly to the right zygoma with a punctum over the right tragus, as shown below. Which type of abscess is most likely indicated in this area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Luc's abscess

Luc's abscess is most likely indicated in the given clinical vignette.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of acute mastoiditis that has occurred as a complication of acute infection of the middle ear. If the pus in this infection breaks through the bony wall between the antrum and external osseous meatus, it results in the formation of a Luc abscess (meatal abscess) and presents as a swelling in the deep part of the bony meatus.

Other abscesses related to mastoid infection:

* Postauricular abscess—the most common abscess that forms over the mastoid. In infants and children, this presents over MacEwen’s triangle.

* Zygomatic abscess—infection of the zygomatic air cells. It is situated at the posterior root of the zygoma

* Bezold abscess—In this case, the pus breaks through the medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck

* Citelli’s abscess—Here, the abscess is formed posterior to the mastoid, occupying a position more towards the occipital bone

questions.text: The image below shows the insertion of transversus abdominis muscle. Identify the conjoint tendon:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C

The structure marked C is the conjoint tendon.

The conjoint tendon is formed from the lower fibres of internal oblique and the lower part of the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis. It is attached to the pubic crest and extends to a variable extent along the pectineal line.

Transversus Abdominis muscle

Origin: internal surface of 7th -12th costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, connective tissue deep to lateral third of inguinal ligament.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following true regarding benzodiazepines and barbiturates: 1. Both act on GABA-A chloride channel 2. Alcohol causes superadded CNS depression 3. Flumazenil reverses the action of both 4. Thiopentone has short duration of action due to its rapid metabolism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both 1 and 2 are correct

Benzodiazepines and barbiturates both act on the GABA-A chloride channel, and alcohol produces additive CNS depression with them.

Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines only, not barbiturates, it is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site on GABA-A receptors.

Thiopentone’s short action is due to redistribution, not rapid metabolism, it moves quickly from brain → muscle → fat.

Metabolism is actually slower. Therefore, statements 1 and 2 are correct.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct about ectopic ureters? 1. They are more common in males. 2. They drain the upper pole of kidney. 3. They are associated with duplex ureter. 4. They may cause incontinence. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Ectopic ureters are more common in females and are usually associated with a duplex collecting system. According to the Weigert-Meyer rule, the upper pole ureter is the one that inserts ectopically and may open below the external urethral sphincter, causing continuous urinary incontinence.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. They are more common in males: Incorrect. They are more common in females.
• 2. They drain the upper pole of the kidney: Correct.
• 3. They are associated with duplex ureter: Correct.
• 4. They may cause incontinence: Correct, especially in females.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old female undergoes emergency laparotomy. Which of the following is the surest sign of wound dehiscence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Copious sero-sanguinous discharge

The surest sign of wound dehiscence is copious serosanguinous discharge.

Burst abdomen/Acute wound dehiscence is the mechanical wound failure causing separation of the closed abdominal wound associated with abdominal content evisceration. It usually occurs between the 5th and 8th postoperative days.

A sudden giving way feeling from the wound precipitated by bouts of cough, and pinkish serosanguinous discharge can be seen. Omentum or coils of the intestine are forced out of the wound.

Management includes delayed closure with initial mesh wrap or Bogota bag, placing a subcutaneous drain, suitable antibiotic therapy, and prevention of abdominal compartment syndrome as described above.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: When the serum ascites to albumin gradient (SAAG) is less than 1.1 gm/dL, then which of the following causes of ascites may be considered? 1. Infection 2. Malignancy 3. Cardiac ascites 4. Portal hypertension Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2 only

The Serum–Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) is the preferred test for determining whether ascites is due to portal hypertension. It is calculated as:

• SAAG = Serum albumin − Ascitic fluid albumin

Interpretation:

• SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL: Indicates portal hypertension (≈97% accuracy).
• SAAG <1.1 g/dL: Indicates ascites not caused by portal hypertension.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Infection: Correct. Infections (e.g., tuberculous peritonitis) typically produce low-SAAG ascites.
• Statement 2. Malignancy: Correct. Peritoneal malignancy (malignant ascites) is a classic cause of low-SAAG ascites.
• Statement 3. Cardiac ascites: Incorrect. Cardiac ascites is caused by elevated venous pressure and produces high-SAAG ascites (≥1.1 g/dL).
• Statement 4. Portal hypertension: Incorrect. Portal hypertension (e.g., cirrhosis) is the prototypical cause of high-SAAG ascites.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A child with a history of night-blindness presented to you with the following findings. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phrynoderma

A child having night-blindness, and multiple keratotic papules on elbows as shown in the image suggests a diagnosis of phrynoderma or toad-skin. This can occur due to the deficiency of vitamin A.

Phrynoderma is not specific to vitamin A deficiency. It may also be associated with deficiencies of B complex, riboflavin, vitamin C, vitamin E, and essential fatty acids. It manifests as groups of papules with a central keratotic plug. The commonest sites are elbows and knees. They are present around the follicles and give the skin a rough texture. Treatment involves the correction of poor diet and administration of a multivitamin preparation containing vitamin A.

Option B: Keratosis pilaris is an inherited abnormality of keratinization. It affects the follicular orifices leading to keratotic follicular plugging, perifollicular erythema, and follicular atrophy. It usually presents during puberty. They present as small, keratotic papules on the extensor aspects of the limbs, particularly the arms which can lead to ingrowing of the hair. Treatment is purely reserved for cosmetic purposes.

Option C: Darier disease is an autosomal dominant genodermatosis characterized by keratotic papules that show acantholysis and dyskeratosis. ATP2A2 gene mutations are present in Darier disease. Histologically, acantholysis (separation of keratinocytes) and blistering are seen in the suprabasal epidermis.

It presents with discrete or confluent rough, greasy, skin-colored papules in seborrheic areas (trunk, face scalp margins) and flexures (perineum, axillae, groin). There may also be isolated nipple hyperkeratosis. Nail findings include fragility, painful longitudinal splits, or distinctive red and white longitudinal bands terminating in V-shaped nicks.

Option D: Follicular eczema is a form of atopic dermatitis that presents with a discoid patch formed due to the coalescence of the follicular lesions with peripheral excoriation marks. The biopsy shows spongiotic dermatitis.
questions.learning: Phrynoderma — A child having night-blindness, and multiple keratotic papules on elbows as shown in the image suggests a diagnosis of phrynoderma or toad-skin.

The laproscopic image above depicts multiple miliary nodules on the uterine and peritoneal surfaces. This guides us towards the diagnosis of female genital tuberculosis (FGTB).

Genital Tuberculosis is caused by M. tuberculosis and almost always occurs secondary to primary infection elsewhere in the extragenital states. Most common route of spread is hematogenous and the most common site is bilateral fallopian tubes (the most common part affected is ampulla and most common pathology encountered is endosalpingitis). 20-30 years age group is affected the most. Infertility is the most common symptom.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male presents with a one-hour history of sudden-onset chest pain. His ECG shows ST- segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. In a multispecialty hospital setting, what is the most appropriate treatment for this case of inferior wall myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with an acute Inferior Wall ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI). In a multi-specialty hospital (which implies the presence of a cardiac catheterization lab), the best (gold-standard) treatment is Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) or Primary Angioplasty. Primary angioplasty is superior to thrombolysis (Option A and B) because it achieves higher reperfusion rates and lower rates of re-occlusion and intracranial hemorrhage. Thrombolytic agents like Alteplase or Streptokinase are only preferred if PCI cannot be performed within 90-120 minutes of first medical contact. Dabigatran (Option D) is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor used for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, not for the acute management of a myocardial infarction. Inferior wall MIs are usually due to Right Coronary Artery occlusion. Immediate mechanical reperfusion is the most effective way to salvage the myocardium and improve patient outcomes

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy is diagnosed with cryptorchidism, and the condition has not resolved spontaneously after a period of observation. Which medication is appropriate for the medical management of this condition?
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) requires management to prevent infertility and reduce the risk of malignancy. While surgery is the primary treatment, hormonal therapy can be considered for cases where the testis is palpable and low in the inguinal canal. Pulsatile administration of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) (Option A) mimics the natural physiological rhythm, stimulating the pituitary to release LH and FSH, which in turn causes the Leydig cells in the testis to produce testosterone. This localized rise in testosterone can facilitate the descent of the testis into the scrotum. Non-pulsatile GnRH (Option B) actually suppresses the pituitary-gonadal axis and is used to treat precocious puberty. Direct testosterone (Option C) or estrogen (Option D) are not appropriate for inducing testicular descent. Hormonal therapy success is generally limited to about 15-20% of cases. If no descent occurs by age 1 or after a hormonal trial, surgical orchidopexy is mandatory to secure the testis in the scrotum
questions.learning: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) requires management to prevent infertility and reduce the risk of malignancy. While surgery is the primary treatment, hormonal therapy can be considered for cases where the testis is palpable and low in the inguinal canal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true for non-parametric tests?
options: ANOVA is an example of a non parametric test
It is used for skewed distributions
It involves the assumption that the data has a normal distribution
It cannot be used for small sample sizes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is used for skewed distributions

Non-parametric tests are tests that do not assume that the data is normally distributed. Thus, they are used for skewed (asymmetric) distributions {skewed either to the lesser side (left-sided skewed) or towards the greater side (right-sided skewed)}.

The chi-square test is an example of a non-parametric test that is used to test hypotheses in relation to nominal scale data or categorical data.

ANOVA is an example of a parametric test.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A psychiatric patient was started on lithium for the management of bipolar disorder. To monitor the blood lithium levels, at what time interval should the blood sample be collected after the administration of lithium tablets?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. After 12 hours

The blood sample for serum lithium estimation is to be collected after a time interval of 10-12 hours from the previous dose of lithium.

Lithium is used in the management of bipolar disorder, mania, and has anti-suicidal properties. It has a narrow therapeutic index, and blood levels in excess of this may cause symptoms of toxicity. Therapeutic drug monitoring is done by measuring trough lithium levels 12 hours after the previous dose, at least 5 days after the initiation of the treatment with lithium.
questions.learning: After 12 hours — The blood sample for serum lithium estimation is to be collected after a time interval of 10-12 hours from the previous dose of lithium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which part of the placenta is attached to the maternal body?
questions.explanation: The placenta is a feto-maternal organ. The maternal part of the placenta is the Decidua basalis, which is the specific portion of the modified endometrium that lies directly beneath the site of implantation and is firmly attached to the maternal body (the uterine wall). The Decidua parietalis (Option A) lines the remainder of the uterine cavity. The Chorionic plate (Option C) is the fetal surface of the placenta, from which the umbilical cord originates and the placental vessels branch. The Spiral arteries (Option D) are the maternal vessels that supply blood to the intervillous spaces but are not a "part" of the placental structure itself. This placental-decidual interface is where the critical exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste occurs. Abnormalities in this attachment lead to serious complications: placenta accreta occurs when the placenta attaches too deeply into the myometrium, and abruptio placenta occurs when the decidua basalis prematurely separates from the uterine wall

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of pressure epiphysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Head of femur

Epiphyses are classified based on their function and role in bone development. One important type is the pressure epiphysis, which is involved in weight transmission and articulation at joints.

Pressure Epiphysis:

• Located at articular ends of long bones.
• Transmits body weight and mechanical pressure across joints.
• Usually covered by articular cartilage.
• Develops secondary ossification centers.

Example: Head of femur – articulates with the acetabulum and transmits body weight at the hip joint.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Tubercles of humerus → Traction epiphysis (site of muscle attachment).
• Coracoid process of scapula → Atavistic epiphysis (represents a bone that was separate in lower animals).
• Trochanters of femur → Traction epiphysis (muscle attachment sites).
questions.learning: Head of femur Epiphyses are classified based on their function and role in bone development. One important type is the pressure epiphysis, which is involved in weight transmission and articulation at joints.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl presents with multiple small skin colored papules with central umbilication over the trunk and face. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Molluscum Contagiosum

The given clinical vignette of multiple small skin colored papules with central umbilication over the trunk and face is suggestive of infection with Molluscum Contagiosum.

It belongs to the Family Pox virus and is transmitted via autoinoculation, sexual or nonsexual contact. The condition is usually self-limiting, but treatment is required for non-resolving symptomatic lesions. Incubation period is 2 weeks - 6 months.

The age of peak incidence is between 2 and 5 years. In children, it is mainly caused by the type I molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV-1). There is a relatively higher incidence of MCV‐2 type in adults and HIV infection. Sexually transmitted molluscum contagiosum may be present over the genital area.

The lesions are shiny, pearly white, hemispherical, umbilicated papules that may show a central pore. These may enlarge slowly. Widespread and refractory lesions are seen most commonly in HIV or patients on immunosuppressive therapy.

Intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies called Henderson-Patterson bodies are seen. There are eosinophilic and are also called molluscum bodies.

Pseudo-Koebner phenomenon is seen i.e., new lesions develop along a line of trauma.

The diagnosis is usually clear when multiple lesions at different stages of evolution are seen and the classical umbilicated papule is observed. Diagnosis can be confirmed by direct microscopy, histopathology, or molecular analysis.

Treatment is usually not required, and lesions are likely to resolve spontaneously. Stimulation of the immune response can be done after destructive or inflammatory therapies with salicylic acid, trichloroacetic acid, and imiquimod. Cryotherapy when done needs to be repeated at 3-4 week intervals. Extensive lesions are treated with an antiviral agent like cidofovir.

The image below shows a characteristic lesion of Molluscum Contagiosum.

Option A: Impetigo contagiosa is a type of bacterial skin infection, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes. It presents as honey-colored crusts.

Option C: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, intensely pruritic, skin condition associated with Celiac disease. It includes intensely pruritic inflammatory papules and vesicles on the forearms, knees, scalp, or buttocks.

Option D: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular and proliferative infection caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana. It mainly occurs in immunocompromised individuals.  It is the second-most-common cause of angiomatous skin lesions in persons infected with HIV.
questions.learning: Molluscum Contagiosum — The given clinical vignette of multiple small skin colored papules with central umbilication over the trunk and face is suggestive of infection with Molluscum Contagiosum.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Thickest portion of sclera is -
questions.explanation: The sclera is the tough, fibrous outer coat of the eye that maintains its shape and protects internal structures. Its thickness varies significantly throughout the globe. The sclera is thickest at the posterior pole, near the optic nerve head, where it measures approximately 1.0 mm. Conversely, it is thinnest at the points just posterior to the insertions of the extraocular rectus muscles (Option B), where it can be as thin as 0.3 mm. This thinness makes the areas behind the muscle insertions particularly vulnerable to rupture during trauma or perforation during surgical procedures like strabismus surgery. The thickness anterior to the rectus insertions (Option A) is intermediate, roughly 0.6 mm. The "anterior pole" (Option D) refers to the center of the cornea; the sclera itself begins at the limbus. Understanding these anatomical variations is critical for surgeons to avoid accidental globe penetration and for clinicians assessing the severity of ocular injuries. Therefore, the posterior pole is the thickest region of the scleral shell
questions.learning: The sclera is the tough, fibrous outer coat of the eye that maintains its shape and protects internal structures. Its thickness varies significantly throughout the globe.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A pulmonary function test shows a Tiffeneau–Pinelli index of less than 0.70. This finding is diagnostic of which of the following lung diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obstructive lung disease

The Tiffeneau–Pinelli index is the ratio FEV₁ / FVC used to assess airflow limitation.

• Normal: ≥ 0.70–0.80
• < 0.70: Indicates airflow obstruction

Seen in obstructive lung diseases:

• COPD
• Asthma
• Bronchiectasis
• Emphysema

In obstruction, FEV₁ decreases more than FVC due to difficulty expelling air rapidly.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32 year old primigravida with chronic hypertension came to the hospital at 36 weeks of gestation with headache and blurring vision. Her BP is 170/110 mm Hg. Urine analysis reveals urine albumin 3+. What is the next step to be done?
options: Injection labetalol and magnesium sulphate and expedite the delivery
Injection labetalol , antenatal steroids and immediate termination of pregnancy
Injection labetalol and magnesium sulphate and deliver at 37 weeks
Injection labetalol to control her blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Injection labetalol and magnesium sulphate and expedite the delivery

The given scenario is suggestive of chronic hypertension with superimposed severe pre-eclampsia. The next step in the management is to give injection labetalol, and magnesium sulfate and expedite the delivery, irrespective of the duration of gestation.

The criteria for diagnosis of superimposed pre-eclampsia are :

• New onset proteinuria
• Aggravation of hypertension
• Development of HELLP syndrome
• Development of headache, scotoma, and epigastric pain.

Pre-eclampsia is further divided into :

• Nonsevere pre-eclampsia: Blood pressure >140/90 mmHg but <160/110 mmHg without significant proteinuria
• Severe pre-eclampsia: Persistent increase of systolic blood pressure above 160 mmHg or diastolic above 110 mmHg, proteinuria, oliguria (<400 mL in 24 hours), platelet count <1 lakh/cu.mm, serum creatinine level of >1.1 mg/dL, persistent severe epigastric pain, marked elevation of liver enzyme levels, convulsions or visual disturbances, intrauterine growth restriction of the fetus, and pulmonary edema.

In a patient with severe pre-eclampsia, ie, systolic BP ≥ 160 mm Hg or diastolic ≥ 110 mm Hg, immediate delivery after single-dose steroids is indicated regardless of the period of gestation. Concurrently, injection labetalol is given to reduce the blood pressure and injection magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis.

Patients with pre-eclampsia may be expectantly managed up to 34 weeks of gestation. After 34 weeks pregnancy, may be prolonged up to 37 weeks if there is adequate BP control, and delivery is recommended at 37 weeks of gestation. However, in the following events, pregnancy is terminated regardless of the period of gestation:

• Uncontrolled severe hypertension
• Eclampsia
• Pulmonary edema
• HELLP Syndrome
• Renal dysfunction
• Coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation)
• Abruption
• Fetal compromise
questions.learning: Injection labetalol and magnesium sulphate and expedite the delivery The given scenario is suggestive of chronic hypertension with superimposed severe pre-eclampsia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Patient undergoes lens implantation folllowing which there's worsening of vision after 1 year. Slit lamp examination finding is shown in the image below. Identify the complication.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior subcapsular cataract

The given clinical vignette supported with the image of vacoulated clusters seen behind IOL is suggestive of Elschnig’s pearls which is a type of posterior subcapsular cataract (after cataract).

Posterior subcapsular cataracts occur mainly due to ageing, other causes include the use of topical steroids, trauma, excessive consumption of alcohol, and exposure to ionizing radiation. Visual impairment is more during the day or exposure to bright light as the pupil constricts which blocks light rays.

After cataract also known as secondary cataract or posterior capsular opacification is a late postoperative complication that follows extracapsular extraction of the lens.

Different types of after cataract include:

• Elschnig’s pearls: where the subcapsular epithelial cells proliferate and develop into vacuolated soap bubble like clusters along the posterior capsule.
• Soemmering’s ring: A peripheral dense ring is formed behind the iris and is enclosed between layers of the capsule.
• Dense membranous after cataract: formed in the pupillary area impairing the vision.
• Thin membranous after cataract : is thickened posterior capsule.

Treatment of after cataract is by

• Nd-YAG laser capsulotomy of the posterior capsule which works on the principle of photodisruption
• surgical posterior capsulotomy.
questions.learning: Posterior subcapsular cataract — The given clinical vignette supported with the image of vacoulated clusters seen behind IOL is suggestive of Elschnig’s pearls which is a type of posterior subcapsular cataract (after cataract).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Type I endometrial carcinoma?
options: It is associated with obesity and diabetes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Smoking is a high-risk factor

Type I endometrial carcinoma is the estrogen-dependent form of endometrial cancer and usually arises from endometrial hyperplasia.

• Associated with unopposed estrogen exposure
• Common risk factors: obesity, diabetes, PCOS, nulliparity
• Histology: Endometrioid adenocarcinoma
• Common genetic mutation: PTEN

Smoking is not a risk factor for Type I endometrial carcinoma; it may actually reduce estrogen levels and slightly lower risk.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following organisms can cause croup except ___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rhinovirus

Croup can be caused by parainfluenza types 1, 2,3, RSV(Respiratory syncytial virus), and influenza viruses and it cannot be caused by Rhinovirus.

Croup, or laryngotracheobronchitis, is a viral infection affecting the upper airway, primarily in children aged 6 months to 3 years. It causes inflammation of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi, leading to characteristic symptoms such as:

* Barking cough (seal-like cough)

* Inspiratory stridor

* Hoarseness

* Respiratory distress in severe cases

The most common causative organism for croup is the parainfluenza virus. While other viruses like influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and adenovirus can also cause croup, parainfluenza is the predominant cause

On X-ray: Steeple/ Church top/ Pencil top sign (obstruction in subglottis) is seen as below:

Management:

* Racemic epinephrine nebulization leads to rapid improvement of upper airway obstruction.

* Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway edema.

* Dexamethasone is indicated in all grades of croup.

* Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %).

* Antibiotics are not indicated in croup.
questions.learning: Rhinovirus Croup can be caused by parainfluenza types 1, 2,3, RSV(Respiratory syncytial virus), and influenza viruses and it cannot be caused by Rhinovirus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Löfgren syndrome: 1. It is an acute illness and is more commonly seen in females. 2. It is a clinically distinct phenotype of sarcoidosis characterized by peripheral arthropathy and uveitis. 3. Clinical features include fever, erythema nodosum and bilateral lymphadenopathy. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 and 3 only

Löfgren syndrome is an acute, self-limiting presentation of sarcoidosis with an excellent prognosis. It is considered a distinct clinical phenotype of sarcoidosis and is seen more commonly in young females.

Löfgren syndrome (acute sarcoidosis, good prognosis):

• Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
• Erythema nodosum
• Migratory polyarthralgia (ankles especially)
• ± Fever
• No uveitis or neuropathy in this triad — that's the trap

Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever) — this is the one with uveitis

• Anterior uveitis
• Parotid gland enlargement
• Facial nerve palsy (cranial neuropathy, not peripheral)
• Fever

Neurosarcoidosis (general):

• Cranial neuropathies (CN VII most common)
• Can also cause peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex or symmetric polyneuropathy) — less classic than the cranial nerve involvement, but tested
• CNS involvement (mass lesions, meningitis, hypothalamic-pituitary axis)
questions.learning: 1 and 3 only Löfgren syndrome is an acute, self-limiting presentation of sarcoidosis with an excellent prognosis. It is considered a distinct clinical phenotype of sarcoidosis and is seen more commonly in young females.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 24-year-old female patient presented with malar rash, recurrent oral ulcers, and multiple joint pain. She has no relevant past history and does not take any medication. On further investigations, thrombocytopenia was seen and the Anti-Sm antibody was positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Systemic Lupus Erythematous

The clinical scenario along with Anti-Sm antibody positivity is suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

SLE is an autoimmune disease that mostly affects women of reproductive age. It is characterized by the formation of autoantibodies and immune complexes that cause widespread systemic damage.

Diagnosis of SLE requires at least four of the following categories:

Clinical features:

* Skin:

* acute, subacute cutaneous manifestations (photosensitivity, malar or maculopapular rash)

* chronic cutaneous manifestations (discoid lupus, panniculitis, lichen planus like)

* Oral or nasal ulcers

* Nonscarring alopecia

* Synovitis involving 2 or more joints

* Serositis (pleurisy, pericarditis)

* Renal:

* Protein/Creatinine ratio of more than 0.5

* RBC casts

* Biopsy

* Neurologic: seizures, psychosis, myelitis, neuropathy, confusional state

* Hemolytic anemia

* Leukopenia/lymphopenia

* Thrombocytopenia

Immunological manifestations:

* Antinuclear antibodies > reference value

* Anti-dsDNA > reference value

* Anti Smith antibody

* Antiphospholipid antibody (lupus anticoagulant, false-positive rapid plasma reagin)

* Low serum complement

* Positive direct Coombs' test in absence of hemolytic anemia.

Four criteria with one in each category must be positive for it to qualify as a diagnosis of SLE. However, if a renal biopsy is suggestive of lupus nephritis and lupus autoantibodies are positive then four criteria are not required.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common presentation of abdominal desmoid tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Abdominal mass

Explanation:

The most common presentation of an abdominal desmoid tumor is an abdominal mass.

Desmoid tumors, also known as fibromatosis, aggressive fibromatosis or desmoid-type fibromatosis are locally aggressive tumors that lack metastatic potential. Desmoid tumors can be sporadic in origin or associated with familial adenomatous polyposis.

These tumors arise from fibro-aponeurotic tissue and typically are manifested as a slowly growing mass. They present as firm, non-painful, non-tender masses in the abdominal wall, shoulder, hip and limbs, mesentery, and pelvis. They are also associated with trauma, pregnancy, and oral contraceptive usage.

The investigation of choice for a desmoid tumor is MRI. It is superior to CT in defining the pattern and the extent of involvement and can determine recurrence after surgery. Diagnosis is established by a biopsy with immunohistochemistry, which stains positive for beta-catenin, actin and vimentin, and negative for desmin, cytokeratin and S-100.

Treatment:

• An initial observation is preferred for stable, asymptomatic, primary or recurrent desmoids, especially if surgery can cause high mortality.
• Surgical resection with negative margin clearance is reserved for patients with small abdominal wall tumors associated with pain or an increase in size.
• Tamoxifen and NSAIDs are used as first-line medical therapy. Other systemic treatment options are low-dose chemotherapy, tyrosinase kinase inhibitors, and full-dose chemotherapy
• Radiotherapy is preferred for candidates unfit for surgery, patients refusing surgery and when surgical resection is associated with high morbidity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the diagram showing the development of ovarian follicles.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antral follicle

The structure marked in the image is of a secondary follicle, also called an antral follicle.

Development of ovarian follicles:

At birth, the ovarian cortex contains numerous primordial follicles which contain primary oocytes surrounded by a single layer of flat follicular cells. Most of these follicles degenerate in the prepubertal life and are called atretic follicles. At puberty, around 20 primordial follicles get activated in each menstrual cycle. Out of these 20 primordial follicles, only one follicle is dominant which reaches maturity and releases the oocyte during ovulation.

The different stages of development of the primordial follicle are:

a) Primary follicle:

* Follicle cells change from flattened cells to cuboidal and the stromal cells surrounding the follicle differentiate into spindle-shaped cells called 'theca externa'.

* The oocyte increases in size and secretes a proteoglycan material around it which forms the layer called 'Zona Pellucida' which is seen between the plasma membrane of the oocyte and the granulosa cells.

b)Secondary follicle(Antral follicle):

* The primary follicles continue to increase in size and the granulosa cells multiply.

* Numerous cavities coalesce to form a single fluid space called antrum.

* The granulosa cells envelop the oocyte to form a structure called Cumulus oophorus.

c) Tertiary follicle (Graffian follicle):

* Numerous secondary follicles are formed but only one tertiary follicle develops while others regress and become atretic follicles.

* As the antrum draws the fhe follicle increase in size and expands to a diameter of 2 cm to become Graffian follicle.

* The oocyte and the surrounding granulosa cells called corona radiata break away from the follicular wall and float in the follicular fluid.

* The primary oocyte completes its first meiotic division to form the secondary oocyte and a polar body.

* The secondary oocyte is arrested in the metaphase of the second meiotic division until fertilization takes place.

* The follicle ruptures to release the oocyte which is captured by for the fimbriae.

d) Corpus Luteum:

* The remainder of the follicle after ovulation is called the Corpus luteum. It synthesizes a carotenoid pigment called lutein which gives it a yellowish colour.

* If the oocyte is not fertilized then corpus luteum degenerates 12-14 days after ovulation to become corpus albicans.

* If fertilization occurs then the hCG produced by the trophoblast maintains the corpus luteum. It releases progesterone, estrogen, and relaxin, and regresses at around 8 weeks when the placenta takes over.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following responses to intravenous adenosine is correctly matched?
options: Ventricular tachycardia — Termination and complete recovery
Atrial flutter — Termination and complete recovery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atrio-ventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia — Termination

Adenosine is an ultra-short-acting antiarrhythmic drug that transiently blocks conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node by activating A1 adenosine receptors, causing hyperpolarization and slowing AV nodal conduction. It is the drug of choice for terminating AV node-dependent supraventricular tachycardias, particularly AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT.

AVNRT depends on re-entry through the AV node. By producing a transient AV nodal block, adenosine interrupts the re-entry circuit, leading to termination of the arrhythmia.

Why not the other options?

• A. Atrial fibrillation — Termination: Incorrect. Adenosine does not terminate atrial fibrillation; it may transiently slow the ventricular rate by blocking AV nodal conduction.
• C. Ventricular tachycardia — Termination and complete recovery: Incorrect. Adenosine is not effective for most ventricular tachycardias (except rare idiopathic outflow tract VT).
• D. Atrial flutter — Termination and complete recovery: Incorrect. Adenosine may produce transient AV block, helping reveal flutter waves, but does not terminate atrial flutter.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant born to an HIV-positive mother presents with recurrent diarrhea. What is the next best step?
options: Test stool for giardia and give antibiotics
Dried spot sample for HIV DNA PCR
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dried spot sample for HIV DNA PCR

In the above scenario, the diagnosis of HIV infection should be established/ruled out before evaluating for secondary infections. Hence, a dried spot sample for HIV DNA PCR is the next best step.

AIDS enteropathy, a syndrome of malabsorption with partial villous atrophy not associated with a specific pathogen, has been postulated to be a
result of direct HIV infection of the gut.

The diagnosis of HIV infection in babies born to HIV-infected mothers is done by HIV proviral DNA or RNA PCR, HIV culture, or HIV p24 antigen. The national program (Early Infant Diagnosis) now uses HIV total nucleic acid (RNA + proviral DNA) PCR test on dried blood spot samples. All positive tests need to be confirmed with an HIV PCR test on another sample.

An infant born to an HIV-positive mother should be breastfed exclusively or by replacement feeds exclusively for 6 months of age. Infants should receive ARV prophylaxis with syrup nevirapine or zidovudine.

Involvement of the gastrointestinal tract is common in HIV-infected babies. Common pathogens identified are bacteria (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Mycobacterium avium complex), protozoa (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Isospora, microsporidia), viruses (CMV, HSV, rotavirus), and fungi (Candida). MAC and protozoal infections are most severe and protracted in children.

Other options:

Option A: Test stool for giardiasis and give antibiotics is not preferred as the immediate next step. First, the diagnosis of HIV infection should be established before treating secondary infections.

Option C: Antibody tests for HIV are not useful in establishing the diagnosis of HIV infection. This is because all infants born to HIV-infected mothers test antibody positive at birth because of the passive transfer of maternal HIV antibodies across the placenta. It can be used as a diagnostic tool after 18 months of age.

Option D: Aerobic culture is not used for the diagnosis of HIV infection.
questions.learning: Dried spot sample for HIV DNA PCR — In the above scenario, the diagnosis of HIV infection should be established/ruled out before evaluating for secondary infections.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A child presents with pinpoint ecchymoses around hair follicles and is not allowing anyone to move his limbs because of pain. He also has tender nodules over the chest, as seen in the image given below. What is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Scurvy

The given clinical scenario and the image showing scorbutic rosary are suggestive of scurvy.

Scurvy results from the deficiency of vitamin C. Vitamin C is required for the hydroxylation of lysine and proline that are used in the synthesis of collagen. Hence, deficiency of vitamin C leads to the formation of defective collagen.

Defective collagen results in capillary hemorrhages which may present as generalized bleeding tendency. It also results in defective osteoid formation. Subperiosteal hemorrhages cause acute pain and swelling mimicking acute osteomyelitis.

Costo-chondral separation leads to the formation of tender nodules, also known as scorbutic rosary. Rickets also presents with similar nodules at the costochondral junctions known as rachitic rosary. They can be differentiated as scorbutic rosary is more sharply angulated and are painful.
questions.learning: Scurvy — The given clinical scenario and the image showing scorbutic rosary are suggestive of scurvy. Scurvy results from the deficiency of vitamin C.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Pompe's disease, the enzyme deficient is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lysosomal alpha glucosidase

Pompe's disease results from a deficiency in the enzyme lysosomal alpha-glucosidase.

Pompe's disease is a type II glycogen storage disorder that results from a deficiency in the enzyme acid maltase/ lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase. It is a rapidly progressive disorder that results in hypotonia and hepatosplenomegaly. Myocardial involvement helps to distinguish it from other similar glycogen storage disorders.

Hepatomegaly results from the ballooning of the lysosomes with glycogen. This creates a characteristic lacy cytoplasmic pattern. Cardiac and skeletal muscles will show enlargement with clear spaces in the cells, representing glycogen storage within the lysosomes. This disease classically has a poor prognosis, but enzyme replacement has helped to prolong survival in recent times.

A muscle biopsy with enlarged glycogen-containing vacuoles can be seen in the image below:

Other options:

Option A: Lactic acid dehydrogenase deficiency is not associated with any disorder.

Option B: Tarui's disease is characterized by a deficiency of muscle and erythrocyte phosphofructokinase 1. This results in abnormal glycogen metabolism and hence muscle cannot generate energy after exercise using glycogen reserves which leads to exercise intolerance.

Option C: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency is seen in McArdle's disease (type V glycogen storage disorder). Patients present with exercise-induced muscle cramping without elevated blood lactate levels which would normally be expected.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism, including weakness, lethargy, marked cold intolerance, and a delayed ankle jerk reflex. Thyroid function tests reveal TSH 16 µIU/mL, low T4, and low T3 levels. What is the most appropriate initial treatment strategy for this patient?
options: Start levothyroxine at 100 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually
Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and increase the dose gradually
Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually
Give T3 and T4 drugs simultaneously
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptomatic, overt hypothyroidism confirmed by a significantly elevated TSH (16 ) and low T4 Levels. In an elderly patient (65 years old), the standard management principle is to "start low and go slow". Therefore, the most appropriate initial strategy is to start levothyroxine at a low dose of 25 micrograms and gradually increase it (Option B). This cautious approach is critical to avoid precipitating acute cardiac issues (like angina or arrhythmias) by rapidly increasing metabolic demand. Starting at 100 micrograms (Option A) is too aggressive for an older male. Decreasing the dose (Option C) is nonsensical for treating a deficiency. Giving T3/T4 simultaneously (Option D) is not the standard primary therapy. Consequently, the low-dose initiation with titrated escalation is the definitive clinical standard of care to ensure patient safety while achieving a euthyroid state

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with joint pain and on evaluation, urine turns black on standing. What is the likely enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase

The urine turning black in color, on exposure to air, along with joint pain is suggestive of alkaptonuria. It occurs due to the defect in the homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase enzyme.

Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine.

Alkaptonuria is characterized by homogentisic aciduria, ochronosis, and arthropathy (joint pain).

Homogentisic aciduria is the black discoloration of urine on prolonged exposure to air caused due to oxidation of the excreted homogentisate.

Ochronosis is the accumulation of oxidized homogentisic acid pigment (alkaptone bodies) in connective tissues leading to bluish-black discoloration of tissues mostly involving ear cartilage, ocular tissue, the skin of the eyelids, forehead, cheeks, and hands, nail beds, and intervertebral discs. The compound that accumulates in the tissues in ochronosis is benzoquinone acetate.

Painful arthritis (arthropathy) may be seen from the fourth or fifth decade.

Diagnosis: Blackish discoloration of urine on standing is diagnostic of alkaptonuria (shown below). The ferric chloride test will be positive.

The image further below shows Ochronosis.

Treatment:  No specific treatment is required. Symptomatic treatment with analgesics, spinal surgery, and arthroplasty along with ascorbic acid and protein restriction can be considered. Nitisinone (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid (pHPPA) oxidase inhibitor) reduces urinary excretion of homogentisic acid.

Other options:

Option B: Tyrosine transaminase deficiency causes type II tyrosinemia (Richner-Hanhart syndrome). Patients present with painful corneal erosions with photophobia, learning disability, and palmoplantar keratosis.

Option C: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes type I tyrosinemia (Tyrosinosis). Patients generally present with failure to thrive, neuropathy, boiled-cabbage urine, and liver failure secondary to cirrhosis.

Option D:  4-hydroxy-phenyl pyruvate dioxygenase deficiency causes type III tyrosinemia (neonatal tyrosinemia). Patients might rarely have a mental disability. The liver function is generally normal.

questions.text: Regarding vitamin D supplementation in an exclusively breast-fed newborn, which of the following is recommended?
options: Immediately, initially 200 IU and after 6 months 400 IU
To be started after breastfeeding is stopped
To be started 400 IU at the time of complementary feeding
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immediately 400 IU

Exclusively breast-fed infants should receive vitamin D supplementation of 400 IU/day starting soon after birth.

• Human breast milk contains insufficient vitamin D (≈20–40 IU/L) to meet the infant’s requirement.
• Therefore, guidelines recommend 400 IU of vitamin D daily from the first few days of life, regardless of maternal vitamin D status.
• Supplementation should continue until the infant consumes adequate vitamin D from fortified formula or diet (≥400 IU/day).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Non-immune hydrops is seen in all, except ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Human immunodeficiency virus

Human immunodeficiency virus is not a cause of nonimmune hydrops.

Hydrops is diagnosed by identifying two or more fetal effusions—pleural, pericardial, or ascites—or one effusion plus anasarca. Hydrops can be seen in association with red cell auto immunization, which is termed immune hydrops. Otherwise, it is nonimmune hydrops.

Pathogenesis of hydrops includes decreased colloid oncotic pressure, increased hydrostatic or central venous pressure, and enhanced vascular permeability. Sonographically measured skin thickness of >5 mm constitutes edema or anasarca.

Etiology of nonimmune hydrops fetalis:

Cardiovascular

• Structural defects:

• Ebstein anomaly
• Tetralogy of Fallot with absent pulmonary valve
• Hypoplastic left or right heart
• Premature closure of ductus arteriosus
• Arteriovenous malformation (vein of Galen aneurysm)

• Cardiomyopathies
• Tachyarrhythmias
• Bradycardia

Chromosomal

• Turner syndrome (45,X), triploidy
• Trisomies 21, 18, and 13

Hematological

• Hemoglobinopathies, such as α4-thalassemia
• Decreased erythrocyte production (myeloproliferative disorders)
• Fetomaternal hemorrhage

Lymphatic Abnormalities

• Cystic hygroma
• Systemic lymphangiectasis
• Pulmonary lymphangiectasis

Infections

• Parvovirus B19
• Syphilis
• Cytomegalovirus
• Toxoplasmosis
• Rubella
• Enterovirus
• Varicella
• Herpes simplex
• Coxsackievirus
• Listeriosis
• Leptospirosis
• Chagas disease
• Lyme disease

Kidney and Urinary Tract

• Kidney malformations
• Bladder outlet obstructions
• Congenital (Finnish) nephrosis
• Bartter syndrome

Placental, Twin, and Cord Abnormalities

• Placental chorioangioma
• Twin-twin transfusion syndrome
• Twin reversed arterial perfusion sequence
• Twin anemia polycythemia sequence
• Cord vessel thrombosis

Idiopathic

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Drug of choice for the treatment of digoxin induced ventricular arrythmia is ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lignocaine

Lignocaine has the least effect on AV nodal conduction and is the most appropriate drug for the treatment of digoxin-induced arrhythmias.

Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside with a narrow therapeutic index and is used in the management of heart failure.

Mechanism of action: Increased accumulation of intracellular sodium is caused by inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase pump in the myocardium. Increased intracellular sodium prevents the efflux of calcium ions. This results in increased intracellular calcium which increases the contractility of the muscle.

It can also cause bradycardia via its vagotonic and sympatholytic activity.

Clinical features of digoxin toxicity:

CNS manifestations - Drowsiness, neuralgia, headache, confusion or giddiness

Ophthalmic manifestations - Visual aberration is an early indication of digitalis toxicity. Yellow-green distortion is most common. Yellow halos around lights (xanthopsia) is seen. Visual acuity is reduced.

Gastrointestinal manifestations- Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea, abdominal pain.

Cardiac manifestations - Palpitations, dyspnea, syncope, hypotension. The most serious side effect of digoxin is arrhythmia. They can present as extreme bradycardia, atrial fibrillation, ventricular extrasystoles, bigeminy, ventricular tachycardia, and fibrillation.

Digoxin should be discontinued whenever toxicity is suspected. An effective antidote for digoxin toxicity is digibind, which is an antidigoxin antibody. Arrhythmias should be treated

Other options:

Option A: Procainamide and other class IA anti-arrhythmic agents are not indicated in digoxin toxicity because of their inhibitory effects on AV nodal conduction.

Option C: Atropine is used for atrial bradyarrhythmias associated with digoxin toxicity.

Option D: Propranolol is used for atrial tachyarrhythmias associated with digoxin toxicity.
questions.learning: Lignocaine Lignocaine has the least effect on AV nodal conduction and is the most appropriate drug for the treatment of digoxin-induced arrhythmias. Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside with a narrow therapeutic index and is used in the management of heart failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old man presents to the surgery department with abdominal pain and tenderness, having developed acute appendicitis three days earlier. Which type of surgical incision would be most appropriate in this clinical scenario?
questions.explanation: The patient has acute appendicitis, and the most appropriate surgical incision is the McBurney’s incision (gridiron incision). This incision is placed in the right iliac fossa, centered over McBurney’s point (junction of lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the line joining the umbilicus and anterior superior iliac spine). In the given diagram, label 3 corresponds to the McBurney’s (gridiron) incision, which is an oblique muscle-splitting incision. It provides excellent access to the appendix while minimizing muscle damage and promoting faster recovery. This incision follows the direction of external oblique muscle fibers, allowing separation rather than cutting of muscles, thereby reducing postoperative pain and complications. Why other options are incorrect: (1) → Subcostal incision (used for gallbladder/liver) (2) → Transverse incision (general abdominal access) (5) → Pfannenstiel incision (used in gynecological surgeries)
