questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An unvaccinated 5-year-old child presents with a sore throat and difficulty in swallowing. On examination, she has a greyish membrane over her tonsils. She has a fully vaccinated 2-year-old brother who was asymptomatic. What is the appropriate management of this contact?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prophylactic dose of penicillin

The given clinical features of sore throat and difficulty in swallowing with a greyish-white membrane over the tonsils in an unvaccinated child is suggestive of pharyngeal diphtheria. The appropriate management for the asymptomatic 2-year-old brother of the child with diphtheria is to initiate prophylactic antibiotic treatment with penicillin, regardless of his immunization status.

Diphtheria is caused by the bacteria Corynebacterium diphtheriae which spreads via droplets through the respiratory tract (most important), cutaneous lesions, and fomites. Management includes antitoxin therapy as a single empirical dose of 20,000-100,000 units and antibiotics. Penicillin G/ Benzylpenicillin is the drug of choice for diphtheria. However, in case of an allergy to the same, Erythromycin is used. Other antibiotics used are clindamycin, rifampin, and tetracycline.

All household contacts of diphtheria should be closely monitored for 7 days. Culture should be taken from both the throat and nose. After culture, all contacts should receive the following:

• Antibiotic prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G or erythromycin), regardless of immunization status.
• If fewer than three doses of diphtheria toxoid have been given, or vaccination history is unknown, an immediate dose of diphtheria toxoid should be given and the primary series completed according to the current schedule.
• If more than 5 years have elapsed since the administration of the diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine, a booster dose should be given.
• If the most recent dose was within 5 years, no booster is required.

At least two successive negative cultures obtained 24 hr apart after completion of therapy are needed to confirm the elimination of the organism.
questions.learning: Prophylactic dose of penicillin — The given clinical features of sore throat and difficulty in swallowing with a greyish-white membrane over the tonsils in an unvaccinated child is suggestive of pharyngeal diphtheria.

>5 meters

questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is brought by her mother, who asks about the normal sequence of puberty. The girl is noted to have Tanner stage 2 breast development and Tanner stage 2 pubic hair. What is the next physiological event expected in her pubertal progression?

• Thelarche (breast budding, Tanner stage 2)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which type of renal calculus is most commonly encountered?
questions.explanation: Renal calculi (kidney stones) are composed of various mineral crystals. Globally, calcium oxalate stones are the most prevalent type, accounting for roughly 75% to 80% of all cases. These stones are radio-opaque and can form in both acidic and alkaline urine. Triple phosphate (struvite) stones (Option C) are associated with urea-splitting bacterial infections (like Proteus) and can form large "staghorn" calculi. Uric acid stones (Option D) are unique because they are typically radiolucent (invisible on plain X-ray) and are linked to high purine intake or gout. Cystine stones (Option B) are rare and result from an inherited defect in amino acid transport. Factors promoting calcium oxalate formation include dehydration, hypercalciuria, and hyperoxaluria. Management focuses on adequate hydration and dietary modifications. Because calcium oxalate is the predominant mineral composition found in the majority of patients worldwide, it is the correct answer to this epidemiological question

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 58-year-old patient with a known malignancy undergoes molecular analysis of tumor cells. RNA sequencing reveals transcripts that are longer than normal, with inclusion of additional exon sequences not seen in healthy tissue. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alternative RNA splicing

Alternative RNA splicing allows a single gene to produce multiple mRNA transcripts with different exon combinations, leading to variation in transcript length and protein isoforms.

Role in Cancer:

• Cancer cells often exhibit abnormal alternative splicing.
• This can generate longer or altered mRNA transcripts.
• These variants may promote tumor growth, survival, and metastasis.

Why not other options:

A) Polyadenylation: Adds a poly-A tail at the 3′ end but does not significantly change transcript length of coding regions.

C) Gene amplification: Increases the number of gene copies, not the length of each RNA transcript.

D) Upstream promoter modification: Affects transcription initiation and expression level, not mRNA length.
questions.learning: Alternative RNA splicing Alternative RNA splicing allows a single gene to produce multiple mRNA transcripts with different exon combinations, leading to variation in transcript length and protein isoforms.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following scan is of a young woman on oral contraceptives. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatic adenoma

The image given is of hepatic adenoma.  It is the most frequent hepatic tumour in young women on oral contraceptive pills.

Hepatic adenomas, also referred to as hepatocellular adenomas, are benign liver tumours. They are well-defined vascular lesions, which are generally solitary. They are almost always seen in women between the age of 25 and 50 years and are associated with the use of the oral contraceptive pill.

On CT, uncomplicated adenomas are usually homogeneous, with a well-defined margin. They enhance markedly and uniformly during the arterial phase and then merge with the surrounding liver during the portal phase.

Hypervascular tumours are often visible as low-attenuation lesions on unenhanced images and may enhance transiently in the arterial phase, some becoming invisible in the portal phase. Venturi mask is a high-flow, fixed-performance oxygen delivery system and the highest oxygen concentration (FiO2) delivered is 60% at a flow rate of 15 L/min. It is useful with patients who require greater FiO2 such as COPD patients, where it is important to provide controlled oxygenation. It is available in different colors, with the green valve venturi mask providing 60% FiO2.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An apparently well male neonate delivered by vaginal route in hospital is discharged on day 2 of life. He is brought to the outpatient department on day 4 of life as the mother complains of pink staining of his diapers. There is no bleeding from urethra or per rectum noticed during examination and urine dipstick test for RBCs is negative. The baby is appearing playful and active. The most likely etiology of pink staining of diapers is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urate crystals in urine

• The pink or reddish-orange staining of a newborn’s diaper during the first week of life, in an otherwise well baby, is most commonly due to uric acid (urate) crystals in concentrated urine. It is often called “brick-dust” or “brick-red” urine.
• The negative urine dipstick for RBCs and absence of actual bleeding support this diagnosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Porphyria: Extremely rare in neonates and not the typical cause of pink diaper staining.
• C. Hemoglobinuria: Would produce a positive dipstick for blood despite absence of intact RBCs.
• D. Hematuria: Would produce RBCs on urine microscopy and typically a positive blood dipstick.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
Regarding urinary tract infection (UTI ) in children, which of the following is true?

1. Most common cause of UTI is Streptococcus pneumoniae.
2. Bowel, bladder dysfunction increases the risk of recurrence.
3. Cotrimoxazole is not given.
4. Micturating cysto-urethrogram (MCU) is done in children with recurrence of UTI.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2,4

The true statements regarding UTI in children are bowel and bladder dysfunction increases the risk of recurrence, and micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) is done in children with recurrence of UTI.

The chief cause of UTI in children is Escherichia coli, others include Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus. Risk factors for recurrent UTI are age <6 months, obstructive uropathy, female sex, vesicoureteric reflux (VUR), bladder dysfunction, constipation, and repeated catheterization.

Clinical features in neonates include fever, vomiting, diarrhea, poor weight gain, and lethargy. If the child cries during voiding or has a weak urine stream with a palpable bladder, it implies urinary obstruction. High fever (>39ºC), persistent vomiting, dehydration, renal angle tenderness, or raised creatinine is considered a complicated UTI.

A colony count of >105/mL of a clean catch sample is considered significant bacteriuria. Any colonies on suprapubic aspiration and >50,000/mL on urethral catheterization are considered significant. Patients with recurrent UTIs need to be evaluated with ultrasonography, DMSA scan (dimercaptosuccinic acid), and MCU.

Evaluation following the first episode of UTI is given below:

Age
Evaluation

<1 year
USG, MCU, DMSA renal scan

1 to 5 years
USG, DMSA scan. MCU is done if USG is abnormal

>5 years
USG. If USG is abnormal,  MCU and DMSA are done.

Third-generation cephalosporins or aminoglycosides are preferred empirical antibiotics for urinary tract infections (UTIs). Treatment duration is 7-10 days for simple UTIs and 10-14 days for complicated UTIs. Asymptomatic bacteriuria doesn't require treatment. Infants <3 months and those with complicated UTIs should receive parenteral antibiotics.

Cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, and cefadroxil are given as prophylaxis to prevent recurrent UTIs. Cotrimoxazole and nitrofurantoin can be given in infants >3 months of age.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A researcher examines the relationship between per capita alcohol consumption and liver cirrhosis mortality rate across 10 countries. Identify the type of study.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ecological study

An ecological (correlational) study examines the relationship between exposure and disease at the population or group level, rather than at the individual level. It compares aggregate data (e.g., countries, states, or communities) to identify associations and generate hypotheses but cannot establish causality due to the ecological fallacy.

• The study compares per capita alcohol consumption and cirrhosis mortality rates across countries, where the unit of analysis is the population (country), making it an ecological study.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cohort study: Follows individuals over time based on exposure status.
• B. Case-control study: Begins with individual cases and controls and compares past exposures.
• C. Cross-sectional study: Measures exposure and outcome simultaneously in individuals at a single point in time.
questions.learning: Ecological study — An ecological (correlational) study examines the relationship between exposure and disease at the population or group level, rather than at the individual level.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: True regarding the difference between adult and pediatric resuscitation.
options: Ventricular dysrhythmias are common in children
The no flow phase precedes the period of cardiac arrest in children.
More ventilation to be given compared to chest compressions in children
Dysrhythmias are most often due to respiratory insufficiency in children
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dysrhythmias are most often due to respiratory insufficiency in children

Dysrhythmias in the pediatric age group are most often the result of respiratory insufficiency or hypoxia and not of primary cardiac causes, as in adults.
Hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis lead to bradycardia, hypotension, and secondary cardiac arrest in children.

Other options:

Option A: Supraventricular tachycardia is the most common tachydysrhythmia that necessitates treatment in pediatric patients. Ventricular dysrhythmia is an uncommon presenting rhythm in infants and children.

Option B: The pre-arrest phase is the period that precedes the period of cardiac arrest.

Four phases of cardiac arrest have been described as follows:

• The prearrest phase- a period that precedes the period of cardiac arrest.
• The no-flow phase- reflects untreated cardiac arrest before it is recognized by a bystander in the community or by a medical provider in the hospital
• The low-flow phase- begins with the onset of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
• The post-resuscitation phase - The post-resuscitation phase begins with the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC).

Option C: The chest compression to ventilation ratio should be 30:2 or 15:2. Excessive ventilation results in decreased venous return into the chest, decreased coronary and cerebral blood flow, diminished cardiac output, and ultimately a decreased likelihood of return of spontaneous circulation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following is the bone marrow biopsy of a 60-year-old man with easy fatiguability, back pain, and multiple lytic lesions in the skull. Likely diagnosis is______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Multiple myeloma

The clinical history along with the biopsy picture showing Russell bodies is suggestive of multiple myeloma.

Russell bodies are eosinophilic, large, homogeneous immunoglobulin-containing inclusions usually found in a plasma cell undergoing excessive synthesis of immunoglobulins. It is characteristic of the distended endoplasmic reticulum in multiple myeloma.

Clinical features

* Bone pain is the most common symptom

* Renal failure -Acute oliguric or non-oliguric kidney failure may be present due to hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, light-chain cast injury, or primary amyloidosis

* Pallor and soft tissue masses

* Fever occurs with infection

* Patients may have neurologic signs related to neuropathy or spinal cord compression

* Hyperviscosity syndrome (mucosal bleeding, vertigo, nausea, visual disturbances, alterations in mental status, hypoxia)

Bone marrow biopsy shows round or oval cells with an eccentric nucleus composed of coarsely clumped chromatin, a densely basophilic cytoplasm, and a perinuclear clear zone containing the Golgi apparatus.

Pearl PF0569: Some Pathological Cells/Bodies in Multiple Myeloma

Description

Russell bodies

They are globular intracellular accumulations of immunoglobulins (Ig).

Plasma cells filled with multiple Russell bodies are called Mott cells.

Dutcher bodies

PAS-positive intranuclear inclusions containing Ig seen in some of the plasma cells are called Dutcher bodies.

Flame cells

Plasma cells with fiery red cytoplasm are called flame cells.

PAS: Periodic acid Schiff

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 72-year-old postmenopausal woman develops sudden severe chest pain and breathlessness following a stressful emotional event. She has no prior history of heart disease. On examination, she is mildly tachycardic with normal blood pressure. Echocardiography reveals systolic left ventricular apical ballooning, and cardiac enzymes are only minimally elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, or "broken heart syndrome," is a transient condition typically triggered by intense emotional or physical stress in post-menopausal women. It is characterized by the classic "ballooning" of the left ventricular apex during systole, resembling a Japanese octopus trap (takotsubo). Symptoms mimic an acute MI, including chest pain and minimal elevation of cardiac enzymes, yet coronary angiography typically shows no significant obstructive disease. Hypertensive heart disease (Option A) results from long-standing pressure and causes hypertrophy, not acute ballooning. Coronary artery disease (Option C) would feature significant plaque obstruction. Pulmonary embolism (Option D) causes acute pleuritic pain but not this specific LV wall motion abnormality. The condition is thought to be mediated by a massive catecholamine surge leading to microvascular dysfunction
questions.learning: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, or "broken heart syndrome," is a transient condition typically triggered by intense emotional or physical stress in post-menopausal women.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In the image shown, which diuretic acts at the site labeled “A” and was prescribed to a 50-year-old woman for the management of hypertension?
questions.explanation: The diagram identifies the Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT) as location 'A'. The class of diuretics that specifically targets this segment is the Thiazides, such as Hydrochlorothiazide. Thiazides work by inhibiting the symporter on the luminal membrane, thereby increasing the excretion of sodium and water. They are considered first-line pharmacological agents for the management of primary hypertension. Mannitol (Option A) is an osmotic diuretic acting primarily on the proximal tubule and descending limb. Acetazolamide (Option C) inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule. Furosemide (Option D) is a loop diuretic that targets the thick ascending limb of Henle's loop. While loop diuretics are more potent, Thiazides are preferred for chronic hypertension because they have a longer duration of action and a favorable cardiovascular profile. Clinicians must monitor for side effects like hypokalemia and hypercalcemia. Correctly localizing the site of action of these drugs is essential for understanding their clinical utility and adverse effect profiles in renal medicine
questions.learning: The diagram identifies the Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT) as location 'A'. The class of diuretics that specifically targets this segment is the Thiazides, such as Hydrochlorothiazide.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the angle subtended by the largest alphabet on the Snellen's chart at 60m distance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5

The angle subtended by the largest alphabet on the Snellens chart at 60m distance is 5 minutes.

Visual acuity is a measure of the spatial resolution of the eye or an estimation of its ability to discriminate between two points. Snellens chart is used for Visual acuity assesment.

In snellens chart the alphabets decrease in size as we move from above-downwards and these lines, from above-downwards should be read at 60, 36, 24, 18, 12, 9, 6, 5 and 4 m respectively. At these distances, the respective letters subtend a visual angle of 5 minutes. Hence, the largest alphabet that should be read at 60 m subtends a visual angle of 5 minutes in the eye.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A young boy from a low socioeconomic background presents with hyperemia and yellowish nodules at the limbus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is an allergic hypersensitivity reaction of the conjunctiva and cornea to endogenous microbial proteins, most commonly those from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is frequently seen in children from poor socioeconomic backgrounds who may have underlying malnutrition or subclinical tuberculosis. The characteristic clinical finding is a small, yellowish-grey nodule at the limbus (the phlycten) surrounded by a localized area of hyperemia. Bitot's spots (Option A) are dry, foamy patches on the conjunctiva associated with Vitamin A deficiency and are not usually hyperemic. Pterygium (Option B) is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth onto the cornea, typically seen in older adults with chronic sun exposure. Pinguecula (Option C) is a common, non-progressive yellowish thickening of the bulbar conjunctiva that does not involve the limbus in the same inflammatory manner. Management of phlyctenular conjunctivitis involves topical steroids and, crucially, investigating and treating the underlying cause, such as tuberculosis or staphylococcal blepharitis
questions.learning: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is an allergic hypersensitivity reaction of the conjunctiva and cornea to endogenous microbial proteins, most commonly those from Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the challenge faced in the operationalization of the concept of Universal Health Coverage (UHC)?
options: Universal Health Coverage aims to provide free health care services to all, regardless of the available resources in the country
Universal Health Coverage aims to provide services despite having unregulated and fragmented healthcare delivery systems
Universal Health Coverage prioritizes the safety of resources in a low-resource setting
Universal Health Coverage targets primary health care delivery based on the needs of the population
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Universal Health Coverage aims to provide services despite having unregulated and fragmented healthcare delivery systems

Universal Health Coverage (UHC) means all individuals and communities receive the health services they need without suffering financial hardship.

UHC includes access to health promotion, disease prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, palliative care.

A major challenge in implementing Universal Health Coverage (UHC) is delivering equitable and continuous care within unregulated and fragmented healthcare systems, where services are split between public and private sectors.

Such fragmentation leads to inefficiencies, variable quality, and gaps in continuity of care, making universal access difficult.

In contrast, UHC is based on resource prioritization and need-based primary health care, not on unlimited or unsafe use of resources.

UHC in India

India’s move toward UHC includes initiatives such as:

• Ayushman Bharat
• Health and Wellness Centres
• Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY)

These programs aim to improve access, affordability, and quality of care.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The recommended temperature of water bath for a patient with frost bite is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 37 degree C

The temperature of the water bath for a patient with frostbite should be maintained between 37- 40°C (Option A). Circulating water is preferred for treatment.

In frostbite, tissue damage results from severe environmental cold exposure or from direct contact with a very cold object. Tissue injury results from both freezing and vasoconstriction. It usually affects the distal aspects of the extremities or exposed parts of the face, such as the ears, nose, chin, and cheeks.

The treatment includes - extraction from cold environment, rapid rewarming, analgesics for pain during thawing, antithrombotics or thrombolytics, cleaning of the injured area with soap or antiseptics, tetanus prophylaxis, monitoring for compartment syndrome and finally, elective late amputation after imaging in severe cases.
questions.learning: 37 degree C The temperature of the water bath for a patient with frostbite should be maintained between 37- 40°C (Option A). Circulating water is preferred for treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 17-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of numbness and tingling in her fingers, especially triggered by stress or exposure to cold. She has no significant past medical history and is otherwise healthy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation and the provided image are pathognomonic for Raynaud’s phenomenon. This condition is characterized by episodic, reversible vasospasm of the digital arteries in response to cold or emotional stress. It classically follows a triphasic color change: white (vasospasm/ischemia), blue (deoxygenation/cyanosis), and red (reactive hyperemia/reperfusion). In a 17-year-old non-smoker with no underlying disease, this is likely "primary" Raynaud’s (Raynaud's disease). Buerger's disease (Option B) causes digital ischemia but typically presents in heavy male smokers and is characterized by permanent vessel inflammation rather than reversible spasms. Atherosclerosis (Option C) and Peripheral Arterial Disease (Option D) are common in older adults with risk factors like diabetes or hypertension and cause permanent claudication rather than episodic color changes in the fingers. Therefore, given the triggers and the classic visual pattern, Raynaud's phenomenon is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation and the provided image are pathognomonic for Raynaud’s phenomenon. This condition is characterized by episodic, reversible vasospasm of the digital arteries in response to cold or emotional stress.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The loading dose of MgSO4 in pre-eclampsia is?
options: 4 ml Mgso4 (50% w/v) in 16 ml NS
8 ml MgSo4 (50% w/v) in 12 ml NS
12 ml MgSo4 (50% w/v) in 8 ml NS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8 ml MgSo4 (50% w/v) in 12 ml NS

The loading dose of MgSO4 is 8ml MgSO4 (50% w/v) in 12ml NS. For loading dose IV infusion of 4g of 20% solution is needed.

One 2mL vial has 1g MgSO4. Therefore, to make a 20% solution containing 4g of MgSO4, we would need to take 8 mL of 50% magnesium sulfate, and dilute it with 12 mL NS. Therefore the final 20mL solution (8+12) would have 4g of MgSO4, making it a 20% solution.

MgSO4 is used as an anticonvulsant in the management of eclampsia and as prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia. The therapeutic level of magnesium in eclampsia is 4–7 mEq/L. Measurement of serum magnesium levels is indicated to monitor magnesium toxicity if serum creatinine >1.0 mg/dL.

MgSO4 regimens for management of eclampsia and severe preeclampsia:

Regimen

Loading Dose

Maintenance Dose

Intramuscular (Pritchard)

4 g (20% solution) IV over 3-5 minute

followed by 10 g (5O%), deep IM

(5 gm in each buttock)

5 g (5O%) IM 4 hourly in the alternate buttock

Intravenous (Zuspan or Sibai)

4g IV slow over 15-20 minute

1-2 g/h IV infusion

Repeat injections of magnesium sulfate are continued only if the patellar reflex is present, respiratory rate is >12, and urine output is >30 mL/h. Magnesium sulfate is discontinued either 24 hours after delivery or 24 hours after the onset of convulsions (whichever is later).

Loss of patellar reflex is the first sign of MgSO4 toxicity and occurs when the plasma magnesium level reaches 10 mEq/L. Elevated magnesium levels above 10 mEq/L weaken breathing, while 12 mEq/L or higher levels can lead to respiratory paralysis and arrest.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency room following a bike accident. Examination reveals the right upper limb in abduction and external rotation. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior Dislocation of the Shoulder

The upper limb in abduction and external rotation and radiograph are both suggestive of anterior dislocation of the shoulder.

The AP view radiograph shows the disturbed articulation between the humeral head and glenoid fossa. The humeral head is seen below and medial to the glenoid socket. This suggests anterior dislocation of the shoulder joint. In young adults, the common cause for anterior dislocation is athletic injuries, while in older adults, falls are a more common cause.

Anterior dislocation is the most common among shoulder dislocations. It occurs due to a fall on the hands. The head of the humerus is driven forwards and tears the capsule resulting in an avulsion in the glenoid labrum (Bankart lesion). Sometimes, the posterolateral part of the head of the humerus is crushed resulting in the Hill-Sachs lesion.

The clinical features include severe pain and the patient usually supports his dislocated arm with the opposite arm. On examination, the arm is usually abducted, externally rotated and the lateral outline of the shoulder may be straightened and sometimes a prominent acromion process or a bulge below the clavicle may be appreciated.

The anteroposterior radiograph shows the humeral head lying below and medial to the glenoid socket. It may also show the Bankart lesion and the Hill-Sachs lesion.

Other Options:

Option A: Luxatio erecta is also known as inferior dislocation of shoulder. This is caused due to severe hyperabduction. The radiograph shows that the head of the humerus is present below the glenoid and the shaft is in an abducted position.

Option B:  Light bulb sign is seen on AP radiographs in the posterior dislocation shoulder. In posterior dislocation of the shoulder, the humerus rotates internally. This causes changes to the normal radiographic contour of the head of the humerus. The humerus appears similar to a lightbulb in AP views.

Pearl PF2105: Tests for anterior shoulder dislocation

Bryant’s test: Anterior axillary fold is at a lower level on the dislocated side.

Dugas test: The patient is made to place the hand on the opposite shoulder. The examiner then applies gentle pressure on the flexed elbow to make it touch the chest. In shoulder dislocation, the elbow cannot be made to touch the chest.

Hamilton ruler test: In a normal shoulder, a ruler (scale) placed on the lateral side of the arm will not touch the lateral condyle of the humerus and the acromion at the same time.

In anterior shoulder dislocation, the ruler will simultaneously touch the lateral condyle of the humerus and the acromion.

Callway Test: The vertical circumference of the axilla is increased on the dislocated side as compared to the normal side.

Pearl PF1173: Methods of reduction of shoulder dislocation

Kocher's technique - TEAM (Traction → External Rotation → Adduction → Medial Rotation)

Hippocratic method- Surgeon applies a firm and steady pull on the semi-abducted arm by keeping his foot on the axilla against the chest wall. The foot is used as the fulcrum.

Stimson's gravity technique: Patient is left prone and weight is attached to the elbow or wrist on the affected side. Gravity stretches the muscle and reduction occurs in 15-20 minutes.
questions.learning: Anterior Dislocation of the Shoulder — The upper limb in abduction and external rotation and radiograph are both suggestive of anterior dislocation of the shoulder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Device shown in the image is used for which purpose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prevent transfusion related reactions

The image shows a leukoreduction filter which is used for filtering out donor WBCs. This helps in reducing the incidence of transfusion-related reactions by removing WBC microaggregates. The optimum time for performing leukoreduction is before the storage of blood.

Potential benefits include reduced risk of:

• Sensitization to HLA antigens (important for transplant patients & preventing platelet refractoriness)
• Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions (FNHTR)
• CMV transmission

Note: CMV also has an affinity for monocytes and macrophages (types of WBCs). Reduction in WBCs is the cause for the decrease in CMV transmission (accidental benefit), and thus, the main purpose of a leukoreduction filter is not the prevention of CMV transmission (options A and C).

Possible reduced risk of:

• Transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA- GVHD)
• Transfusion-related immuno-modulatory (TRIM) effects
• Transmitting variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease

Other Methods of Leucodepletion are:

• Specific leucodepletion filters (Most Efficient)
• Washing
• Freezing
• Buffy coat removal
• Micro-aggregate filtration
• Low leucocyte apheresis devices
questions.learning: Prevent transfusion related reactions — The image shows a leukoreduction filter which is used for filtering out donor WBCs. This helps in reducing the incidence of transfusion-related reactions by removing WBC microaggregates.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with recurrent vomiting undergoes an X-ray (shown below). What is the most likely electrolyte imbalance in this patient?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays the "double bubble sign," which is pathognomonic for duodenal atresia or stenosis, leading to gastric and duodenal distension. This condition causes profuse, recurrent vomiting. Prolonged vomiting of gastric contents results in the loss of hydrogen ions (acid), chloride, and potassium. This leads to a state of hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. As the body tries to conserve hydrogen ions in the kidneys in exchange for potassium, potassium levels drop significantly. Hyperkalemia (Option B) and hypernatremia (Option D) are not typical outcomes of vomiting; they usually occur in renal failure or severe dehydration without fluid loss. While hyponatremia (Option C) can occur due to total body sodium loss, hypokalemia is the more hallmark and clinically significant electrolyte deficit associated with the metabolic alkalosis of high intestinal obstruction. Correcting these imbalances is essential before surgical intervention to repair the duodenal obstruction
questions.learning: The X-ray displays the "double bubble sign," which is pathognomonic for duodenal atresia or stenosis, leading to gastric and duodenal distension. This condition causes profuse, recurrent vomiting.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 33-year-old woman presents for evaluation of multiple painless oral lesions and a long history of “small bumps” on her face. Physical examination shows numerous facial trichilemmomas and papillomatous papules on the oral mucosa. She also has a history of multiple thyroid nodules. Family history reveals that her mother had breast cancer at age 41. Genetic testing shows a germline mutation in a tumor suppressor gene that normally inhibits the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Colonic adenomatous polyposis beginning in adolescence
Increased risk of breast and thyroid malignancies
Increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased risk of breast and thyroid malignancies

The clinical features describe Cowden syndrome, caused by a germline mutation in the PTEN gene.

• PTEN normally:

• Inhibits the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway
• Acts as a tumor suppressor regulating cell growth and survival

• Mutation → loss of inhibition → uncontrolled cell proliferation
• Mucocutaneous lesions:

• Facial trichilemmomas
• Oral papillomas

• Multisystem involvement:

• Thyroid nodules
• Hamartomas in various organs

Increased risk of:

• Breast cancer
• Thyroid cancer (especially follicular)
• Endometrial carcinoma

Why not other options:

A. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas: Seen in Neurofibromatosis type 2

B. Colonic adenomatous polyposis: Seen in Familial adenomatous polyposis

D. Medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma: Seen in Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2
questions.learning: Increased risk of breast and thyroid malignancies — The clinical features describe Cowden syndrome, caused by a germline mutation in the PTEN gene. • PTEN normally: • Inhibits the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway • Acts as a tumor suppressor regulating cell…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A wildlife photographer presents with a blackish lesion at the site of a mite bite from a few days back. He also gives a history of fever and rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scrub typhus

In the above clinical scenario, a history of mite bite followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever and rash suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases.

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for both adults and children.

In Scrub typhus both the adult and nymphal stages of mites are free living in nature, hence they do not feed on vertebral hosts. The larval stage(chigger) feeds on the vertebrate host and pick up the rickettsiae. Rodents are the mammalian reservoir for scrub typhus. Eschar can be seen in the image below:

Other options:

Option A: Anthrax- Cutaneous anthrax (Hide Porter’s disease) present as a black eschar at the site of entry. At the site of entry of organism or spores, a papule develops in about 1–7 days. This develops into a vesicle that later breaks down into an ulcer with a black, central, necrotic eschar surrounded by edematous skin. The disease used to be common in dock workers, carrying loads of hides and skins on their bare backs. Renal involvement is unlikely to be seen in this condition.

The image below shows its characteristic rash:

Option C : Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a rickettsial infection transmitted by ticks (Dermacentor andersoni). It is the most serious type of fever. Symptoms include fever, headache, Rash, muscle pain and lack of appetite. Early treatment with doxycycline is recommended to prevent death and severe illness.

The rash is shown in the image below:

Option D : Epidemic typhus: Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and the vector is louse. Its incubation period is 10 to 14 days. The disease starts with fever and chills. A characteristic rash appears on the fourth or fifth day, starting on the trunk and spreading over the limbs but sparing the face, palms, and soles.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Menke’s disease, which of the following enzymes would be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lysyl oxidase

Menke’s disease is due to defective lysyl oxidase.

It is an X‐linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in ATP7A, which encodes for a copper-transporting ATPase‐α polypeptide.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought with fever, fatigue, and left ventricular dysfunction. An endomyocardial biopsy is shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lymphocytic myocarditis

The clinical scenario of a child with complaints of fever, fatigue, and left ventricular dysfunction, and a biopsy showing lymphocytic infiltration in myocardial tissue, is suggestive of lymphocytic myocarditis.

The inflammatory process of the myocardium is termed myocarditis. Patients mostly present with fatigue, chest pain, cardiogenic shock, and even cardiac arrest. Viruses are the most common among the infectious causes of myocarditis. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for the diagnosis, and it shows diffuse, mononuclear, lymphocytic infiltration, as shown below.

Myocarditis begins with the direct invasion of an infectious agent. it subsequently replicates within and around the myocardium, causing myonecrosis. This infiltration and replication of the infectious agent lead to the destruction of cardiac tissue.

They are treated with supportive management.

Other Options:

Option A: Aschoff's bodies are the lesions found in the heart during acute rheumatic fever. They are composed of foci of T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump-activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells. Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and central round-to-ovoid nuclei with chromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence, they are also called caterpillar cells.

This condition classically occurs a few weeks after an episode of group A streptococcal pharyngitis or, less commonly, skin infections, and Aschoff's bodies are seen in the image below.

Option B: The myocarditis of Chagas disease has distinctive features of the parasitization of scattered myofibers by trypanosomes accompanied by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils, lymphocytes, macrophages, and occasional eosinophils. The clusters of amastigotes cause swelling of individual myocardial fibers and create intracellular pseudocysts. There is focal myocardial cell necrosis accompanied by extensive, dense, acute interstitial inflammatory infiltration throughout the heart.

The image below shows the amastigotes within a myocyte (arrow) and the surrounding inflammatory response.

Option C- In most bacterial infections, the heart can be involved through direct invasion and abscess formation. Causes include diphtheria, brucellosis, legionella, Meningococcus, and Mycoplasma, and require treatment of the systemic infection.
questions.learning: Lymphocytic myocarditis — The clinical scenario of a child with complaints of fever, fatigue, and left ventricular dysfunction, and a biopsy showing lymphocytic infiltration in myocardial tissue, is suggestive of lymphocytic myocarditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Tigroid white matter on MR imaging is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease

Tigroid white matter on MR imaging is seen in Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease.

It is a rare, X-linked recessive disorder characterized by central nervous system dysmyelination.

The proteolipid protein gene (PLP1) is affected, leading to the failure of axon myelination by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system.

Clinical Features:

• Nystagmus
• Developmental delay
• Psychomotor delay
• Seizure
• Stridor
• Feeding difficulties
• Ataxia
• Hypotonia progressing to spasticity.

The degree of dysmyelination is correlated with the severity of the clinical manifestations.

Genetic analysis can confirm the diagnosis. MRI shows a lack of myelination and MR spectroscopy reveals aberrant N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) and choline concentrations that reflect axonal and myelination abnormalities.

Unlike other demyelinating leukodystrophies such as metachromatic leukodystrophy and adrenoleukodystrophy, where myelin is formed but subsequently destroyed, PMD shows a failure of myelin formation.
questions.learning: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease Tigroid white matter on MR imaging is seen in Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease. It is a rare, X-linked recessive disorder characterized by central nervous system dysmyelination.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Arrange the following in the sequence of auditory pathway:

1. Cochlear nucleus
2. Spiral ganglion
3. Superior olivary nucleus
4. Inferior colliculus
5. Medial geniculate body
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2-1-3-4-5

The correct sequence of the auditory pathway is spiral ganglion (2) - cochlear nucleus (1) - superior olivary nucleus (3) - inferior colliculus (4) - medial geniculate body (5).

The spiral ganglion contains bipolar cells whose dendrites form the afferent supply for inner and outer hair cells of the organ of Corti and whose axons form the cochlear division of CN VIII that end in the cochlear nuclei.

The auditory pathway can be remembered with the mnemonic E.C.O.L.I.M.A

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve is not the content of superior orbital fissure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. II

The correct answer is Optic nerve (CN II).

CN II passes through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.

The superior orbital fissure transmits CN III, CN IV, CN VI, and the ophthalmic division of CN V (V1) along with sympathetic fibres.
questions.learning: II The correct answer is Optic nerve (CN II). CN II passes through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with schizophrenia was started on risperidone. After taking the medication last night, the patient rushes to OPD today with complaints of upwards rolling of his eyes. What is the management of the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Promethazine

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of oculogyric crisis and promethazine is used for the management.

Oculogyric crisis refers to the spasm of the extraocular muscles, usually causing upward and outward deviation of the eyes. It is a severe form of acute dystonia, an extrapyramidal side effect of antipsychotics like risperidone. It can be treated by drugs with antimuscarinic activities like promethazine.

Dystonia is acute in onset and occurs within 1-5 days of starting treatment. It is more common in the younger population. The proposed mechanism of action is D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway. There is typical involvement of head and neck muscles and presents in a variety of forms, such as torticollis, trismus, mouth opening dystonia, grimacing, dysarthria, oculogyric crisis, blepharospasm, and swallowing difficulties.

Risperidone is an atypical antipsychotic with D2 blocking but strong 5HT2 antagonistic activity. Its main side effects include weight gain, hyperglycemia, hyperprolactinemia, dyslipidemia, fatigue, etc. At low doses, extrapyramidal side effects are less, but can be significant in higher doses. Extrapyramidal side effects include;

• Parkinsonism: Features are bradykinesia, rigidity, variable tremor, masked facies, and shuffling gait.
• Acute dystonia: Which causes spasms of muscles of the tongue, face, eyes, neck, back, etc.
• Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: Extreme rigidity, fever, unstable blood pressure,myoglobinemia, etc.
• Rabbit syndrome: Perioral tremors occur as a delayed variant of parkinsonism.

Other options:

Option A: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine. Its adverse effects include sedation, light-headedness, confusional state, weight gain, etc.

Option C: Olanzapine is also an atypical antipsychotic. Its adverse effects are dry mouth, constipation, weight gain, impaired glucose tolerance etc.
questions.learning: Promethazine — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of oculogyric crisis and promethazine is used for the management. Oculogyric crisis refers to the spasm of the extraocular muscles, usually causing upward and outward deviation of the eyes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In RMNCHA+, all of the indicators in your area are in the Red zone. Which of the following statements is true? 1. Infant Mortality Rate in the area is <20% than the national average 2. Total Fertility Rate in the area is >20% than the national average 3. Children born with low birth weight are <20% than the national average 4. Care seeking for ARI is >20% than the national average
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 only

RMNCHA+ (Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health) prioritizes districts using a color-coded system based on key health indicators. A Red zone indicates that the indicator is performing more than 20% worse than the national average, requiring urgent programmatic intervention.

• Red zone: Indicator is >20% worse than the national average.
• For adverse indicators (e.g., Total Fertility Rate, IMR, MMR, Low Birth Weight), higher values indicate poorer performance.
• For positive service coverage indicators (e.g., institutional delivery, immunization, care-seeking for ARI), lower values indicate poorer performance.
• Thus, a Total Fertility Rate >20% above the national average is classified as a Red zone indicator.
questions.learning: 2 only RMNCHA+ (Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health) prioritizes districts using a color-coded system based on key health indicators.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was done on asthma and pollution. P value was found to be 0.03. What do you infer from this?
options: 3% probability that the result occurred due to chance alone
There is 95% confidence that the null hypothesis is true
The observed difference is not statistically significant
Null hypothesis is rejected at the probability of effect is less than 0.03
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3% probability that the result occurred due to chance alone

A p-value of 0.03 means that there is a 3% probability of noting the result “by chance only”.

Since p < 0.05, the result is statistically significant, and the null hypothesis is rejected at the 5% significance level.

It does not indicate the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor does it measure the size or importance of the effect.

⭐ p-value ≠ probability that hypothesis is true

⭐ p < 0.05 → statistically significant

⭐ p-value depends on sample size

Large samples may show significant results even for small effects.

⭐ Statistical significance ≠ clinical significance.
questions.learning: 3% probability that the result occurred due to chance alone A p-value of 0.03 means that there is a 3% probability of noting the result “by chance only”.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with complaints of greenish frothy vaginal discharge for 1 month and a burning sensation in her vaginal area for the past 5 days. There is no history of fever. Vitals are within normal limits. On speculum examination, you are able to see the below finding. Which of the following kits would you prescribe to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Green kit

The given clinical scenario and the image showing  strawberry cervix is suggestive of Trichomoniasis and the green kit containing Tablet Secnidazole 2 gm, to be taken orally as a single dose is recommended in its treatment.

Trichomoniasis: Infection of the female genital tract with the Trichomonas vaginalis protozoan

Trichomoniasis characteristically causes a copious, frothy, offensive yellow-green discharge with vaginal soreness or irritation and urinary frequency.

The vagina looks red and inflamed. The inflamed cervix looks like a strawberry with punctate hemorrhagic spots.

Management: The CDC recommends one of the following treatment regimens.

* Metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose (Standard treatment) or Secnidazole/Tinidazole 2 g orally in a single dose

* The alternative regimen includes Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice a day for 7 days

* Metronidazole gel does not reach therapeutic levels in the urethra and perivaginal glands. Because it is less efficacious than oral metronidazole, it is not recommended.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Hand washing during COVID-19 is what level of prevention?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary prevention

Hand washing during COVID-19 is a method of Primary prevention.

COVID-19 is an infectious respiratory illness caused by the coronavirus. Infection control measures like immunization, hand washing, personal hygiene and public health measures such as sanitation serve as a holistic primary prevention strategy.

Primary prevention is defined as an action taken prior to the onset of a disease, whose aim is to prevent the disease from occurring. Its target population is healthy individuals. It commonly institutes activities that limit risk exposure or increase the immunity of individuals at risk to prevent a disease from progressing in a susceptible individual. The approaches can be as follows:

* Population (mass) strategy where the target group is the whole population

* A high-risk strategy is where the target group is limited to the people who are most at risk of developing a particular disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: On a color Doppler, the blue color typically represents: (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Flow away from the transducer

On color Doppler ultrasound, the color assignment follows a standardized convention where blue color represents blood flow moving away from the transducer. This color coding is based on the Doppler effect principles and not on the oxygenation status of blood or vessel type.

Other Options:

Option A. Deoxygenated blood flow - INCORRECT. Color Doppler doesn't distinguish between oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. The colors represent direction of flow relative to the transducer position\, not blood oxygenation.

Option C. Flow towards the transducer - INCORRECT. Flow toward the transducer is conventionally displayed as red on color Doppler\, not blue. This is a fundamental convention in vascular ultrasound.

Option D. Venous flow pattern - INCORRECT. While venous flow often appears blue (because veins typically carry blood away from superficial transducer positions)\, the color assignment is based on direction of flow relative to the transducer\, not vessel type. Arteries can also appear blue if blood is flowing away from the transducer.

Educational Objective:

In color Doppler ultrasound, blue color specifically indicates flow moving away from the transducer, while red indicates flow moving toward the transducer - this convention is standardized across ultrasound systems regardless of vessel type or blood oxygenation.
questions.learning: Flow away from the transducer On color Doppler ultrasound, the color assignment follows a standardized convention where blue color represents blood flow moving away from the transducer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 24-year-old man presents with anemia, with a similar condition reported in his father and paternal aunt, both of whom showed significant improvement after splenectomy. Examination of his peripheral blood smear raises suspicion of a hereditary hematological disorder. Based on the familial pattern and favorable response to splenectomy, which additional blood abnormality is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture is suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis, an inherited disorder caused by defects in red blood cell membrane proteins such as spectrin. This leads to the formation of spherocytes, which have a reduced surface area-to-volume ratio and are less deformable. As a result, these cells are more prone to destruction in the spleen, causing hemolytic anemia. A key laboratory finding in hereditary spherocytosis is increased osmotic fragility. When placed in hypotonic solutions, spherocytes cannot accommodate osmotic swelling effectively and therefore rupture more easily than normal red blood cells. This increased fragility is a hallmark diagnostic feature of the disease. Other options are incorrect: Decreased reticulocytes is wrong because hemolysis stimulates the bone marrow, leading to an increased reticulocyte count. Heinz bodies are seen in G6PD deficiency, not hereditary spherocytosis. Howell–Jolly bodies appear after splenectomy due to loss of splenic function, not as a primary feature of the disease. Thus, the most appropriate abnormality is increased osmotic fragility
questions.learning: The clinical picture is suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis, an inherited disorder caused by defects in red blood cell membrane proteins such as spectrin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient who sustains trauma leading to rupture of the bulbar urethra, in which anatomical space is urine most likely to collect?
questions.explanation: The bulbar urethra is the portion of the male urethra located within the superficial perineal pouch. A rupture of this structure, often caused by a "straddle injury" or a fall into a manhole, leads to the extravasation of urine and blood into the superficial perineal space. This space is bounded by Colles’ fascia, which is continuous with the Dartos fascia of the scrotum and Scarpa’s fascia of the abdominal wall. Consequently, urine tracks into the scrotum, penis, and anterior abdominal wall, but not into the thighs or the anal region. The deep perineal pouch (Option B) contains the membranous urethra; a rupture here would have a different extravasation pattern. Options C (Rectouterine pouch/Pouch of Douglas) and D (Uterovesical pouch) are intraperitoneal structures in females and are irrelevant to a male bulbar urethral injury. Clinical signs include a "butterfly-shaped" hematoma in the perineum and blood at the external urethral meatus, requiring retrograde urethrography for definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not used in heart failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trimetazidine

Trimetazidine is not used in heart failure.

Trimetazidine is a newer antianginal drug that is a pFOX inhibitor which partially inhibits the fatty acid oxidation pathway in the myocardium. This decreases the oxygen requirement of the heart.

Nesiritide (natriuretic peptide), sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) and metoprolol (beta-blocker) are used in the treatment of heart failure.
questions.learning: Trimetazidine Trimetazidine is not used in heart failure. Trimetazidine is a newer antianginal drug that is a pFOX inhibitor which partially inhibits the fatty acid oxidation pathway in the myocardium.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old diabetic male presents with a history of decreased vision. Fluorescein angiography showed the following image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy

The given clinical vignette and Fluorescein angiography findings of neovascularization are suggestive of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR).

Neovascularization is a hallmark of PDR. So this rules out Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy-NPDR (Option A,B).

Option C: Birdshot retinochoroidopathy is an idiopathic bilateral chorioretinitis characterized by creamy yellow spots of chorioretinal hypopigmentation resembling a birdshot scatter. It most commonly affects middle aged females who are HLA-A29 positive.

PDR is most common in patients with Type Ⅰ diabetes after a period of 15-20 years and is characterized by proliferation of new vessels at the optic disc (NVD) or elsewhere in the fundus (NVE).

( NVD- neovascularization at the optic disc ; NVE-neovascularization elsewhere in the fundus )

Complications of PDR include recurrent vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment and pre retinal hemorrhages.

It is treated by administration of Anti-VEGF drugs followed by pan retinal photocoagulation which destroys the hypoxic retina that has been producing the vasoformative factors responsible for neovascularization.

Duration of diabetes mellitus is the most important factor for the development of diabetic retinopathy.

Ophthalmoscopic features of NPDR include:

• Microaneurysms: due to loss of pericytes around the capillaries
• Retinal hemorrhages: both superficial (flame shaped) and deep (dot & blot) hemorrhages.
• Hard exudates: composed of lipoproteins and lipid laden macrophages. They are yellow waxy looking and arranged in clumps or circinate patterns.
• Cotton wool spots: which are small whitish fluffy lesions which represent areas of nerve infarct.
• Intra retinal microvascular abnormalities(IRMA): are arteriovenous shunts in retina
• Venous abnormalities such as beading,looping and dilatation.

The below given image is that of Hard Exudates.
questions.learning: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy — The given clinical vignette and Fluorescein angiography findings of neovascularization are suggestive of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of childhood blindness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A deficiency

The most common cause of preventable childhood blindness is vitamin A deficiency.

The most common cause of blindness in adults, is however, cataract.

Vitamin A deficiency is a major cause of childhood blindness, particularly in developing countries. Lack of sufficient vitamin A can lead to conditions like xerophthalmia, which includes night blindness and can progress to more severe forms, ultimately causing irreversible damage to the cornea and leading to blindness.

Other options:

(a) Refractive error: Refractive errors, such as myopia (nearsightedness), hyperopia (farsightedness), and astigmatism, can cause vision problems, but they are usually correctable with glasses or contact lenses. While refractive errors can affect children's vision, they are not typically a direct cause of childhood blindness.

(c) Retinopathy of prematurity: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a condition that primarily affects premature infants and is related to abnormal blood vessel development in the retina. While it can lead to vision impairment or blindness in severe cases, it is not as prevalent as vitamin A deficiency, especially on a global scale.

(d) Injuries: While injuries can certainly lead to vision impairment or blindness in children, they are not as prevalent on a population level as vitamin A deficiency.
questions.learning: Vitamin — A deficiency The most common cause of preventable childhood blindness is vitamin A deficiency. The most common cause of blindness in adults, is however, cataract.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 48-year-old patient, with HIV presented to the casualty with shortness of breath, and fever with chills. On examination, there was marked hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse rales were auscultated in all lung fields.The chest X-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Miliary TB

The history, clinical features, and chest X-Ray point towards a diagnosis of miliary tuberculosis.

There is widespread dissemination of M. tuberculosis, via the hematogenous route that leads to the seeding of bacteria in various organs (hepatosplenomegaly).

It is a form of disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis, not extrapulmonary.

The risk factors of miliary TB include-

* Extremes of age

* Alcohol use

* Malignancy

* HIV

* Corticosteroids

* Connective tissue disease

* Renal failure

* Diabetes, and pregnancy

questions.text: Which of the following has the worst prognosis?

Semon’s Law – RLN (Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve) Palsy

• In progressive (compressive) lesions of the Recurrent laryngeal nerve:

• Abductors are affected first
• Adductors are affected later

Reason: Abductor fibers (posterior cricoarytenoid) are more vulnerable than adductors.

B/L Partial RLN palsy: Only abductors paralyzed

• Vocal cord position → Paramedian
• Clinical features: Abductors lost, adductors intact
• Airway → severely compromised

Most dangerous situation

While in Complete B/L palsy:

• Airway → relatively better

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A new drug combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy for metastatic melanoma was prescribed by a radiotherapist. It prolongs the survival. Which of the following is true in this situation?
options: Incidence reduces and prevalence remains the same
Incidence remains the same and prevalence increases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Incidence remains the same and prevalence increases

By the new drug combination, the survival of the patient has increased, hence incidence remains the same while prevalence increases.

Incidence: Number of new cases in a defined population in a specified period of time.
Prevalence: Number of old and new cases at a given point of time over a period of time.

Options A, B, D: The treatment only prolongs the disease, it has nothing to do with the occurrence of cases thereby nothing to do with incidence.
questions.learning: Incidence remains the same and prevalence increases By the new drug combination, the survival of the patient has increased, hence incidence remains the same while prevalence increases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain and morning stiffness that improves with activity. He also reports pain and redness in one eye associated with photophobia. On examination, there is restricted lumbar spine mobility and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints. Which of the following is most likely associated with this condition?

HLA-B51 is linked to Behçet’s disease.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient presented to the casualty department with torticollis and dystonia. His attender reported that he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and had recently started treatment with Haloperidol. What is the next best step to treat the patient's presenting symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Give Benzhexol

This patient on haloperidol developed extra-pyramidal symptoms of torticollis and dystonia. The next best step in his management to alleviate his symptoms would be to administer benzhexol, an anticholinergic medication

Benzhexol, also known as trihexiphenidylis an antimuscarinic agent. Drug-induced parkinsonism is a condition that is caused by certain drugs that have D2 antagonistic action like typical antipsychotics. Due to the decrease in dopaminergic activity, they result in an unbalanced cholinergic activity. Benzhexol acts by restoring the balance of the cholinergics in the striatal interneurons.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
False statement regarding rabies immunoglobin is:

RIG- Rabies immunoglobulin
options: It is exclusively given in the deltoid
Not given after 7 days of the 1st dose of the vaccine
If human RIG is unavailable, equine is preferred
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is exclusively given in the deltoid

The false statement regarding rabies immunoglobulin is it is exclusively given in the deltoid. Rabies immunoglobulin is given as much as possible into the wound site or around it.

Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is passive immunization. It is administered only once, preferably within 24 hours of the exposure, ie, on day 0 of the anti-rabies vaccine (ARV). If RIG was not given with the ARV 1st dose, it can be given up to the 7th day after the first dose of ARV. It is not given after 7 days of receiving the 1st dose of ARV.

The dose is 20 IU/kg body weight for human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) and for equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG), the dose is 40 IU/kg body weight. When HRIG is not available, ERIG can be used. They are potent, safe, and less expensive.

The entire RIG dose or as much as anatomically possible should be infiltrated into the wound or as close as possible. If it is likely that there are additional small wounds, the remaining RIG should be given IM as close as possible to the site of wound or exposure.

All patients with category III exposures should be given RIG. This includes:

• single/multiple transdermal bites/scratches
• licks on broken skin
• contamination of mucous membranes with saliva
• contact with bats

In immunocompromised patients, RIG should be given to both category II and III exposures.
questions.learning: It is exclusively given in the deltoid — The false statement regarding rabies immunoglobulin is it is exclusively given in the deltoid. Rabies immunoglobulin is given as much as possible into the wound site or around it.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-month-old baby presents with jaundice and clay-colored stools. Lab investigation reveals that the baby has conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The liver biopsy shows periductal proliferation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Biliary atresia

The most likely diagnosis in this infant with jaundice, clay-colored stools, and periductal proliferation is biliary atresia.

Biliary atresia presents with progressive jaundice, persistent acholic stools, and palpable liver with abnormal consistency. Laboratory investigations show conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Ultrasonography reveals a triangular-cord sign (cone-shaped fibrotic mass cranial to the bifurcation of the portal vein).

HIDA test is used for screening and liver biopsy is diagnostic for biliary atresia. Biopsy shows proliferation of the bile ductule, the presence of bile plugs, and portal or perilobular edema and fibrosis, with the basic hepatic lobular architecture intact.

Other options:

Option A: Crigler-Najjar type 2 is an autosomal recessive disease with non-hemolytic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia caused by homozygous missense mutations in UGT1A1, resulting in reduced (partial) enzymatic activity.

Option B: Rotor syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder presenting with asymptomatic mild and fluctuating conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver histology.

Option C: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder due to the absent function of multiple drug-resistant protein-2.  It presents with abdominal pain, mild icterus, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Biopsy shows black liver due to an accumulation of epinephrine metabolite.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with history of ischemic stroke was started on clopidogrel. However, she had another attack of stroke after 6 months. Which of the following is likely to be responsible for the failure of clopidogrel in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Downregulation of CYP2C19

Downregulation of CYP2C19 is responsible for the failure of clopidogrel in this patient.

Clopidogrel is a prodrug and its metabolic activation occurs in the liver. It is bioactivated by the CYP2C19 enzyme. If there is downregulation of this enzyme it will cause a decrease in the efficacy of clopidogrel and can lead to thrombotic events like stroke. Drugs that inhibit CYP2C19 can also decrease the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel. Proton-pump inhibitors may cause inhibition of CYP2C19 and when they are given in combination there would be a decrease in the efficacy of clopidogrel.

Therapeutic uses: Clopidogrel is used to reduce the rate of stroke and myocardial infarction. It also decreases the rate of deaths in patients with recent myocardial infarction or stroke. Other uses are acute coronary syndrome and peripheral arterial disease.

Adverse effects: Increased risk of bleeding especially when given with an anticoagulant or aspirin. Rarely thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura can occur.

CYP2C19: Common drugs that are metabolized include omeprazole, phenytoin, diazepam, and propanolol. Inducers of the CYP2C subfamily are rifampicin and carbamazepine. Omeprazole is an inhibitor.

Other options:

CYP2D6: Drugs metabolized include SSRIs,  tricyclic antidepressants, antiarrhythmic drugs, beta-blockers, and opiates. It is inhibited by quinidine and it will prevent the formation of morphine from codeine. Hence quinidine decreases the analgesic effect of codeine.

CYP1A1/2: It metabolizes few drugs like theophylline, paracetamol, caffeine and carbamazepine. It plays an important role in the activation of procarcinogens. Inducers are rifampicin, carbamazepine, polycyclic hydrocarbons, charbroiled meat, and cigarette smoke.

CYP2E1: It is involved in the oxidation of alcohol, halothane, and minor metabolism of other drugs. It is important to note that it is involved in the formation of hepatotoxic N-acetyl benzoquinone imine from paracetamol. Chronic alcoholism is responsible for the induction of this enzyme.
questions.learning: Downregulation of CYP2C19 Downregulation of CYP2C19 is responsible for the failure of clopidogrel in this patient. Clopidogrel is a prodrug and its metabolic activation occurs in the liver.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent Staphylococcus infections. Laboratory evaluation reveals markedly reduced levels of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE) along with a decreased number of B cells, while skin tests show a normal response to environmental antigens. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bruton's X-linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA) is caused by a mutation in the BTK gene, leading to a failure in B-cell maturation. Clinically, it presents as a near-total absence of mature B cells and very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes (IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE). A critical diagnostic clue is the "normal reaction to environmental antigens," which signifies that T-cell function and cellular immunity are intact. DiGeorge syndrome (Option B) involves T-cell deficiency due to thymic hypoplasia, making skin reactions abnormal. Hyper IgM syndrome (Option C) would show elevated IgM levels. Common Variable Immunodeficiency (Option D) presents similarly but usually manifests later in life, whereas XLA appears in infancy as maternal antibodies wane. Treatment requires lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy, and patients must avoid live vaccines
