questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly woman involved in a road traffic accident presents with respiratory distress and altered sensorium. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated D-dimer levels, and the chest X-ray demonstrates suggestive findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of respiratory distress and altered mental status following a high-energy accident (likely involving long bone fractures) is diagnostic of Fat Embolism Syndrome. This occurs when fat globules from bone marrow are released into the bloodstream and travel to the lungs and brain. Respiratory distress usually manifests 24–72 hours after trauma due to capillary obstruction. Gas gangrene (Option A) presents with crepitus and foul discharge. Acute infection (Option C) typically presents with fever rather than sudden post-traumatic hypoxia. While pulmonary embolism (Option D) also causes respiratory distress and elevated D-dimer, it is less likely to cause early altered mental status or the classic petechial rash often seen in fat embolism. The suggestive X-ray likely shows bilateral patchy infiltrates mimicking ARDS, which is characteristic of this syndrome. Thus, fat embolism is the most consistent post-traumatic diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of respiratory distress and altered mental status following a high-energy accident (likely involving long bone fractures) is diagnostic of Fat Embolism Syndrome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following can not be used for emergency contraception?
options: Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours

Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours would not be enough for emergency contraception. Levonorgestrel (LNG) 1.5 mg, i.e., 2 tablets of LNG 0.75 mg, can be used as a single-dose emergency contraceptive. This should be taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse. Alternatively, one tablet of LNG 0.75 mg can be followed by another tablet 12 hours later.

Advantages of LNG:

* It does not contain estrogen and therefore precludes the associated side effects.

* It can be used in hypertensive, cardiac, and diabetic patients.

* It is suitable for lactating women.

* It can be given up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse.

* It can be given as a single-dose therapy.

Combined oral pills consisting of both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH) and thus inhibit ovulation.

Emergency contraception refers to backup methods for contraceptive emergencies that women can use within the first few days after unprotected intercourse to prevent an unwanted pregnancy. Administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy.

The various emergency contraceptive methods, along with their mechanism of action, have been described below:

* Ethinyl estradiol 50 μg + norgestrel 0.25 mg is administered as two tablets within 72 hours of coitus, followed by the 2 tablets after 12 hours. The hormone may delay ovulation if taken soon after intercourse.

* Ulipristal is given as a 30 mg tablet and should be taken within 5 days. It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator. The drug attaches to the progesterone receptor, delays ovulation, and suppresses the endometrium, thereby preventing implantation.

* IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium.

* Centchroman is administered as two tablets of 60 mg, taken twice over a duration of 24 hours and within 24 hours of intercourse. It acts by preventing the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium.

Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives

Oral pills:

* Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC)

* Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate

* Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost)

* Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women

* Norethisterone 350 μg

* Norgestrel 75 μg

* Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg

* Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results

* Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone

* Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia

* Post-coital pills or interceptive

* Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg, 2 doses, 12 hours apart

* Mifepristone 10-600 mg

* Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse

* Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse

* GnRH agonists

* CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days

Injectable contraceptives

* Progesterone only injectables

* DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months

* NET-EN 200 mg IM every 2 months

* Combined injectables

* Cyclofem - DMPA 25 mg + Estradiol cypionate 5 mg

* Mesigyna - NET-EN 50 mg  + Estradiol valerate 5 mg

Subdermal implants

* Norplant I - Levonorgestrel 35 mg

* Norplant II or Jadelle - 2 rods with levonorgestrel 70 mg in each and released at a rate of 50 μg/day

Others

* Hormonal IUCD - Mirena which contains LNG 52 mg with release rate of 20 μg/day

* Orthoevra patch - Norelgestomin + Ethinyl estradiol weekly for 3 weeks, then patch free for 1 week

* Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week
questions.learning: Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours would not be enough for emergency contraception. Levonorgestrel (LNG) 1.5 mg, i.e., 2 tablets of LNG 0.75 mg, can be used as a single-dose emergency contraceptive.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following is not a differential diagnosis of chronic inversion of uterus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gartner’s cyst

Chronic uterine inversion is a rare condition in which the uterine fundus remains inverted for more than 4 weeks, usually following mismanaged third stage of labor or due to a fundal uterine tumor (e.g., submucous fibroid). It presents as a mass protruding through the cervix or vagina, often associated with irregular bleeding, foul discharge, pelvic pain, and anemia.

Because it presents as a vaginal mass, it must be differentiated from other causes of protruding genital tract masses.

• Gartner’s cyst is a remnant of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, located in the anterolateral wall of the upper vagina.
• It presents as a vaginal cystic swelling and does not resemble an inverted uterus, making it not a differential diagnosis of chronic uterine inversion.

Why not the other options?

• A. Fibroid polyp: A prolapsed submucous fibroid may present as a vaginal mass and closely mimics chronic uterine inversion.
• B. Fungating cervical malignancy: An advanced cervical cancer may present as an irregular bleeding vaginal mass and should be differentiated from uterine inversion.
• C. Cervical prolapse: Cervical or uterovaginal prolapse presents as a protruding vaginal mass and is an important differential diagnosis.
questions.learning: Gartner’s cyst Chronic uterine inversion is a rare condition in which the uterine fundus remains inverted for more than 4 weeks, usually following mismanaged third stage of labor or due to a fundal uterine tumor (e.g., submucous fibroid).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the cranial nerve that arises from the marked part.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abducens nerve

The structure marked in the image is the abducens nerve that arises from the pontomedullary junction.

In the groove between the medulla and pons, abducens, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves emerge arranged medially to laterally.

The abducens nerve is the 6th cranial nerve that arises from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, passes through Dorello's canal, and enters the cavernous sinus where it lies lateral to the internal carotid artery. It then enters the orbit through the common tendinous ring in the superior orbital fissure to supply the lateral rectus.
questions.learning: Abducens nerve — The structure marked in the image is the abducens nerve that arises from the pontomedullary junction. In the groove between the medulla and pons, abducens, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves emerge arranged medially to laterally.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with diabetes has high increased LDL and VLDL because of ?
options: Hormone sensitive lipase and lipoprotein lipase both increased
Hormone sensitive lipase increased & lipoprotein lipase decreased
Lipoprotein lipase increased & hormone sensitive lipase decreased
Lipoprotein lipase and hormone sensitive lipase both decreased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hormone sensitive lipase increased & lipoprotein lipase decreased

In diabetes mellitus (especially uncontrolled diabetes), insulin deficiency or resistance alters lipid metabolism, leading to hypertriglyceridemia and increased VLDL and LDL levels.

1. Effect on Hormone-Sensitive Lipase (HSL)

• Insulin normally inhibits HSL in adipose tissue.
• When insulin is deficient → HSL activity increases.
• This causes enhanced lipolysis in adipose tissue, releasing large amounts of free fatty acids (FFA) into the circulation.
• The liver takes up these FFAs and converts them into triglycerides, which are packaged as VLDL → increased VLDL production.

2. Effect on Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL)

• Insulin normally stimulates LPL, which hydrolyzes triglycerides in VLDL and chylomicrons to allow uptake into tissues.
• In diabetes → LPL activity decreases due to lack of insulin.
• This results in reduced clearance of VLDL and chylomicrons, further increasing plasma triglycerides.
questions.learning: Hormone sensitive lipase increased & lipoprotein lipase decreased In diabetes mellitus (especially uncontrolled diabetes), insulin deficiency or resistance alters lipid metabolism, leading to hypertriglyceridemia and increased VLDL and LDL levels.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of trauma, presented with diplopia, epistaxis, and restricted eye movements. Looking at the CT image given below, what will be your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blow out fracture

The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

Blow-out fractures are isolated comminunited fractures caused from direct trauma to the orbit that results in a backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in the intraorbital pressure. This causes a fracture at the weakest point of the orbital wall which is usually the posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone in the orbital floor. The second most common site for orbital blowout fracture is the medial wall of the orbit.

The patient with blow out fracture usually presents with immediate periorbital edema and blood extravasation in and around the orbit. Proptosis of the eyeball secondary to orbital edema or hemorrhage with paresthesia along the infraorbital nerve are also very common.

Imaging by a plain x-ray in water's view or by CT demonstrates depression of bony fragments and orbital contents herniating through the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum. This is called as the "hanging drop sign" or "tear drop sign".

Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotics.

Le fort fracture- Is the term used to describe different types of maxillary fractures.
questions.learning: Blow out fracture — The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 40-year-old male comes with an intracapsular fracture of the femur. What is the surgery of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Closed reduction internal fixation

Closed reduction internal fixation is the surgery of choice for a 40-year-old patient with an intracapsular fracture of the femur.

A displaced fracture neck of the femur in an adult who is physiologically less than 65 years of age is best treated by closed reduction and internal fixation with multiple cannulated cancellous screws. Open reduction is only done if closed reduction fails, as the complication rate is higher.

Proximal femur fractures are classified based on their location near the hip joint. The main types include:

1. Intracapsular Fractures:: It occurs within the joint capsule and involves the femoral neck and head.

Subtypes:

• Femoral head fracture
• Femoral neck fracture (common site for avascular necrosis and non-union).

2. Extracapsular Fractures: Occur outside the joint capsule.

Subtypes:

• Intertrochanteric fracture: Between the greater and lesser trochanters.
• Subtrochanteric fracture: Below the lesser trochanter.
• Trochanteric fracture: Isolated fracture of the greater or lesser trochanter.

Management of Intracapsular Fractures depends on the age of the patient:

1. > 65 years: Replacement - Hemi/Total Replacement (Option C and D)

2. < 65 years: is based on duration of fracture

• <3 weeks- CRIF with cannulated cancellous screws (avoid hematoma)
• >3 weeks- Check the viability of head- further management depends on the viability of head
questions.learning: Closed reduction internal fixation Closed reduction internal fixation is the surgery of choice for a 40-year-old patient with an intracapsular fracture of the femur.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A sewage worker presented with abdominal pain, jaundice, conjunctival suffusion, and blood in the urine for the past 5 days. Which of the following is the investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Microscopic agglutination test

Leptospirosis (e.g., in sewage workers exposed to contaminated water) is best confirmed by the Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT)--> is the gold standard serological test.

Etiology: Leptospira interrogans (spirochete)

Risk factors: exposure to water contaminated with animal urine (rats, sewage) Enters via: Skin cuts, eyes, nose (mucosal surface)

Clinical features (Weil disease):

• High fever, chills
• Severe muscle pain (calf tenderness )
• Conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without pus → classic clue)
• Jaundice (liver involvement)
• AKI (kidney injury)
• Bleeding tendencies (platelets ↓, capillary damage)

Diagnosis:

MAT (Microscopic Agglutination Test) → detects antibodies against leptospira (gold standard)

Early phase: PCR may be used

Why not others:

• Widal test: Done for typhoid fever
• Weil-Felix reaction: Done for rickettsial infections
• Paul-Bunnell test: Done for infectious mononucleosis (EBV)
questions.learning: Microscopic agglutination test Leptospirosis (e.g., in sewage workers exposed to contaminated water) is best confirmed by the Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT)--> is the gold standard serological test.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old lady was brought to the hospital by her daughter, with episodes of falls, confusion, chronic diarrhea, and cough. The intern decided to conduct a geriatric assessment. Which of the following factors indicated such an examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Age, fall, confusion

This patient's age, history of falls and episodes of confusion necessitate a comprehensive geriatric assessment.

Various comprehensive geriatric assessment programs use the following before performing a full-fledged assessment:

• Age
• The presence of concurrent medical conditions, such as heart failure or cancer.
• The presence of psychosocial illnesses like depression or isolation.
• Diseases unique to the elderly, include cognitive decline, mobility issues, and falls
• Prior or anticipated high health-care utilization
• Changes in living situation (for example, from independent living to assisted living, nursing facility, or in-home caretakers)

The inclusion of geriatric evaluation is imperative within the broader framework of the patient's health trajectory, taking into account their future care objectives and personal preferences. Functional status refers to the comprehensive assessment of an individual's health effect within the framework of their surroundings and social support network. It encompasses the individual's capacity to do the physical and social tasks required for their typical activities and duties. The constituents of functional status encompass activities of daily living (ADLs), instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), and advanced activities of daily living (AADLs). Two often employed measures in the field are the Katz index, which assesses activities of daily living (ADLs), and the Lawton scale, which evaluates instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). The most effective approach for ascertaining AADLS involves the utilization of open-ended inquiries, such as "In what manner do you allocate your time throughout the day?" or "What activities do you find enjoyable?"

There is a growing trend in geriatric assessment to integrate perspectives from non-clinical office workers, patients, and their relatives or loved ones. This collaborative approach may encompass the use of standing orders, forms, and questionnaires. An advisable strategy involves doing an annual evaluation of functional status, commencing at the age of 65 years, using the Medicare Annual Wellness Visit. For individuals below the age of 75 years with multiple comorbidities or those aged 75 years and above, it is recommended to augment this assessment with supplementary components. Furthermore, it is recommended that some components of geriatric assessment, such as evaluating activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), measuring gait, balance, and the risk of falls, evaluating mood and affect, as well as assessing cognition, be conducted following significant illnesses, particularly those necessitating hospitalization.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most common cause of seizures in a 2-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Febrile seizures

The most common cause of seizures in the said age group is febrile seizures.

Febrile seizures are defined as seizures that:

Occur between the age of 6 to 60 months
Associated with a temperature of ≥38°C (100.4°F)
Do not occur as a result of central nervous system infections or any metabolic imbalance.
Occur without a history of afebrile seizures in the past.

Depending on the duration and recurrence of the febrile seizure, they are classified as follows:

Simple febrile seizure
Complex febrile seizures
Febrile status epilepticus

Generalised, tonic-clonic seizure
Focal seizure
Febrile seizure

Last for ≤15 minutes, without another episode in 24 hours
Lasts >15 minutes and/or recurs in 24 hours
Duration of >30 minutes

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glucose is stored in the form of glycogen because __________
options: It can be stored at multiple organs
It can provide glucose for about 1 week when needed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is compact

Among the given options, the most appropriate answer would be option A i.e Glucose is stored in the form of glycogen because it is compact.

Glycogen is the major storage carbohydrate in animals, corresponding to starch in plants. It is a branched polymer of α-d-glucose.

Other options:

The major sites of storage are liver and muscle, that is, it can't be stored at multiple sites.

It does not have multiple reducing ends. It instead has multiple non-reducing ends.

Liver glycogen functions as a reserve to maintain the blood glucose concentration in the fasting state. After about 18 hours of fasting, most of the liver glycogen is depleted and hence it can not provide glucose for up to 1 week.
questions.learning: It is compact Among the given options, the most appropriate answer would be option A i.e Glucose is stored in the form of glycogen because it is compact.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A child is diagnosed with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which among the following can be seen in this child?

1. Bilious vomiting
2. Visible peristalsis from right to left
3. Hypochloremia and hypokalemia
4. Metabolic alkalosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 and 4 only

Patients with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) will present with non-bilious projectile vomiting and visible peristalsis observed moving from left to right (not from right to left). Metabolic abnormalities include hypokalemia, hypochloremia and metabolic alkalosis.

CHPS occurs due to hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus, which results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet.

• Patients commonly present between 2 and 8 weeks of age.
• First-born male infants are at the highest risk.
• Infants usually present with projectile, non-bilious vomiting.
• Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right (not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting.

Metabolic abnormality:

• Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e. hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.
• Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid, leading to metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).
• Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, sodium loss stimulates aldosterone secretion through the RAAS pathway.
• Aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions leading to the development of hypokalemia and paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially loses H+ ions due to the loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine.

Management:

• The child should be rehydrated and the metabolic abnormality must be corrected before surgery.
• Ramstedt pyloromyotomy remains the standard surgical procedure for its treatment.
questions.learning: 3 and 4 only Patients with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) will present with non-bilious projectile vomiting and visible peristalsis observed moving from left to right (not from right to left).

questions.text: Which of the following is seen in all kinds of shock?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reduced tissue perfusion

Shock is defined as a systemic state of low tissue perfusion that is inadequate for normal cellular respiration.

The classification of shock and its features are as follows:

Hypovolemic shock: It is due to reduced circulating volume. Causes include hemorrhage, dehydration, vomiting, and third spacing.

Obstructive Shock: This leads to a reduction in preload due to mechanical obstruction of cardiac filling. Causes include cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolus, or air embolus.

Cardiogenic shock: Due to the failure of the heart to pump blood to tissues. Causes include myocardial infarction, cardiac dysrhythmias, valvular heart disease, blunt myocardial injury, and cardiomyopathy.

Distributive shock: Distributive shock is the condition of reduced oxygen delivery where the primary physiologic disturbance is a reduction in systemic vascular resistance leading to vasodilation. It is unique among the types of shock in that there is a compensatory increase in cardiac output. Causes include spinal shock, anaphylaxis, and septic shock.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Korsakoff psychosis is true except? 1. Amnesia 2. Confabulation 3. Ophthalmoplegia 4. Ataxia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4

Korsakoff psychosis is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B₁) deficiency, most commonly seen in chronic alcoholism. It is characterized by anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation (fabrication of stories to fill memory gaps).

Ophthalmoplegia and ataxia are features of Wernicke encephalopathy, the acute stage of thiamine deficiency.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient who is a teacher by profession presents to the clinic with hoarseness of voice. The fiberoptic laryngoscopy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vocal nodule

The swollen area in the given image and the clinical scenario is suggestive of vocal nodules.

Vocal nodules are also known as singer’s or screamer's nodes. It is present at the junction of anterior one-third with the posterior two thirds. It is the area of maximum vibration of the cord and thus is subjected to maximum trauma.

Vocal nodules occur due to vocal trauma when person speaks in unnatural low tones for prolonged periods or at high intensities. They mostly affect teachers, actors, vendors or pop singers.

Nodule:

* Early stages soft, reddish and oedematous swellings

* Later stages - greyish or white in colour

Symptoms:

* Hoarseness

* Vocal fatigue

* Pain in the neck on prolonged phonation

Treatment:

* Educating the patient in proper use of voice.

* Surgery is required for large nodules or nodules of long standing in adults. They are excised with precision.

Other options:

Option A: Vocal polyp is caused by sudden shouting which results in hemorrhage and edema of the vocal cord.Affected individuals present with hoarseness of voice and diplophonia(double voice). Other factors associated with it are allergy and cigarette smoking. It presents as a benign swelling on the free edge of the vocal cord.

Option B: Vocal cysts: These are retention cysts due to blockage of seromucinous glands of the laryngeal mucosa. They occur in the false vocal cords.

Option D: Reinke's edema is the collection of fluid in Reinke's space. Affected individuals present with diffuse swelling of the vocal cords. Treatment involves the removal of gelatinous collection by a longitudinal incision on the vocal cord.
questions.learning: Vocal nodule — The swollen area in the given image and the clinical scenario is suggestive of vocal nodules. Vocal nodules are also known as singer’s or screamer's nodes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Labyrinthitis

In the above options, labyrinthitis is a cause of sensorineural hearing loss while all others are causes of conductive hearing loss.

Causes of sensorineural hearing loss:

* Congenital

* Anomalies of the inner ear or the hearing apparatus due to prenatal or perinatal factors

* Acquired

* Labyrinthitis—viral, bacterial, or spirochaetal

* Trauma to labyrinth or VIIIth nerve

* Noise-induced hearing loss

* Ototoxic drugs

* Presbycusis

* Ménière’s disease

* Acoustic neuroma

* Systemic disorders-diabetes, autoimmune disorders, multiple sclerosis

Causes of conductive hearing loss:

* Congenital

* Meatal atresia

* Fixation of stapes footplate/malleus head

* Ossicular discontinuity

* Congenital cholesteatoma

* Acquired

* External ear

* Obstruction in the ear canal-wax, foreign body, furuncle

* Middle ear

* Perforation of tympanic membrane

* Fluid in the middle ear-acute otitis media, serous otitis media

* Tumors in the middle ear

* Disruption of ossicles-chronic suppurative otitis media, cholesteatoma

* Fixation of ossicles-otosclerosis, tympanosclerosis, adhesive otitis media

* Eustachian tube blockage-retracted tympanic membrane, serous otitis media

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis made from the MRI image given below?
questions.explanation: The MRI image reveals destruction of adjacent vertebral bodies and the intervening disc space, accompanied by a large prevertebral and paravertebral fluid collection. This is the hallmark of Pott’s spine (Spinal Tuberculosis). The fluid collection is known as a "cold abscess" because it lacks the intense acute inflammation of a pyogenic infection. Multiple myeloma (Option A) causes multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions but usually spares the disc space. Ankylosing spondylitis (Option B) shows fusion and syndesmophytes without abscess formation. Pyogenic spondylitis (Option C) presents with more acute, rapid bone destruction and systemic toxicity compared to the subacute nature of TB. Because Pott’s spine characteristically involves two adjacent vertebrae, destroys the disc, and forms large paravertebral abscesses, it is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The MRI image reveals destruction of adjacent vertebral bodies and the intervening disc space, accompanied by a large prevertebral and paravertebral fluid collection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A lady presents with abdominal pain. USG reveals multiple gall stones with no wall thickening. CBD diameter is 12 mm and serum bilirubin was 0.8. Alkaline phosphatase is 380 and GGT is raised by 5 times. What is the next best step of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRCP

In this clinical scenario, a patient with gallstones, a dilated common bile duct, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase level raises suspicion for common bile duct stones. The next best step would be to perform magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) to confirm their presence.

A dilated common bile duct (>8 mm) detected on ultrasound in a patient with gallstones, jaundice, biliary pain and an abnormal liver function panel (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases; but these can be normal in some cases) strongly indicates the presence of common bile duct stones (choledocholithiasis).

If there is uncertainty regarding the presence of bile duct stones, as in this case where bilirubin levels are normal, MRCP offers precise anatomical visualization and exhibits high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing choledocholithiasis.

While endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is also highly effective in diagnosing choledocholithiasis, due to its invasive nature and the risks associated with the procedure, it is rarely used as a purely diagnostic modality. Instead, it is reserved for cases in which a therapeutic intervention, such as stone extraction or sphincterotomy, is planned.

Treatment options:

• ERCP along with sphincterotomy and stone removal.
• Laparoscopic common bile duct exploration
• Open common bile duct exploration is only done when endoscopic and laparoscopic methods are not feasible or when concomitant biliary drainage is needed.
questions.learning: MRCP — In this clinical scenario, a patient with gallstones, a dilated common bile duct, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase level raises suspicion for common bile duct stones.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the dye used to stain the anterior capsule of the lens in cataract surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trypan blue

Trypan blue dye can be used to stain the lens capsule for better visibility. It is used in anterior capsulotomy like capsulorrhexis.

In capsulorrhexis, an opening is made in the anterior capsule of the lens. Continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC) is considered to be superior to all the pre-existing methods because when done correctly, it does not leave any edges or tears.In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydrodissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed.
questions.learning: Trypan blue Trypan blue dye can be used to stain the lens capsule for better visibility. It is used in anterior capsulotomy like capsulorrhexis.
